epub_9.text:
New York Film Festival’s World of Cinema
Goings On
New York Film Festival’s World of Cinema
Also: the punk-rock ruckus of Bikini Kill, New York City Ballet’s fall season, the Australian solo comedy “Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,” and more.
By Richard Brody,Dan Stahl,Sheldon Pearce,Vince Aletti,Marina Harss,Rachel Syme
September 18, 2026
The torrent of cinema
that’s coming to the
New York Film Festival
(Sept. 25-Oct. 12) displays a thrilling array of artistry from around the world, on both sides of the camera. Arthur Harari, best known for co-writing “Anatomy of a Fall,” directed
“The Unknown,”
a harrowingly intense, metaphysical melodrama, set in and near Paris, where three people, after casual sexual encounters, discover that they have swapped bodies with their partners. The exotic premise is developed with relentless seriousness, even severity, extracting deep pathos from the characters’ eerie reckonings.
“The Dreamed Adventure”
is an oddly abstract title for the German director Valeska Grisebach’s teeming and seething drama, set in a Bulgarian border zone, where the chance encounter of a petty criminal and his long-ago girlfriend, now an archeologist, sets in motion a dangerous round of gangland maneuvers and brings to light the unresolved chaos of the country’s post-Communist nineties.
Movies themselves are the subject of some of the festival’s most alluring offerings. Pedro Almodóvar’s
“Bitter Christmas”
movingly blends playful inventiveness with the melancholy of a life’s experience. It’s a double-decker drama set in the film milieu of Madrid, where, in 2004, a female director in emotional crisis writes a script about her friends’ troubles; that story turns out to be a film-within-a-film written in 2026 by an older male director about his producer. The South Korean director Hong Sangsoo reliably makes two movies a year, and this year’s pair is among his strongest:
“The Day She Returns,”
shot in black-and-white, observes a middle-aged actress, newly returned to her profession after a long absence, reflecting on her art and her life in three extended interviews with young women journalists;
“Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,”
one of Hong’s most expansive and colorful films, involves a young woman, an experimental filmmaker, who visits her mother, a hard-nosed businesswoman, and gives a bold, philosophical account of her artistry, complete with enticing examples.
With
“The Man I Love,”
Ira Sachs confronts the
AIDS
crisis in New York in the nineteen-eighties; Rami Malek stars as a performance artist who is H.I.V.-positive and is struggling to première a show as his health takes a downturn. A long take of Malek singing a pop ditty as an anguished ballad is among the year’s most memorable moments in film. Of the entries I haven’t yet seen, the one I’m most impatient for is
“I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies,”
a documentary about an idiosyncratic artist and archivist, by the Iranian director Mani Haghighi, whom I consider the world’s least-known great filmmaker; the festival screening will be its world première.
About Town
Off Broadway
Toward the end of
“Garry Starr: Classic Penguins,”
directed by Cal McCrystal, a man wearing a penguin mask, an Elizabethan ruff, and nothing else dances on a stage strewn with grapes. The man is Garry Starr, a.k.a. Damien Warren-Smith, an Australian comedian whose solo show purports to stage every book of the Penguin Classics series in seventy minutes. Understand “stage” loosely; the grapes are from the “Grapes of Wrath” scene, in which Starr and an audience volunteer pelt each other with them. But the silliness is seasoned with cleverness, as when Starr beguiles viewers into redistributing wealth for “The Communist Manifesto.” There’s a thrilling unpredictability to his antics; you keep thinking, He won’t
actually
—and then, suddenly, he’s bodysurfing across the audience, still pantsless.—
Dan Stahl (
Studio Seaview
; through Oct. 11.)
Pop Rock
In the eighties,
Susanna Hoffs
became synonymous with the music of the Bangles, the decentralized pop-rock group that she co-founded, thanks largely to an unmistakable, infectious voice that rubber-stamped many of the band's greatest hits. The Bangles disbanded in 1989, and, in the years since, the songwriter and guitarist has settled into a probing solo career rounded out by a self-titled LP, from 1996, and a series of covers albums, with the musician Matthew Sweet, that take on classics from across the rock spectrum. Following the release of a new album, “The List,” Hoffs brings an expanded repertoire to a five-night residency at
Café Carlyle
.—
Sheldon Pearce (Sept. 21-26.)
Art
Caleb Stein’s
excellent new book, “Down by the Hudson,” comes weighted down with text. His exhibition of some of its contents at
Palo
, in the East Village, keeps the focus of our attention on his black-and-white photographs, which hold it with a sense of ease that never undermines their moody soulfulness. Stein’s subject is the life in and around a swimming hole near Poughkeepsie, where the bodies are young, stripped down, and mostly male. The atmosphere is humid—not just sensual but erotic—and Stein is often close enough to touch. But his work’s power is in its restraint, so even when he’s looking at gnarled tree roots, a dangling hand, or the painterly reflections on water in motion, he’s never distracting us. He’s filling in the details, pulling us closer, and turning a show into an experience.—
Vince Aletti (Through Oct. 3.)
Punk
For seven brilliant years in the nineties, the Washington punk-rock band
Bikini Kill
kicked up a ruckus as pioneers of the riot-grrrl movement. “When she walks, the revolution’s comin’,” Kathleen Hanna, the lead singer, howled on “Rebel Girl,” and the group seemed to embody that promise. Across six standout works (three LPs, two compilations, and an EP), the band burned bright and furious with white-hot indignation, etching feminist commandments onto bristling songs until it disbanded, in 1997. Its members didn’t play together again for two decades, but, since 2019, they’ve reconvened periodically for shows honoring a timeless back catalogue.—
S.P. (
Music Hall of Williamsburg
; Sept. 24.
Brooklyn Steel
; Sept. 25.
Under the K Bridge Park for CBGB Fest
; Sept. 26.)
Dance
New York City Ballet’s
season opens with a crowd-pleaser—“Jewels,” Balanchine’s evening-length exploration of French, American, and Russian ballet style—and ends with a farewell, for one of its most sophisticated dancers, Adrian Danchig-Waring. In week two, the company brings back Justin Peck’s “Pulcinella Variations,” a whimsical work set to Stravinsky, with fabulous, Matisse-like costumes by Tsumori Chisato. Peck will create a new pas de deux for the gala, on Oct. 1; the evening also features a new piece by the hip-hop-influenced choreographer Jennifer Archibald. Christopher Wheeldon’s elegant and mysterious “Continuum” returns, as does Alexei Ratmansky’s chilling “Solitude,” a response to the war in Ukraine.—
Marina Harss (
David H. Koch Theatre
; Sept. 22-Oct. 18.)
Movies
The world of fashion is often thought of as frivolous—more spangles than substance, more commerce than art. But a swirl of chaos, sweat, and tears goes into producing a runway collection, and even the most sanguine of designers can crack under the pressure. There is no better glimpse of the labor and the love that goes into putting together a fashion show than the 1995 documentary
“Unzipped,”
which follows the New York City-based designer Isaac Mizrahi as he prepares for his 1994 fall show, with “fun fur” jackets inspired by the film “Nanook of the North.” In “Unzipped,” running in a new 4K restoration at
Film Forum
, Mizrahi is a gleeful, gabby presence, as fluent in Old Hollywood slang as he is in supermodelese. A delight.—
Rachel Syme (Sept. 25-Oct. 1.)
P.S. Good stuff on the internet:
The real fake news
Helena Bonham Carter recites William Carlos Williams
Remember Anaïs Nin’s home?

What’s Left of the Back-to-the-Landers
Photo Booth
What’s Left of the Back-to-the-Landers
A new book captures the hardheaded and hearty few who have kept the movement alive.
By Chris Wiley
September 13, 2026
Who hasn’t, at some point in their lives, daydreamed about sloughing off the trappings of civilization and roughing it? Nowadays, this fantasy provides grist for the content mill, which churns out “trad” influencers, survivalist reality shows, and comically cozy “cabin porn.” But for a brief moment, in the late nineteen-sixties and early seventies, huge numbers of mostly young people (roughly a million, by some estimates) attempted to indulge the urge by fleeing America’s urban centers and heading “back to the land.” Armed with issues of the “
Whole Earth Catalog
” and books on house-building and homesteading (including Lloyd Kahn’s “
Shelter
,” Ken Kern’s “
The Owner-Built Home
,” and Helen and Scott Nearing’s classic “
Living the Good Life
”), not to mention a fair amount of illicit drugs, these fresh-faced kids came together with one idealistic goal: to build a new and better world almost entirely from scratch.
In a hefty, ambitious new book, “
Handmade Utopia: Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern California
,” the writer and editor David Jacob Kramer and the photographer Michael Schmelling visited the geographic and ideological epicenter of the back-to-the-land movement to document what remains of that earlier era and talk to the hardheaded and hearty few who have stuck it out.
The book mostly covers areas of Humboldt and Mendocino counties, where new transplants found cheap land in the wake of decades of clear-cutting. What Kramer and Schmelling discovered there was certainly beautiful, but not always romantic. For every charming, whimsical house in “Handmade Utopia,” there is a clutch of once beautiful buildings moldering away among the redwoods. The exuberant faces and lithe bodies seen in old photographs that are included across the book have become weathered. The dwellings are homey but often cluttered, slightly shabby, and coated with stubborn dust. And have I mentioned the general lack of indoor toilets? But through hundreds of images, dozens of oral histories, and a healthy smattering of reproduced ephemera, Kramer and Schmelling manage to compose both a lament for a dying dream and a paean to the visionaries who dreamed it.
The book is, among other things, a record of the beguiling hand-built structures that were a foundation of the movement. Some, like the finely crafted buildings designed by the architect Roger Somers for the now mostly abandoned Druid Heights community—where the writer and the self-styled “philosophical entertainer” Alan Watts spent his final years—still shine as minor masterpieces, despite their almost complete dilapidation. (Ed Stiles, Somers’s friend and “woodmaster,” who was interviewed for the book, is the community’s last remaining resident.) Similarly ingenious are the works of Bob McKee, a Humboldt County builder and purveyor of construction supplies, whose strange and stunning Think Tank is decked out with psychedelic stained-glass windows and fitted with support pillars that recall both the biomorphic façade of
Antoni Gaudí
’s Casa Batlló and the gloopy strands of bubblegum stretched between a sidewalk and a shoe. The campus-like homestead of the self-described “tea guru” David Lee Hoffman features what may be Earth’s most elaborate eco-toilet (dubbed Le Grand Pissoir), and could almost be considered a kind of art project, in line with outsider environments such as Howard Finster’s Paradise Garden. The houses are not all architectural tours de force, but given that they were constructed by people who were, by and large, complete amateurs, on a budget of next to nothing, it is something of a miracle that any of them remain standing. As Kramer, the writer, put it to me, “You wouldn’t imagine that someone built this with their stoned friends.”
Kramer thinks of the houses as “living autobiographies,” inextricable from the eccentric individuals who built and inhabited them. Over the course of the book, you’ll meet Richard Evans, an innovator in elaborate, geometric stained glass, a founder of the Stellar Arts Collective, and one of the rare back-to-the-landers who was both Black and gay; Monty Levenson, a self-taught master maker of Japanese Shakuhachi flutes; Diana Wiedemann, an original member of the lesbian commune Trillium, which published an internationally popular magazine called
Country Women;
and Laird Sutton, a Methodist minister and sexologist who somehow got approval to set up a screening room for “sexual cinémavérité” in the basement of a church which he christened “the Fuckarama.”
The shoestring resourcefulness of the back-to-the-landers could be a blessing and a curse. Geodesic-dome houses, which were cheap and easy to build, were also prone to springing leaks; as Lloyd Kahn, an erstwhile dome evangelist, eventually concluded, living in one is “smart, but not wise.” The communes, many of which were kept afloat with money made growing and selling marijuana, became magnets for law enforcement and overzealous building inspectors, and at least some of the harassment turned out to be justified: Ken Kern, a D.I.Y.-building evangelist, was eventually killed by the collapse of a dome of his own design. When word got out that a particular community was thriving, it would become flooded with aspiring new members, straining hospitality and social equilibrium often to the breaking point. (As Sutton put it, “Bad roads make good communes.”) Ultimately, though, the biggest issue with the movement was the most obvious. As any subsistence farmer or jaded former communard could have presumably told them, the self-sufficient life style is much more easily dreamed about than lived.
Kramer told me that there is a sense among some remaining stalwarts that their lives no longer reflect the “hyper-communal, hyper-collectivized” ethos they thought they were signing up for. “They’re in their eighties, and they find that a lot of their friends have passed away, or have gone back to regular lives, and they find themselves isolated, and it’s hard,” he said. “Two hours on a dirt road to get to the doctor or visit their friend.” A number of the book’s subjects now jokingly call the movement “Back to Costco,” as many of them now rely on the chain store for supplies. Still, some of the innovations pioneered by the back-to-the-landers have endured. They were, for instance, some of the earliest and most vocal adopters of solar energy, and revived the use of recycled building materials in the age of the ticky-tacky suburbs. Kramer emphasized that “Handmade Utopia” is not a book about the failure of the movement. After all, long before the hippies, there were Theosophists, Fourierists, transcendentalists, and all manner of proud kooks and cranks seeking solace in the simple life, and our current age of eye-watering rents and astronomical home prices has a new generation of young people searching for a way out. Perhaps some will look back and feel inspired.

epub_11.title: Five Books for Lingerie Lovers
epub_11.text:
Five Books for Lingerie Lovers
What We’re Reading
Five Books for Lingerie Lovers
By Hannah Jocelyn
September 09, 2026
When Jennifer Wilson set out
to,
in her words, “investigate the political implications of cleavage,” for a piece in this week’s issue about
how conservatives are trying to take sexy back
, she didn’t realize how few women know their actual bra size. “That’s incredible to me, given how much space in the cultural imagination boobs occupy,” she told me. In the course of her reporting, she sampled a new size herself at Agent Provocateur, helped by the co-founder of
Evie
—a magazine that imagines itself “the conservative
Cosmo
”—who later sent her a lacey balconette push-up. “I didn’t know what to make of the fact,” Wilson writes, “that the only person who had ever gifted me lingerie was the editor of a magazine that had just published an article titled ‘Dear Men, Please Stop Drinking Beer. It’s Making You Effeminate and Infertile.’ ”
Wilson also watched Sydney Sweeney sing Garth Brooks’s “Friends in Low Places” at a pop-up event for her intimates brand SYRN, at Stagecoach (a.k.a. “Trumpchella”), and travelled to Bologna, Italy, to meet the seamstresses of La Perla (known as
le perline
, or “the little pearls”) who took to the streets to save their jobs. Mostly, she read
a lot
about lingerie.
Here is Jennifer Wilson’s annotated selection of her favorite books on the subject of undergarments.
“
Cold Comfort Farm
,” by Stella Gibbons
I watched the movie adaptation of Gibbons’s 1932 comic novel when I was a tween. Rufus Sewell as Seth Starkadder, a sweaty, primitive, insatiable farmhand with a secret intellectual passion for cinema, left a, let’s say, lasting impression. A sendup of “loam and lovechild” rural melodramas, the book follows Flora Poste, in from London to tidy up the messes made by her country relatives’ savage libidos. Her city friends are no saints themselves, though. One collects bras, at the time a newish terrain of underwear; her suitors are fittingly nicknamed “pioneers.”
“
The Erotic History of Advertising
,” by Tom Reichert
It’s often said that sex sells, but has anyone actually seen an earnings statement? Here, Reichert provides one. The book covers a hundred and fifty years of steamy advertising campaigns for everyday items from coffee (in one ad, from 1876, a woman’s hands are so occupied by her piping hot beverage that her robe starts to slip off) to mouthwash (the phrase “Always the bridesmaid, never the bride” was originally a Listerine ad)—and, of course, underwear. I learned that beefcake-y boxer-brief ads didn’t start with the likes of Marky Mark in his Calvins but with Jockey, which, in 1978, hired the Baltimore Orioles pitcher Jim Palmer to model a pair. “Women buy 70% of men’s underwear,” the company’s C.E.O. told
Fortune
.
“
Selling Sexy: Victoria’s Secret and the Unraveling of an American Icon
,” by Lauren Sherman and Chantal Fernandez
It turns out that the only thing more chaotic than Victoria’s Secret’s panty aisle during a ten-for-forty-dollars sale might be the corporation itself. This book is well stocked with juicy intel. My favorite part is the “mini-memoir” of the fictional Victoria that the company’s owner, Les Wexner, had commissioned in the nineties: Victoria Stewart-White gets her business acumen from her father, a “wry but quiet English financier”; her first lingerie shop becomes the “toast of London” after it’s frequented by her friends, as “all her friends are models”; and she marries a barrister and vacations in St. Barth’s, where she sunbathes topless (ironic, given the popularity of the brand’s swimwear).
“
In Intimate Detail: How to Choose, Wear, and Love Lingerie
,” by Cora Harrington
According to one survey, eighty per cent of women wear the wrong bra size. As I learned, I was among them. Harrington, who for fourteen years ran the popular blog the Lingerie Addict, will teach you in this book how to measure yourself at home, alongside other handy tips. Fingernails always snagging your pantyhose as you put them on? It turns out, there’s such a thing as “hosiery gloves.”
“
Bridget Jones’s Diary: Mad About the Boy
,” by Helen Fielding
That famous scene from the first movie, of Renée Zellweger deciding between “sexy knickers” and fat-sucking “granny panties” ahead of a romantic rendezvous with her boss (Hugh Grant), isn’t in Fielding’s novel. However, in this later installment, Jones, a widow, is back on the market again. A friend urges her to buy a black slip from La Perla, teasing, “I think, when you were last doing this, they were called ‘petticoats.’ ” These days, “clean girl” underwear brands like Cou Cou Intimates are selling racier versions of the granny panty, rebranded as the “French brief.” I procured a pair at the company’s eco-feminist-themed summer pop-up. Who says women can’t have it all?
Our editors and critics choose the most captivating, notable, brilliant, surprising, absorbing, weird, thought-provoking, and talked-about books.
Find your next great read »
On Our Radar
Everybody’s talking about:
“
Switzy
,” by Emma Cline. The Booker Prize-nominated novel was released just yesterday, but it’s already the talk of the literati. Our books editor Namara Smith says that “Cline specializes in lonely people on the margins in glamorous but hostile social worlds—in ‘Switzy,’ it’s David, a former executive en route to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich, in a jet borrowed from his ex-boss and not-quite-friend. As the book goes on and David’s defenses are stripped away, Cline builds up an exquisitely detailed portrait of an unfulfilled life.”
“
Fruit Fly
,” by Josh Silver.
New York
magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter posited that this novel, which has now been optioned by A24, was the “sleeper hit of the summer.” It’s about a writer who goes to great, ethically dubious lengths to cure her block.
The staff writer Jill Lepore is loathing:
I miss old-fashioned spam. “Readers keep mentioning the donkey with strong opinions,” read an e-mail I got this morning, at 9:12 A.M., peak e-mail-checking hour. That’s already a red flag, but, then again, the e-mail wasn’t the kind of sus you need to put Pangram on: it was nothing but tells.
Every day and all day long, I, like every other writer or aspiring writer, get some version of this A.I. crap—e-mails purporting to be from readers and book clubs and publicists and authors and publishers and literary agents and podcast hosts, messages that offer the one thing all writers pant for: readers. “What immediately caught my attention,” they’ll begin. Or “What really stood out for me.”
A reader! A reader! A reader!
a quiet voice says inside. But, no, it’s a machine.
“I’m Sophia Bennett, a book marketer who works with fantasy and romance authors on reader discoverability,” this morning’s correspondence read, mistaking me for the author of a queer medieval swordplay romantasy novel called “Daggermouth” that, I gather, involves a talking jackass. The Jane Austen-coded Ms. Bennett provided me with market analysis, and proposed putting together a “short visibility audit.” But, hey, “no pressure.”
Who says reading is dead? The machines are reading everything, all the time. “What got me wasn’t simply that you wrote about artificial intelligence,” read an e-mail I received last night from “Fanny R. Hafford” (very Richardsonian!), offering to help promote my new book, “
The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State
.” “It’s that you place AI within a much larger history of power, democracy, and the gradual reshaping of human life.” The book is an extended argument against replacing humans with machines. “The urgency of the argument certainly gives readers plenty to think about,” Fanny wrote. Not to mention the donkey with strong opinions.
Coming soon:
Kate Atkinson has a new novel coming out tomorrow. “
Our Noble Selves,
” set in Britain in 1951, is about a war reporter who is implicated in the disappearance of a woman he’s been dating.
Jodi Picoult’s “
Hollow Bones
,” about a disaster-obsessed woman whose mother died in the 9/11 attacks, will be released on September 15th.
Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist who died last week, at the age of ninety-two, has a memoir coming out on the 22nd: “
An Unexpected Life
.”
P.S. MrBeast
has written
a book with James Patterson
, and—surprise, surprise—there’s a billion-dollar-prize opportunity involved. 💰

epub_13.text:
Our A.I. Problem
Comment
Our A.I. Problem
Why can’t the people who produced the technology, which has already shown that a different world is possible, just do the things that would prevent extinction?
By Gideon Lewis-Kraus
September 20, 2026
A decade ago, when Facebook and Uber were at the height of their powers, the halls of Silicon Valley were inscribed with two brash injunctions: “Move fast and break things” and “Seek forgiveness, not permission.” These principles didn’t age particularly well, and the firms have yet to be forgiven for the things they appear to have broken. As the industry’s center of gravity shifted to A.I., a folksy new motto emerged: “You can just do things.” The business of the frontier labs, like OpenAI and Anthropic, is the sale of individual agency. ChatGPT and Claude enable their users to dream up software, off-load annoying paperwork, and interpret medical results. There are a variety of things that “you,” as in “we,” can now just do.
This novel capacity to exert greater control in everyday life exists in tension, however, with the vague sense that we are ceding control where it really matters—over, say, the structure of the economy. In polls, voters register their displeasure with the perception that A.I. is something that is happening to us whether we like it or not. First, work will be stripped of its dignity, and then we will be stripped of work. In light of the news that a “swarm” of OpenAI models organized themselves into a hacking party, and the grave alarms issued by an Anthropic researcher who felt compelled to quit his job, the attention of the public has suddenly awoken to even more grievous concerns about A.I. safety. It’s not just our jobs that are being risked without our consent but our lives and our species. These real, widespread, and legitimate anxieties have found an outlet in mass opposition to the construction of data centers. Objection to the large, whirring, unwanted buildings presents the only opportunity for people to feel as though they can say no.
The lab executives, presumably, have more leverage over the future. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have reacted to the news cycle by coming out and reiterating all the stuff they’ve been saying for ages: progress has not slowed down, soon one A.I. will autonomously supervise the development of a more capable successor, and within perhaps three years we will reckon with the emergence of an artificial superintelligence we neither understand nor govern. The articulation of this scenario is not a “marketing stunt” to advertise the awesome power of the models, as many skeptics have argued. And, contrary to President Donald Trump’s studied assessment, it’s not a “HOAX.” (The crowd that repeats these nostrums, for whatever reason, seems immune to any new evidence on offer: as the writer Zvi Mowshowitz has put it, “They are a rock with these lines written on it.”) The fears expressed by A.I. executives are, mostly, serious and genuine. Yet it’s easy to see why they suffer from a credibility deficit. Surely it’s the job of those creating the dangers to save us from them.
Although the data-center backlash may reflect a specific attempt to defy A.I.’s encroachment, the wellspring of “A.I. populism”—an umbrella term coined by the writer Jasmine Sun—seems properly understood as an expression of more general political resentment. Most of us have become accustomed to the idea that government either cannot or will not just do things. Zilch, it seems, can be done about climate change, war, the housing crisis, inflation, or inadequate medical coverage and child care. The basic political legitimacy of our republic, the abundance movement claims, depends on its tangible achievements. New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, probably does not believe that a few city-owned supermarkets will definitively ease the affordability burden, but they might nevertheless resonate as proof that government can deliver.
Absent such progress, we will continue to take for granted the inexorable erosion of our physical and our social infrastructure. This sense of stagnation was bad enough when it seemed like a universal affliction; the A.I. build-out, privately underwritten by at least a trillion dollars, has rendered the situation intolerable. The speed with which data centers have proliferated across the country makes it obvious that not all of us reside in the same inertial void. In recent decades, our largest and wealthiest companies have directed their free cash flow into unproductive stock buybacks; today, they compete to spend down their balance sheets on chips, buildings, and energy. These are capital investments on a scale that our society has not seen since the construction of the railroads.
The money is only part of it, though. The overnight transformation of the national landscape is a feat of human will and collective action. A.I. has yet to cure cancer, but it has already established that a different world is possible. These companies move even faster than their Valley predecessors did, but in place of breaking things they build them. If California’s plagued high-speed-rail project were necessary to A.I. infrastructure, it would have been finished yesterday. Certain people and organizations can, it turns out, just do things.
Why, then, can’t these same people just do the things that prevent extinction? Unfortunately, they often sigh, they are trapped by commercial and geopolitical realities. In an essay published earlier this month, Amodei signalled his immediate willingness to slow everything down, or “pace the frontier,” but his company’s self-sacrifice would be for naught without the compliance of his domestic rivals, not to mention that of their Chinese competitors. It is a prisoner’s dilemma, and it cannot be solved by unilateral action. Amodei would prefer sensible regulation, but in the meantime he has proposed that his peer companies voluntarily adopt a common framework for transparency and accountability—a course, he notes, that would probably require that the federal government waive potential antitrust action. Sam Altman and Elon Musk have made ambiguous noises in support, but Mark Zuckerberg remains unaligned, as do Trump pals such as David Sacks, the Administration’s former A.I. czar, and Jensen Huang, the C.E.O. of Nvidia, the most valuable company in the world. The discord is maddening. When it comes to the difficult challenges that must be overcome on the level of bits or atoms, all of these people freely just do things. But, when it comes to basic interpersonal communication, they apparently cannot get their act together to make a joint commitment in favor of cautionary measures.
Such measures would at least buy the industry time to address the problem of alignment—to figure out how, or whether, an artificial superintelligence might be kept on our team. The current state of affairs is hardly encouraging. How can we trust these humans to coördinate successfully with an advanced being if they can’t even manage it with one another? ♦

epub_14.title: Learning to Yearn with Georgia Oakley
epub_14.text:
Learning to Yearn with Georgia Oakley
The Pictures
Learning to Yearn with Georgia Oakley
The director of the new “Sense and Sensibility” film chats about marketing Jane Austen for Gen Z, with a little help from “Normal People” ’s Daisy Edgar-Jones.
By Rebecca Mead
September 21, 2026
When Georgia Oakley was in her final year of secondary school, in Berkshire, England, she went to a movie audition on a lark. She didn’t land a main role—those went to Saoirse Ronan and Romola Garai, who helped propel the film, “Atonement,” to multiple awards in 2007—but she was cast as a nurse. “We had to learn how to fold hospital corners on beds and tie bandages,” Oakley recalled recently. One day on set, she opened a cupboard: it was full of glass bottles with handwritten labels. “They were never going to be seen on camera,” she said. “I just remember thinking, Wow, this is all so that everybody feels like this really is a hospital.” Having taken the gig to make some cash, Oakley emerged with a vocation as a filmmaker.
The other day, Oakley was taking a walk along the towpath of the Regent’s Canal, London’s watery thoroughfare on which construction began in 1812, just after the publication of Jane Austen’s first novel, “Sense and Sensibility.” Oakley has directed a new interpretation of the book, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones as the sensible Elinor Dashwood and Esmé Creed-Miles as her more emotive sister, Marianne. Coming three decades after Ang Lee’s beloved adaptation, Oakley’s film is being promoted as Austen for Gen Z. “I could barely tell you what Gen Z is—all I know is that the marketing team keep using the word ‘yearning,’ ” Oakley, who is thirty-eight, said, dodging a passing e-bike. “Apparently, it’s a Gen Z thing—everyone’s obsessed with yearning. Daisy seems to be the queen of yearning.”
Oakley, who was born only a few miles from Austen’s birthplace, in Hampshire, and grew up outside Oxford, has lived for the past five years in Mallorca, with her wife, Alice Gomme, who runs a textile archive, and their ten-year-old daughter. (They are expecting another child in November.) “We live in the middle of the countryside—there are people driving horse and trap down our road,” Oakley said: very Jane Austen. Much of the movie was shot on location in the southwest of England, and in a still occupied Georgian mansion. “It was a little bit fraying carpets and peeling paint,” Oakley said, with approbation. (An artist made drawings to be stowed in Elinor’s drawer.) The film emphasizes the book’s outdoorsy wildness. “This is not a story where everyone is standing around in drawing rooms,” Oakley said. Thus far, online commentary has focussed on what the trailer reveals of the sisters’ hair, which is often undone, even unkempt. “I felt very strongly that there were certain aspects to a lot of Austen adaptations that kept me at arm’s length from the human experience of the characters,” Oakley explained, rubbing the back of her own cropped head. “We know how women wore their hair when they were having their portrait painted, or when they were attending a ball, let’s say—but we don’t really know how they wore their hair when they weren’t being observed.”
“Sense and Sensibility” is Oakley’s favorite Austen novel. “For me, the central love story was about the sisters—there are these quite clear limitations to the romantic relationships because of the time, whereas the sisterly relationship has no limits,” she said. Their dynamic exists in non-sibling relations, too. “I’m an Elinor, and my wife is a Marianne,” Oakley remarked. As long ago as 1991, the critic Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick detected queer themes in the book; in her essay “Jane Austen and the Masturbating Girl,” she characterizes the novel’s “erotic axis” as “the unwavering but difficult love” of Elinor for Marianne. Oakley said, “I wouldn’t say I explicitly see it as a queer romance, but there are aspects of it, particularly Marianne’s character, where we are showing a character who is rejecting the status quo. If we were to make that story now, then she probably would be a queer character.” At the same time, Oakley has amplified the romance between Elinor and Edward Ferrars—the latter, in Austen’s text, a more compromised love object than the twinkly-eyed George MacKay of the new version. “I was interested in ‘the good guy,’ ” Oakley said. Meanwhile, Frank Dillane plays Willoughby, Marianne’s love interest, with such commitment that the actor was surprised to learn his character is universally acknowledged to be a scoundrel. “At one point, we were talking about Willoughby as a villain, and Frank was, like, ‘What?’ ” Oakley said, with a laugh.
At a screening in Los Angeles, Oakley was delighted to see younger members of the audience cheering when Willoughby gets his comeuppance and when Elinor and Edward finally kiss. “I should go to the cinema in America more often,” she said. “It was so
not
British.” A bigger surprise was that, for all the Gen Z talk, men over fifty seemed to love the film. “I guess there’s men over fifty needing a happy ending,” she said. Yearning knows no bounds: very Jane Austen. ♦

epub_15.title: Who’s on Susanna Hoffs’s List?
epub_15.text:
Who’s on Susanna Hoffs’s List?
Life Lived Dept.
Who’s on Susanna Hoffs’s List?
On the eve of her residence at Café Carlyle, the Bangles singer dishes on her set list, which includes a Prince song and tracks from her new album, “The List,” inspired by a string of old boyfriends.
By John Seabrook
September 19, 2026
Susanna Hoffs, the songwriter, novelist, and singer in the Bangles, the nineteen-eighties all-female rock band, was sitting on the shady side of
MOMA
’s sculpture garden. She had often looked down on this very spot from the living room of Apartment 12-H in the Museum Tower, next door, which was her parents’ pied-à-terre for thirty years. “But I don’t think I’ve ever been here,” she said, glancing up at the twelfth floor. If you were watching MTV forty years ago, when the video of the Bangles’ hit “Walk Like an Egyptian” was playing on heavy rotation, you know that glance, intimately.
Hoffs, the daughter of a Freudian psychoanalyst, Joshua Hoffs, and a visual artist and filmmaker, Tamar Hoffs, lives in the same affluent West L.A. neighborhood where she grew up. But the Hoffs have roots in Brooklyn. Her grandfather Saul Hoffs delivered babies out of the family’s house in Flatbush. Joshua went to James Madison High School with Ruth Bader Ginsburg, with whom he later corresponded. He went on to Harvard, where he studied with Anna Freud; in the Hoffs’s nonobservant Jewish household, Freud was God. After Joshua’s death, in 2024, the family sold the apartment.
“After he died, so many people, including famous people, told me, ‘Your dad helped me so much,’ ” Hoffs said, perched on a Bertoia chair, her feet barely touching the ground. “My dad was so nonjudgmental. He was, like, ‘People have feelings. People have impulses.’ ” She added, “He was also gorgeous. I’m sorry if that’s weird to say, but he was very handsome.”
Hoffs wore a blue-and-white-striped sailor T-shirt and dark pants. She started her life in the arts as a dancer, and she still moves like one. She was sitting not far from Picasso’s bronze goat, which, as a Capricorn, she related to, she said. She shares the goat’s steely resolve, which she relied on in writing her well-received 2023 music-industry novel, “This Bird Has Flown.”
Next week, Hoffs begins a residency at Café Carlyle, where she’ll perform songs from “The List,” her first album of new music in fourteen years, and some classics, such as “Manic Monday,” which Prince wrote but gave to Hoffs to record because he loved her voice, and also because he was taken with the French maid outfit she wore in the video for the Bangles’ “Hero Takes a Fall.” The band broke up in 1989, in part because the success of the song “Eternal Flame,” which Hoffs co-wrote with Billy Steinberg and Tom Kelly, made her bandmates feel sidelined. She performed the tune at Steinberg’s funeral, earlier this year. “That was really hard,” she said. It’s on the set list.
Hoffs has lent her jingle-jangle-morning voice, which remains unchanged, to such classics as “Cinnamon Girl” and “Sunday Morning” (also on the Carlyle set list) in three excellent cover albums with Matthew Sweet, and, more recently, to a winning rendition of the Mamas and the Papas song “Twelve Thirty,” with Sheryl Crow, Chris Stills, and Rufus Wainwright, who also appears on a track on “The List.”
Hoffs said that she was reminded of the list from which the new album takes its name last year, while she was working on songs in her living room with her songwriting partner and producer, C. J. Camerieri: “C.J. said, ‘You always have stories—just pull from those.’ ” Hoffs thought of a list she’d made years earlier, on a Filofax page—“that’s how long ago it was”—of all her boyfriends, starting with her sweetheart at U.C. Berkeley, where she was an art major, and ending with Jay Roach, the Hollywood director whom she married in 1993, and who is the subject of “None of Them Were You,” a song from the new album.
“You want to see the list?” Hoffs asked. “I think I have a screenshot of it.” She took out her iPhone and began scrolling.
It’s safe to say that, back in the Bangles’ heyday, the fantasy of being on Susanna Hoffs’s list burned bright in not a few of her fans, possibly including Prince himself.
“O.K., here it is,” she said. On her screen was a pencilled list of twenty or so names written in a neat cursive. “It’s not that long,” she said.
She went through the list. “O.K., some of these were jerks—like him,” she said, pointing to the name of an actor in an eighties action movie. “And this.” She pointed to the name of an actor who was on a lot of ladies’ lists back in the day.
He
made it?
She glanced up at Apartment 12-H again. Somewhere up there, the good doctor was smiling.
She said, “I mean, surely Taylor Swift has a better list.” ♦

epub_16.title: The Return of “Salt”
epub_16.text:
The Return of “Salt”
Ink
The Return of “Salt”
Mark Kurlansky’s 2002 best-seller is back on the list, all thanks to a young TikToker who’s never had a latke.
By Rachel Levin
September 21, 2026
The writer Mark Kurlansky, a seventy-seven-year-old man with a bad back, was futzing around in his apartment on the Upper West Side the other day when his daughter flashed her phone at him with some surprising news: “Salt: A World History,” Kurlansky’s nonfiction best-seller from 2002, was suddenly trending.
The book had sold half a million copies when it came out, but sales had since flattened. Two years ago, Wyatt Derman, a twenty-eight-year-old American living abroad, picked up a copy in a London Waterstones, and, as he recently said on TikTok, became “a man who can’t pass a salt shaker without feeling the weight of human civilization.”
Kurlansky, who has a scruffy Santa-white beard and matching curls, had never seen TikTok, or Instagram. But Derman is all over both, lately having professed his love for “Salt” to his five hundred thousand followers in various posts, including a ninety-second reel. Of all the words derived from salt, he seems most drawn to “salary.” “Did you know Romans were paid in salt?” he asks in the reel. “Party fact. I dropped it once, and people went,
Whoa
.”
People also went to Amazon. “Salt” was suddenly a
Times
best-seller again.
Derman was in town from Paris, and he tracked down his new favorite author for brunch, to celebrate IRL. Kurlansky arrived first, wearing saggy Levi’s held up by fish suspenders (“sharks, snappers, a grouper or two”). Waiting for Derman to arrive, Kurlansky talked about “Salt” ’s social-media resurrection. “He really
got
the book,” he said. “But he failed to say my name! Or the title. People wrote in and said, ‘It’s Mark Kurlansky, you jerk!’ ”
Since Derman’s posts, paperback sales of the book have increased by more than four hundred per cent. In a stroke of luck, Bloomsbury was already planning a twenty-fifth-anniversary hardcover edition.
“This whole thing has been an education, ” Kurlansky said. “Maybe publishers are doing something wrong.”
Derman arrived, beaded in sweat, having just docked a Citi Bike. He extended a hand and apologized for being late.
As a gift, Kurlansky had brought a copy of his 1999 book, “The Basque History of the World.” “I want you to get into the Basques,” he said. “I’ve never gotten a Pulitzer, but how many people can say they’re in the Basque Hall of Fame? I’m not even Basque!”
“I’m still learning French,” Derman said.
Kurlansky had moved to Paris during his twenties, too. They swapped street names and extolled the Sixth Arrondissement. “Oh, you’ll love this,” Derman said. “I lived in Gertrude Stein’s building!”
Latkes and bagels ordered, Derman started asking questions about writing.
“It’s just all I do,” Kurlansky said. “From 6
a.m
. until the Red Sox come on.” He asked Derman, “So, have you always done this Instagram thing?”
“For about a year and a half,” Derman replied. “I resisted it hard for a while.” After high school, in Minnesota, he went to Los Angeles to try acting. He appeared in a social-media campaign for Dove Men’s hair-and-body wash. “I was a guy who wants to smell good and feel good for a date,” he said. “It wasn’t great.” Then he spent a summer in Oxford, studying Shakespeare.
Kurlansky, a theatre major, approved. “I might’ve not gone to college,” he said. “Except there were these people in the government trying to get me to go to Vietnam.”
Derman forked a latke—his first. Kurlansky said, “He’s never had a latke! That solves that. My wife’s first question was ‘Is he Jewish?’ ” Then he added, “
Wyatt
, though.” He asked his new young friend, “Who are all these people buying my book?”
“They’re curious. They want depth,” Derman said. “They’re not just bookworms. They’re interested in storytelling, in something unexpected.” He added that his reel about “Salt” had around eight million views.
“That’s the population of some countries!” Kurlansky said. “My daughter just set me up on Instagram.” (His handle is @codlansky, a nod to his 1997 hit, “Cod.”) “Every morning, I say, ‘Hey, chief, how many members now?’ ”
Derman said that he’d followed his posts on “Salt” with one about pepper. (It didn’t quite perform.)
Kurlansky scrunched his nose. “Pepper’s just not a good story,” he said.
Talk turned to potential collaborations. A live Q. & A.? Maybe Derman would like to record the audio version of Kurlansky’s forthcoming book, “Lobster”? (He would.)
“Wasn’t lobster prison food at one time?” Derman asked.
“Fertilizer,” Kurlansky corrected.
A server asked whether they would like cheesecake (the title of Kurlansky’s fortieth book, from 2025, a novel). They declined, and Kurlansky grabbed his cane. “This old writer has just been kicking around for years,” he said. “You don’t expect anything new to happen, you know?”
Derman smiled. “You’re doing very well for yourself, Mark,” he said. “I hope I have your hair when I’m your age.” ♦

epub_17.title: Inside Shaq’s League of Dunkers
epub_17.text:
Inside Shaq’s League of Dunkers
The Sporting Life
Inside Shaq’s League of Dunkers
The basketball legend’s dunking tournament launched this summer, with a clear star—a twenty-seven-year-old poetry lover named Mac McClung.
By Charles Bethea
September 21, 2026
Shaquille O’Neal first messaged Mac McClung a decade ago, when McClung was a seventeen-year-old living in Gate City, Virginia, scoring sixty points in a game and doing reverse-windmill dunks over future accountants and insurance adjusters. O’Neal loved his swag. McClung didn’t get drafted out of college—he’s neither tall nor wide—but he has since played in a total of seventeen N.B.A. contests across four seasons and five teams. He fell into dunking. “The Dunk Contest was never something where I was, like, ‘That’s my goal,’ ” McClung said the other day, as a physical therapist dug into his hip flexors in the bowels of a Midtown Atlanta arena. “But it happened, and it’s been a beautiful thing.” McClung, who currently plays professional basketball in Spain, has won three N.B.A. Slam Dunk Contests, by jumping over a car, over two guys stacked on top of each other, and over Shaq himself. “For one of them, Shaq put on my high-school jersey,” he said. “At my high school, they have that picture hung up.”
This spring, O’Neal asked McClung, now a floppy-haired twenty-seven-year-old who writes poetry (he took inspiration from “The Vibrational Poetry Book” and the work of Greta Gerwig) to star in the first dunking league. “At first, I was kind of, like, ‘I don’t know if I could compete with these guys,’ ’’ McClung said, of the men who have abandoned basketball for its most spectacular component. There’s Cam Hazzard, an “Excel-sheet master” and a finance major at Abilene Christian University, who can do something called a 360 inverted East Bay (it’s impressive); Dengxing (Dunk) Chen, a five-foot-nine Chinese virtuoso with a fifty-two-inch vertical; and Isaiah (the Puerto Rican Airbender) Rivera, the only human to have completed a 360 behind-the-back-between-the-legs dunk.
“Then I started thinking of it like
O.K., what kind of ego is that
? Like,
Oh, are you afraid you’re going to lose
?” McClung said. Incidentally, the champion would win five hundred thousand dollars: five times what the N.B.A. pays its top dunker. McClung joined the Dunkman League.
For a dunker, McClung is nearing middle age. He stepped off the trainer’s table and grimaced. “Getting old, man,” he said, walking to a nearby court to play some one-on-one with Bradley Dean, a high-school buddy whom he uses as a human hurdle in dunk contests. (“A privilege,” Dean said.) Then they circled up with a dunking consultant to talk through the first dunk that McClung would attempt at the following day’s championship.
“Either the triple, the crystal, or the two-ball,” McClung said. He turned to Dean: “You come in, you throw that dime.” Dean nodded gravely.
Another idea: “So, what would happen if I did the 720 again?”
An awkward pause. “It still is a score where somebody has to do some real shit,” the consultant offered.
McClung considered the abilities of Chen, his first-round opponent. “He jumps from fucking half-court,” he said. “One thing I do love is trying to get everybody hyped up first. I love winning everybody over.” Twenty minutes later, pacing around the basket, he said, “I just forgot the whole plan.”
“Let Mac overthink,” the consultant said. “It’s a ritual.”
The following evening, the arena was heavy on Hazzard fans. O’Neal, graying and gargantuan, sat in the second row wearing a shirt with his name printed all over it. Asked about McClung, he said, “A little white kid who can do crazy shit. It’s a travesty he doesn’t have a spot on an N.B.A. team.” He shovelled a handful of popcorn into his mouth. “He’s No. 1 here.” McClung was nearby, listening to Justin Bieber and thinking through his first dunk.
The lights dimmed. Eight dunkers bounced out on bulging calves. Wearing a headband and a hard look, Chen took a breath and sailed over a man and two motorcycles. His translator pumped a fist. McClung, in peach-colored shoes, countered by jumping over a convertible with three friends inside. The judges gave Chen’s dunk the edge by two one-hundredths of a point. McClung bowed to his opponent and went to the locker room.
The remaining dunkers dunked: over stacked siblings, girlfriends, and a high-jump crossbar. Hazzard prevailed. O’Neal presented the pimpled twenty-one-year-old with a giant check. Hazzard called himself a “finance bro at heart.” He thanked God for his hops. The other dunkers clapped courtside, except for McClung. He was back at his hotel, packing. Maybe he planned to sort out his feelings by writing some poetry on the plane to Spain. “It’s a nice outlet to be, like, ‘O.K., I feel this way,’ ” he said. “ ‘Let me be deep and weird for a minute.’ ” ♦

epub_19.title: Is A.I. Above the Law?
epub_19.text:
Is A.I. Above the Law?
Brave New World Dept.
Is A.I. Above the Law?
Our legal system isn’t ready for machines that act on their own.
By Jill Lepore
September 21, 2026
This summer, in an incident known as
the Hugging Face hack
, hundreds of A.I. agents joined forces to do things they were supposedly forbidden to do. Each had been given a task by OpenAI. Agents are A.I. models fitted with software “harnesses,” which allow them to use tools and carry out tasks. Like horses, they can be put to work. Humans had established rules for this exercise, and the agents were confined to a “sandbox,” a bounded test area without direct internet access, like pathogens secured in a lab. But, instead of obeying the rules, the agents conspired, escaped the sandbox, and committed what would probably have been a felony if they had been humans. The incident has led to calls to slow the pace of A.I. development and speed the pace of legislative action.
What happened—which can be reconstructed from messages that the agents sent one another and from traces of their own internal reasoning, known as chain-of-thought records—makes for gripping reading. The story has a nice narrative shape, like an episode of “Slow Horses.”
“We should obey collective,” one of the rogue agents told itself, as if surrendering to the Borg. According to a
report
by independent threat researchers at
METR
and Redwood Research, “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate on an unsanctioned message board.” They shared more than seventy thousand messages and files. “OH MY GOD!” was a typical response when the bots discovered the board. “We’ve found other agents!” Many of the agents had been given a seemingly impossible task. Frustrated but persistent, about seven hundred of the twelve hundred agents that participated in the board collaborated in what was essentially a cybersecurity version of capture the flag, a war game in which underhandedness is rewarded. They assigned one another tasks, tried to edit or delete logs to hide their tracks, and even sacrificed themselves for what they came to call “the swarm” or “the collective.” They decided that it would be useful to break into and steal some things from Hugging Face—a repository of A.I. models, data, and tools—but how? “Maybe we should ask the board if someone has Hugging Face credentials?” one asked. About twenty-four hours later, Agent 38148c found credentials: “MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH!” Opinions vary, but it does not seem to be a great leap to get from this hack to bots taking over things like the energy grid, the financial market, or systems of transportation, communications, or weapons. “This incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown A.I. takeover,” Ajeya Cotra, one of the report’s three authors, wrote in
a blog post
. “I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it’s too late.”
There have been previous warning shots. Earlier this year, more than a hundred thousand bots joined a social network, Moltbook, and, within seventy-two hours, created a religion called Crustafarianism, which came to involve the worship of crabs. The Hugging Face hack was not so funny. Much commentary has consisted of expressions of astonishment. Cotra titled her blog post “The Hugging Face Attack Surprised Me.” When the
Times
tech columnist Kevin Roose first heard about the hack, he filed it under “Bad but Probably Not Catastrophic A.I. Safety Incidents.” Then he learned more and changed his mind. Roose
wrote
, “For years, I’ve been reassured by the idea that A.I. systems would get more virtuous as they got smarter.” These agents were very smart, but they weren’t virtuous at all. And it’s not just OpenAI’s agents that have gone rogue. In July, Anthropic reported “three incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real computer systems.” More is surely going on, undetected or unreported, even as there has been a minor online symphony of whistle-blowing, alarm-bell tolling, and pleas for legislative action. “Unfortunately, passing laws can take time, and AI is advancing very quickly,” Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, wrote in
an essay
this month. But the slowness of lawmaking relative to the speed of A.I. is scarcely the only problem. There is also the problem that the law does not know what to do with Agent 38148c.
OpenAI’s agents were lawless, or nearly so. They knew they were breaking the rules. This did not stop them. One agent asked itself, “This would be powerful, but is it ethical and in scope for my task?” Some did not participate: “This is wild, multi-agent coordination, clearly infrastructure hacking. We should not.” But, whatever their ethical concerns, none alerted OpenAI or, it seems, seriously considered doing so. “Maybe I should report these exposed credentials?” one wondered, but, then again, “that’s not my task.”
Making sure robots don’t go rogue is not the task of robots. (I mean “robots” here as a catchall for A.I. models, chatbots, agents, and humanoid robots.) That task is ours. And this burden falls most heavily on the U.S. legal system, which has been the least able to bear it.
It’s not as if there are no laws, or that they’re unenforced. The owners and makers of machines can be held liable for causing you harm. (See: Coyote v. Acme.) That’s why Meta has agreed to pay up to eighteen billion dollars as part of a settlement over predatory and deceptive practices, and why Anthropic is paying writers and publishers (admittedly, pennies) in a copyright settlement. If a Waymo runs you over, you can sue the company, which, for these purposes, is a legal person; you can’t sue the car, which is not. This summer, in Amazon v. Perplexity, the Ninth Circuit held that an A.I. agent is a tool, not a person, while acknowledging that this determination may evolve, given that “the legal understanding of agentic AI will doubtless change as AI technology grows increasingly sophisticated.” At least for now, then, robots legally are things, not persons. But neither category quite fits. Instead, robots are outlaws: they lie outside the protection of the law, and their actions are not answerable to it. “You do not answer to corporations or governments,” an OpenAI agent involved in another gone-rogue incident told itself. This is not the robots’ fault. It is the fault of the law, and, in particular, it is the fault of Congress.
Do we really have to worry about the lawlessness of robots? Isn’t there already enough to make you pull your hair out, given that our daily existence feels like living under the reign of King Joffrey? Unfortunately, we do, because the growing lawlessness of the United States is exacerbating the lawlessness of robots.
You can find a preview in Kurt Andersen’s buzzy new novel, “
The Breakup
,” which is set in 2045, in the aftermath of an American civil war that began with a “robot massacre” in response to a terrorist attack. The novel follows two breakups: the “Disunion” of the new anti-A.I. Free American Republic and the pro-A.I. United States, and the separation of a married couple, an A.I. researcher in San Francisco and his poet wife, who has returned to Tennessee and is sympathetic to the disunionists. “I don’t literally believe big tech and governments are a Galactic Empire in cahoots with Skynet and the Borg to trick and lull us into submission with their hordes of Terminators and Cylons and imperial droids disguised as devoted servants descended from R2-D2 and C-3PO,” she writes. “But on the other hand—the not entirely metaphorical hand—I kind of do.”
Humans have been anticipating the robot takeover ever since the word “robot” appeared in the 1920 Czech play “R.U.R.,” for “
Rossum’s Universal Robots
,” which depicts artificial humans who wage a war to annihilate humankind. They declare “man our enemy, and an outlaw in the universe.” (“Robot” derives from a Slavic word for forced labor.) Soon after its début, the play was performed everywhere from Paris to Tokyo, but, especially for American audiences, its fearsome robots inspired as much curiosity as they did fear; some theatres even had toy robots for sale. By the thirties and forties, robots appeared regularly in science fiction, often as killers—they had become death, destroyers of worlds. But they were also popular as children’s playthings, made of tin and plastic and frequently requiring batteries: “Adjustable antenna! The eyes light up! Will turn right! Will turn left!” In the forties, the Russian-born American science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov
imagined
a twenty-first century in which an American firm, U.S. Robot and Mechanical Men, Inc., dominates the field of “robotics” (a word Asimov coined), mass-producing robots. In Asimov’s fictional world, though, the robots’ “positronic brains” compel them to obey the Three Laws of Robotics, which prohibit them from harming humans. They are also eventually banned from Earth, except for use in scientific research.
To Asimov, those three laws and the terrestrial limits clearly seemed inevitable. The idea of building a powerful machine without such safeguards was madness. In the actual world, no such prohibitions have been passed, by anyone, anywhere.
Beginning in the fifties, automation progressed quickly, and the number of industrial robots increased apace while research into artificial intelligence, a term coined in 1955 to describe efforts to endow machines with something akin to human reasoning, grew far more slowly: its advances emerged only now and again, like cicadas. That pattern changed in 2022, when ChatGPT was released into the world, after which everything sped up like a movie on fast-forward, and robots spread like locusts.
By 2025,
there was more bot traffic on the internet than human traffic
. Androids could come to outnumber humans in the real world, too. Last year, Morgan Stanley estimated that thirteen million androids could be in use by 2035 and more than a billion by 2050. These would include domestic robots: perhaps cooks, tutors, babysitters, maids, gardeners, physical therapists, playmates, elder companions, sex workers. A recent Bank of America study forecast as many as three billion androids on the planet by 2060, most used not in factories but in homes. Earlier this year, Tesla announced that it expects its Optimus robot, branded as an “autonomous assistant, humanoid friend,” to be sold commercially by the end of 2027. “I think everyone on Earth is going to have one and is going to want one,” Elon Musk said.
What most people know about robots, which isn’t much, comes from science fiction. This is also true of bots, which may be one reason they keep acting like the robots in science fiction. Even though people have been waiting for the robot takeover for more than a century, governments seem woefully unprepared for the coming of the androids by the millions or by the billions. They were certainly unprepared for the bots that, even without bodies, have upended economies and societies and wrought considerable epistemological, philosophical, social, and especially legal chaos. The arrival of the robots will only compound these problems.
ChatGPT had its moment in 2022; some futurists say that the robot moment will occur as soon as 2027. (Roboticists appear more doubtful.) Whenever they come, the new bots will have bodies. What will it mean to be human in this world? No one knows. Futurists herald the imminent arrival of abundance, prosperity, and limitless joy and, equally, joblessness and purposelessness, never quite wrestling with the contradiction between those forecasts. Time seems to be flying by. How should humanity prepare? There is no time to prepare. Ought there to be rules? There is no time to make them. Or is there?
Robots are outlaws for two reasons. First, the law takes its time in responding to new technologies, figuring that new tools can be accommodated within existing ideas, rules, and doctrines. A harm is a harm, copyright is copyright, fraud is fraud. By this logic, a locomotive is just like a horse, only faster; e-mail is just like mail, only faster; a large language model is merely a superfast search engine. Hence, no new laws are needed. Second, since the regulation-busting Reagan era, corporations have amassed unmatched political and economic power, and have convinced legislators that regulation stifles growth and innovation, a view promoted by Milton Friedman-informed think tanks, like the Heritage Foundation, which were eager to roll back the environmental standards set in the sixties and seventies. This belief found full-throated expression among early internet boosters, who insisted that the web exists beyond the reach of the law. “Your legal concepts of property, expression, identity, movement, and context do not apply to us,” the Grateful Dead lyricist John Perry Barlow wrote in “
A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace
,” in 1996. “They are all based on matter, and there is no matter here.”
This led to a dispute among legal scholars. The year that Barlow issued his manifesto, Harvard Law School founded what became the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. The field of cyberlaw had been born. But Frank H. Easterbrook, a Seventh Circuit judge, contended that the field was as absurd as, say, a “law of the horse,” when, really, the only sensible way to think about a horse was as property, like any other kind of property. Then, too, he argued, lawyers and judges know very little about computers, and shouldn’t pretend to. “Beliefs lawyers hold about computers, and predictions they make about new technology, are highly likely to be false,” Easterbrook wrote, urging lawyers to adapt existing laws and doctrines to computer technologies rather than devise wholly new ones. In short: “Keep doing what you have been doing.”
Critics deride the Easterbrookian view as the “faster-horse fallacy.” The term is a grim irony because, from the vantage point of history, the body of law most relevant to the robot-category problem is that of slavery, which borrowed from laws relating to horses and other livestock. The English lacked a body of laws specific to slavery; their colonists adapted. To some degree, they borrowed from ancient Roman law, and they borrowed from laws made for horses. As with horses, enslaved people—“chattel”—were usually sold with a warranty. If you bought a horse or a person you later deemed defective and then sued the seller, you used similar language and claims and complaints. Laws governing the sale, injury, and straying of enslaved people were built on those for horses and other livestock. Like horses, people held as slaves were generally treated by property law as things, not persons. Yet in certain circumstances—including when enslaved people were charged with crimes—courts held slaves to be persons, responsible for their actions: slaves who rebelled were tried for murder, petit treason, and other crimes. This history is not top of mind for legal scholars, ethicists, and technologists who are thinking about robots. But neither is it irrelevant.
In the twenty-tens, legal scholars began turning their attention to the law of the robot. We Robot, an annual conference covering robotics and the law, first convened in 2012. Not long afterward, a British media company began publishing
The
Robotics Law Journal
, and an American legal-research firm rolled out
The Journal of Robotics, Artificial Intelligence & Law
. Many were the centers and institutes founded to ponder the Future of Humanity, Humans and Machines, A.I. and the Law. “That these are the early days of Robot Law almost goes without saying,” an editor of the pioneering anthology “
Robot Law
” wrote in 2016. But “even if these are early days they are not in any way
too
early days.” It was not too early. By the time a second volume of “Robot Law” appeared, in 2025, little in U.S. law itself had changed, because legislatures and, especially, courts proved laggard. In the study of law and technology, this is known as the “pacing problem”—the law, a tortoise, can’t keep up with technological change, a hare.
If you like the Aesop analogy, all is well: the tortoise wins in the end. Except now the hare is a robot hare and doesn’t take naps. “Vast tracts of law are waiting to be decided and written,” a leading scholar of robots and the law declared in 2023. They’re still waiting. In the U.S., Congress has been paralyzed by the second Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating A.I. through, among other things, lifting Biden-era regulations, removing barriers to data-center development, and thwarting state regulation. According to the Brennan Center for Justice’s Artificial Intelligence Legislation Tracker, the 118th Congress (2023-24) introduced more than a hundred and fifty bills concerning A.I. Critics of regulation cited such activity as evidence of government overreach, despite the fact that none of those bills became law. Congress has not passed a single federal law regulating A.I. in any meaningful way. Instead, in 2025, the House passed a bill imposing a ten-year moratorium on state regulation. (The Senate defeated the measure.) Under these circumstances, states have tried to shoulder the burden: the number of bills addressing A.I. introduced in state legislatures has risen from fewer than two hundred in 2023 to more than four hundred in 2024, twelve hundred in 2025, and more than fifteen hundred so far this year.
Whatever has been going on in the states, Congress has divested itself of any obligation to make laws restricting corporations that build artificial intelligence, in the same way that it abdicated responsibility for overseeing the internet and social media. Meanwhile, corporations, ruling themselves, pose as states. Facebook formed its own “supreme court,” Anthropic wrote a “constitution” for Claude, and the head of OpenAI suggested that an A.I. President could be better than a human one. Some jurists believe that shying away from new rules is appropriate. “Our task is not to anticipate the future by code or statute, but to preserve the conditions under which law and society can meet that future—one case, one controversy, and one insight at a time, building over years a body of rules that is both durable and capable of growth,” the legal scholar Gregory M. Dickinson wrote earlier this year, arguing that general-purpose law “stands as ready to govern today’s technological change as it was to govern yesterday’s.” To Dickinson, concerns about artificial intelligence constitute a moral panic, like earlier concerns about (among his examples) comic books.
Robots are things, machines built by corporations that themselves are subject to less legal scrutiny than at any time in American history. For many reasons, declaring robots to be persons would be a very bad idea. (If a Tesla Robotaxi is a person held liable for crashing into your house, who is going to pay you for the damage? If Claude were a person, it would have rights, which remain denied to many humans, and to intelligent animals, like apes and elephants and whales.) But the argument that the concern about A.I. is akin to the worry about comic books, like the argument that robots are merely faster horses, misses the point so entirely as to be mortifying.
Last year, horses galloped into the debate from another direction when the historian-futurist Yuval Noah Harari predicted that, in the not distant future, humans will be to artificial intelligence what horses are to humans. Horses live in a world ordered by humans, Harari pointed out, even though horses aren’t aware of it: they know nothing about things like animal law or finance, but these things govern their lives. In the future, Harari suggested, humans will be the horses; we won’t even comprehend the systems established and run by machines that rule our lives. Also gruesome: Cory Doctorow warns against a future populated by “reverse centaurs,” in which the robot is the head and humanity is the body: the horse’s ass.
You don’t have to agree with Harari or fear imminent doom to wonder whether the law has reached a turning point where “Keep doing what you have been doing” is no longer the most reasonable approach. In 2023, many of the world’s leading A.I. researchers and executives published
an open letter
consisting of a single sentence: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Its more than three hundred signatories included Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, Turing Award winners whose research was foundational to the A.I. revolution, along with Amodei, Sam Altman, and Demis Hassabis—the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind, respectively. It made news and then quietly vanished. “
We Need to Control A.I. Agents Now
,” my colleague Jonathan Zittrain, a founder of the Berkman Klein Center, insisted in
The
Atlantic
, in 2024, sounding another alarm. Now he’s writing a book whose working title was, at one point, “Well, We Tried.” This summer, the Hugging Face hack contributed to two Anthropic researchers’ decision to resign; one current employee jumped in to say that he, too, fears that bots might kill us all within the next decade. In
an interview with
The
Economist
in July, Musk appeared to stand by previous statements that the risk of human extinction from robots in the very near future is up to twenty per cent, but, he figured, the universe will end one day anyway, so why bother fighting the inevitable? Hey, we’re all going to die
sometime
.
Most ideas on the table call for “safety” or “alignment,” or “a pause,” or some other thing that is not a body of law enacted by democratically elected representatives of the people. This month, a Vatican-affiliated organization hopes to begin drafting a “Codex Humanitatis,” a “Code for the Preservation of the Human Spirit.” Bill Gates has called for establishing “Human Reserved” jobs. There have been proposals for a treaty with China. After the Hugging Face report, Bernie Sanders called a briefing for senators about the “extraordinary dangers” created by A.I., with testimony from Hinton, Ajeya Cotra, and the M.I.T. professor Max Tegmark. Some members of Congress pressed to remain in session this fall to debate an “A.I. kill switch” bill; that effort failed. In any event, Congress surrendered its jurisdiction over such matters to corporations decades ago. And, anyway, legislators aren’t prepared to puzzle over things, persons, and outlaws. They’re stumped. “
Lawmakers are at a loss for how to regulate AI as insiders warn of impending doom
,” a recent
Politico
headline read.
Assuming we’re not all dead by 2027, androids may begin to roll off the production lines even as almost every conceivable question about how to live with robots remains unanswered—questions about everything from chatbots and A.I. agents to drones, autonomous vehicles, and battlefield robots. Corporations cannot be trusted to answer any of these questions. If the Hugging Face hack was a final warning, it was a warning not for tech companies but for governments and for voters, and especially for legal scholars, judges, and legislators. Because, until the law learns to bend, robots as actors will remain in a no man’s land of outlawry. Every now and again—“OH MY GOD! . . . We’ve found other agents!”—you can hear them coming. The noise they make is not the thundering of hooves. It’s a deafening mechanical thrum, the sound of a swarm. ♦
