What Barbara Kingsolver Believes the Novel Can Do
Profiles
What Barbara Kingsolver Believes the Novel Can Do
One of the country’s most popular novelists writes what she calls socially engaged fiction. In her new book, she considers the role of art—and who it’s for.
By Casey Cep
September 21, 2026
Barbara Kingsolver always struggles with beginnings. “I write probably one hundred pages to get to page one of any novel,” she told me recently. “Not all at once—like, eight or nine pages a day. And then the next day I start over completely.” She’s looking for the voice and the tone that she wants, the vein of silver in the mine that she’s digging, and ten novels into her career, at age seventy-one, it hasn’t got any easier. “I still begin with the feeling that this is just a load of crap,” she said. “Every single time, I think, This is going to suck.” For each book, “there’s page minus one hundred to page zero.”
Her new novel, “Partita,” was even harder to start than most, but she eventually found her way to three different beginnings, each with a heading borrowed from classical music: Overture, Prelude, and Allemande. Like Kingsolver, the narrator of “Partita” once had a promising career ahead of her as a pianist, and she thinks in musical terms. I have in mind to ask Kingsolver about a fourth beginning to the novel—a “Note on the Music” that prefaces those other beginnings, directing readers to a “Listening List” with selections from Bach, Beethoven, Chopin, Ravel, and Miriam Makeba—but, before I can do so, she insists that I eat some more cucumbers. We picked a basket full of them from her garden the day before, and today she’s cut some into spears and bathed them in balsamic vinegar.
It’s almost pickling time in southwest Virginia—late July, on what Kingsolver calls a “dog breath” day, hot and humid, with the threat of thunderstorms in all directions. Although it’s lunchtime, what sun there is still hasn’t fully cleared the holler where Kingsolver lives; light flashes here and there between the leafy branches of all the maples, oaks, and poplars, illuminating various patches of the two hundred and forty acres that she shares with her husband, their Border collie, a flock of guinea fowl and laying hens, and a herd of Icelandic sheep. Readers of Kingsolver know this farm from her memoir, “Animal, Vegetable, Miracle: A Year of Food Life,” which describes her family’s efforts to eat only what they or their neighbors could grow or raise. The book makes an environmental and civic case for doing so, but it’s also true that Kingsolver doesn’t like to go too far from home. “My family has this running joke,” she says, explaining her love for this part of Appalachia and her stubborn reluctance to abandon it. “ ‘How long since Mom left the holler?’ ”
The answer today turns out to be not that long, and not just because she went to the post office in the nearby town of Meadowview or to the farmers’ market in Abingdon. Kingsolver and her husband have recently returned from Greece, where she taught a writing workshop in Patmos before they toured the Pindus Mountains and the monasteries of Meteora and paid a visit to the old neighborhood in Athens where she’d lived for a few vagabond months during college. They take a trip together whenever she finishes a book. Otherwise, if she had her way, she’d seldom leave the farm.
“I’m as extreme an introvert as they make,” she says, moving strands of gray hair away from her face. Kingsolver has hazel eyes that follow you from behind round scholarly glasses, and, although that self-characterization may contain a touch of hyperbole, she does seem to have roughly the same attentiveness, curiosity, and social needs as an owl. “I’ve learned to be comfortable in front of an audience,” she tells me. “When I was a kid and we’d play that game of wishing for our superpowers, the one I always wished for was invisibility. And I still wish for invisibility.”
That desire is somewhat at odds with Kingsolver’s career. She’s published nineteen books—in addition to the novels and the memoir, there’s a story collection, a children’s book, a photography book, a work of narrative nonfiction, two volumes of essays, and two poetry collections—which have cumulatively sold more than twenty million copies in this country alone. She’s won most of the major literary prizes, some of them twice, and her commercial success has launched her into a tier of celebrity rare for novelists, with her work appearing in “Jeopardy!” clues and crossword-puzzle answers and her name bantered about by characters on “The Sopranos” and “King of the Hill.” Her last novel made her more visible than ever: “Demon Copperhead,” the story of a dirt-poor Appalachian boy orphaned by the opioid epidemic, won the Pulitzer Prize in 2023, sat on the
Times
best-seller list for more than a year, and was voted the best book of the twenty-first century by the newspaper’s readers.
Kingsolver talks about that novel’s success as we rock in parallel chairs on the front porch of her hundred-year-old farmhouse, sipping coffee and watching butterflies and birds through its cloister-like arches. She relays the history of those arches like a fairy tale: how they were made by the original owner’s eleven children, each of them paid ten cents a day to help their father soak boards in the creek and bend them into shape, covering the arched wood and framed flower boxes with mortar and river stones that he’d gathered by the trunkful while working for the railroad on the Nolichucky River in Tennessee. “You can see the little ones got a little sloppy down at the bottom,” she says, laughing.
Kingsolver can turn anything into a story, so I’m surprised to learn that she struggled with writer’s block after “Demon Copperhead.” “I think it should actually be called writer’s fear,” she says. She had the idea for her next book, but she couldn’t stop worrying about whether readers would like it, and how it would do, and other things that real artists are supposed to at least pretend not to care about. She was well and truly stuck when a Substack post, of all things, got her writing again.
The headline was “Barbara Kingsolver Is a Fraud,” a charge that literary critics have debated, usually in more polite terms, for most of her career, but not the sort of proposition I expected Kingsolver to entertain. “I had to know why,” she says, explaining her decision to click on the link. “Maybe I
am
a fraud!” The writer of the post “had done her Wiki research,” she recalls. “She had read my dad was a doctor, so obviously I had to be in the country-club set. What would I know about working-class people? And I went to college on a piano scholarship, but how could any working-class person ever play classical piano? That pissed me off.”
Kingsolver writes what she calls socially engaged fiction, novels in the tradition of Charles Dickens and John Steinbeck that take on whatever political, economic, or cultural issue she feels a moral urgency to address. Her books, like theirs, are sometimes knocked as preachy and sentimental, but Kingsolver says it wasn’t the criticism of her work that irked her as much as the stereotypes about people on the margins of American life. “There are assumptions in both directions,” she told me. “Rural working-class people don’t necessarily feel at home in a concert hall, and therefore they might not support the N.E.A., because of all the snooty people who look down on us. And those snooty people think, How could someone from Appalachia know anything about classical music?”
Kingsolver has always believed that the arts belong to everyone, and has spent her life writing books that she hopes can be read by anyone. “Partita” clicked into place when she realized that its narrator, the daughter of a dairy farmer, would need to justify her musical ambitions not only to her family and to herself but to her peers at the conservatory she attends and to the man with whom she falls in love, a Marxist organizer who has his own doubts about the purpose of the arts. A smaller and more intimate novel than “Demon Copperhead,” it nonetheless addresses, in Kingsolver’s usual manner, a host of politically charged topics, among them abortion rights and access to health care. More strikingly, it wrestles with the questions that have fuelled her whole career—namely, who is art for, what makes it good, and what can it actually accomplish?
There’s a difference between beginnings and origins. Kingsolver came into the world in 1955 in Annapolis, Maryland, where her father, Wendell, was stationed after being drafted into the Navy, and where her mother, Virginia, suffered from what was likely postpartum depression. Far from home and raising two children while her husband was busy in the service, Ginny, as she was known, struggled to bond with Barbara, her second baby. The family soon moved to Kentucky, where Kingsolver’s parents, high-school sweethearts, had been born and raised, and settled in the small town of Carlisle, where another daughter was born. Dr. Wendell, as everyone called him, opened a medical practice for the people he thought most needed one, and Kingsolver grew up surrounded by alfalfa and tobacco fields and neighbors who made their living working them. Her parents were founding members of a Disciples of Christ church and the Kentucky chapter of the Sierra Club, and they raised their children in the gap between God and His green earth.
As Kingsolver tells it, she and her siblings—older brother Robert and younger sister Ann—grew up as wild as Peter Pan or Pippi Longstocking. They tried to tame a baby snapping turtle in a pickle jar, caught crawfish with their bare hands and cooked them over a campfire, counted to a million together in the back seat of the family’s VW bus, and divided the encyclopedia into shares with the aim of collectively reading the whole thing. But it wasn’t just facts that interested Kingsolver. “Barbara was a wonderful storyteller as a child,” Ann recalls. By age ten, Kingsolver had a “menu” of recurring characters from which she’d let her little sister pick each night: the Maya stories, the Henry stories, the Annie stories, all of which grew new chapters whenever needed.
Dr. Wendell sought to serve the impoverished and imposed a kind of poverty on his own family: the kids wore hand-me-down and homemade clothes; much of what they ate came from their garden or whatever food his patients had brought for barter. “The spiritual truth my father lived by is that your value is not what you have but what you do,” Kingsolver says. Exceptions were made for books, travel, and musical instruments. “Our dad took literature very seriously,” Robert recalls, “and every Friday night, we’d sit down by the fire in the winter or out on the porch in the summer, and he would read novels to us, classics like Robert Louis Stevenson or Jack London.” The family also had a hi-fi, which is how Kingsolver first heard the classical compositions that form the repertoire of “Partita,” and a piano, which she and her mother both played, plus a bass and a flute for her sister and guitars for her father and her brother.
Kingsolver’s parents aspired to live a humble life in an even humbler part of the country, but they were set apart by their education, and so was she, not always in ways that benefitted her. She remembers being bullied by students and teachers alike, first for learning how to read so early—she figured it out at three, when the word “o-r-a-n-g-e,” in one of her father’s newspapers, tempted her like Augustine’s pear—then for reading more than people thought a girl should. Once, in middle school, her teacher abandoned her desk and had Kingsolver lead the lessons. “I wasn’t just the teacher’s pet, I was her emotional-support animal,” Kingsolver says. “She was in the back painting her fingernails and reading romance novels, and I was up front talking about Lord Halifax.”
Around this time, Kingsolver was accused of cheating in a regional essay contest. “They rejected her essay,” Robert tells me, “and sent it back and said, Obviously this girl had her parents write her essay, no seventh grader could write this.” Kingsolver, furious over the false accusation and offended because she felt she was already a better writer than both of her parents, sent a letter of protest with supporting evidence from her teacher. “The judges reconsidered, I won, and my authorship was never questioned again,” she recounts.
Early on, Kingsolver fantasized about ways of getting out of school, and when she was in the second grade the Lord, or at least Dr. Wendell, provided: the family spent half that year on the Wamba River in the Republic of the Congo. “A colleague of his told him, ‘Yes, the people of eastern Kentucky need you, but the people in Congo need you even more,’ ” Kingsolver says. It was the first of a handful of medical mission trips he undertook with his family—first to Congo, then to St. Lucia, and later to the rural coast of Newfoundland. In the village of Kikongo, the kids picked up Kituba and learned not to pick up spitting vipers, got close but not too close to the leper colony nearby, and made a treasure hunt out of searching for the parachuted packages of medical supplies that aid workers dropped off every month by plane. Those supplies were essential—penicillin, antivenom, surgical tools—but never enough.
“I think my father just thought it would be a grand adventure for all of us,” she says. “He was a real believer in what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.” It fell to Ginny, she adds, “to keep us all alive.” Kingsolver never felt close to her mother, but she could see how hard it was for her. “She loved him, but being a mother and a housewife was not her thing. As soon as I knew that people—adults, I mean—had feelings, I knew that hers were not good. He was doing all this to save lives. She was doing it because she’d gotten married at nineteen, and, even though she was completely dismayed by most of it, whatever he said, she did. I decided then I didn’t want to be a wife, because it was obvious wives got a really bad deal.”
Kingsolver likes to say that she learned the power of prose after an essay she wrote about the need for a new elementary school ran in the local newspaper ahead of a successful tax levy. She is pleased to take a little credit for the overdue upgrade. But one of her first awards for the sort of ventriloquism that would shape her career came from channelling a woman like her mother. When the girls in her high school were sent to participate in the Betty Crocker Search for the All-American Homemaker of Tomorrow exam, Kingsolver closed her eyes and imagined the antithesis of what she wanted for her life, then began to write.
In truth, the 1973 winner for Nicholas County High School wanted to be anything but a homemaker. She stuffed her days with Drama Club, Speech Club, French Club, Honor Society, and whatever else she thought might help her escape the miserable domesticity she knew from Scrubgrass Road. A benevolent librarian had taught her the Dewey decimal system, and she found her way to categories like “323.34: Women’s Rights and Feminism”: the novels of Gordimer, Nadine; Lessing, Doris; and Woolf, Virginia; later, the polemics of Betty Friedan, Germaine Greer, and Gloria Steinem.
Those women provided a genealogy of aspirations and ideas from which Kingsolver fashioned herself and her sense of the world. A piano scholarship landed her at DePauw University, in Greencastle, Indiana, though she soon switched her major from music to zoology. She dropped her accent just as quickly, changed her clothes, and leaned into a life as far from Carlisle as she could.
Alongside her classes, Kingsolver marched for abortion rights and against the Vietnam War, and worked as a housecleaner and a typesetter. She sent self-righteous letters home to her mother “on the great freedom women could experience if only they would throw off the bondage of housewifely servitude.” But she did not reveal in those letters that she’d been raped in her sophomore year, by a man she’d met a few nights before, worried her mother would say that it was her own fault for going to a bar. Kingsolver cut off her waist-length hair and started wearing combat boots and an Army overcoat. Somehow, even as the world collapsed into a “knot of nothingness,” it also opened wider than ever: she moved abroad the next year, first spending a semester in Greece, where she trained as an archeologist’s assistant, then heading to France and to England, where she found work on a Viking dig in York. After that, she cobbled together whatever other gigs she could until her visa ran out: copy editor, translator, even art model. She soon stopped telling her parents where she was. “My mother deserved the daughter who ran away,” she says.
Whatever Kingsolver studied, wherever she went, she filled notebooks with poems and stories and kept a diary, as she had been doing since she was seven years old, when she opened the lock on the little red one she’d been given for Christmas before leaving for Congo and carefully crafted words that now seem as if they were meant to be read: “When I first saw Africa I thought it was a cloud.” In her early twenties, she wanted to write “War and Peace” but figured she’d settle for “Cannery Row.” When neither materialized, she enrolled in graduate school, but not for creative writing: she earned a master’s degree in ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Arizona, in Tucson, where she studied subterranean termites—specifically, why it is they behave so altruistically toward one another.
She dropped out of the Ph.D. program she was in to take a job as a technical writer in the university’s Office of Arid Lands Studies, and began dating a quiet, lanky chemistry professor named Joseph Hoffmann. The pair wrote a few science papers together, mostly related to his research on alternative uses for native desert plants; they collaborated on political work as well, volunteering with the sanctuary movement to provide support to refugees and to document human-rights violations along the border. She and Hoffmann married in 1985, sending her parents a postcard from Spain: “Having a wonderful time. Weather’s great. Got married. Wish you were here.”
Back in Arizona, she quit her day job and freelanced full time, writing for local newspapers, literary journals, and left-leaning magazines. She got a break when some outlets sent her to report on copper miners and mill workers striking against the Phelps Dodge Corporation over wages. She was supposed to file a few quick stories, but the strike dragged on, and Kingsolver kept talking to the workers; eventually, they started introducing her to others as “the gal that’s writing the book about us.”
Kingsolver wrote that book, “Holding the Line: Women in the Great Arizona Mine Strike of 1983,” about the wives, daughters, and sisters of the miners, who formed a picket line when the men were prohibited from doing so. But no one wanted to publish it. She’d found an agent in a directory at the public library, Frances Goldin, whom she chose because her entry had indicated that her agency would not represent “pornography or ageist, sexist, racist, or homophobic material.” Kingsolver emphasizes how radical that was for the time, and how heartened she is that literary culture has caught up to the mission-driven agency, whose marquee clients were Adrienne Rich and Dorothy Allison. Although Goldin couldn’t sell Kingsolver’s book, the pair grew close, and Goldin, already beloved at Pride parades for the sign she carried in support of her two lesbian daughters, became a kind of surrogate mother to the author.
When Kingsolver got pregnant, in 1986, she developed severe insomnia, and used those “extra hours” to write fiction. It came slowly until she began drawing on aspects of herself that she’d spent nearly fifteen years suppressing. “I was in this little writing group,” she tells me, “and there were four other women writing stories and sharing them with each other, and I kept sharing these stories about all these people who lived around Dog Doo Park”—the nickname her characters gave to their small urban park—“and one of the women said, ‘These people don’t seem like they’re from anywhere.’ ”
Kingsolver, chastened and inspired, apprenticed herself to the working-class characters of Bobbie Ann Mason and the neo-agrarian works of Wendell Berry. Those Kentucky authors helped her find the voice of Taylor Greer, the narrator of “The Bean Trees.” “I have been afraid of putting air in a tire ever since I saw a tractor tire blow up and throw Newt Hardbine’s father over the top of the Standard Oil sign,” it begins. “I’m not lying. He got stuck up there.” A prolonged pregnancy gave Kingsolver more time to finish; instead of opting for induction when her due date passed, she waited out her baby for another three weeks, long enough to send the manuscript off to Goldin with a note: “I’m sorry, you probably don’t want this. I think it’s a novel.”
The day that Kingsolver came home from the hospital with her daughter Camille, there was a message on the answering machine from Goldin with two offers for the book. The novel, published in 1988, foreshadowed the career to come by taking on, with disarming frankness, everything from child abuse to transracial adoption. It also divided critics in ways that her work has done ever since. “Only a Dickensian villain could fail to like this book,” Carolyn See wrote in the Los Angeles
Times
, adding that “this novel goes beyond ordinary storytelling in its noble intent.” But that intent seemed like a flaw to others: a reviewer in the New York
Times
lamented Kingsolver’s “overmanipulation” of characters, from the unfailingly honorable victims to the impossibly perfect heroine, saying that the book, for all its virtues, sometimes read like “an upbeat novel for teenagers.”
Although “The Bean Trees” sold modestly, book clubs and independent booksellers adored it and kept it in print. But, while Kingsolver’s professional life was taking shape, her personal life began falling apart. “When the attention started coming to me, not to him—that was not in the contract,” she tells me. In the early nineties, she and Hoffmann moved with Camille to the Canary Islands for a year, partly because Kingsolver, who had been protesting the Gulf War, wanted a break from American politics, but also because she and Hoffmann were trying to reset their life. When that failed, they divorced. “A nonfunctioning marriage,” Kingsolver wrote not long afterward, “is a slow asphyxiation. It is waking up despised each morning, listening to the pulse of your own loneliness before the radio begins to blare its raucous gospel that you’re nothing if you aren’t loved.”
Kingsolver still has insomnia but doesn’t write in those late-night hours anymore. Instead, she keeps a special stack of books by her bed which she essentially uses as soporifics, and which she diplomatically asks me not to name. Despite all the lost sleep, she gets up early to write, which she does in a long and gorgeously renovated L-shaped office she jokes should have a plaque for Oprah Winfrey, who has twice chosen Kingsolver novels for her book club. Every edge, ledge, and surface is covered with books, pictures of her children, and cards from her grandchildren, plus art, letters, and tchotchkes from her readers—everyone, she says, from prisoners to Presidents.
She works at a standing desk, taking a break whenever her feet fall asleep. She generally wakes up with a few sentences, occasionally even whole paragraphs, in mind, and starts typing; after she gets those written up, she reads what she wrote the day before, often aloud, and keeps doing it over and over until she’s satisfied, which can sometimes take dozens of drafts. These days, her process can be slow for another reason: she suffers from Dupuytren’s contracture, a painful disease that causes the tissues of the palms to thicken and tighten, forming hard cords that curl the fingers until they cannot lie flat. She has had corrective surgery on both hands and is grateful to still be able to play the piano and to knit. Some days, she can type only with one hand, but she quips that, much of the time, you really just need one finger: “Whenever people ask for writing advice, I say, Fall in love with your Delete key.”
Kingsolver tends to alternate between smaller novels and grander ones. Two years after “The Bean Trees,” she published “Animal Dreams,” which is not only about a woman who moves home to take care of her ailing father but also about her sister, who has been murdered by the Contras in Nicaragua while trying to help the Sandinistas grow cotton. That was followed quickly by “Pigs in Heaven,” in 1993, which returned to Taylor Greer and her adopted Cherokee daughter, Turtle. By then, Kingsolver was already well into the decade she spent writing what she came to call the D.A.B.: the Damned Africa Book.
The rest of the world would know it as “The Poisonwood Bible.” The novel is narrated by the five female members of the Price family of Bethlehem, Georgia, who collectively tell the tragic story of Western intervention in Congo. It occupied the
Times
best-seller list for more than six months, largely thanks to its gripping sweep, but also because of Kingsolver’s knack for producing the right book for the moment. It appeared in 1998, a few months after the Congolese President, Laurent-Désiré Kabila, banished Rwandan and Ugandan troops from the country, leading his former allies to support rebel uprisings, and eventually pulling some two dozen armed groups and nine African countries into the deadliest conflict since the Second World War. But some critics found the book as preposterous as the Betty Crocker cake mixes the Prices tote with them across the Atlantic. In
The New Republic
, Lee Siegel crowned Kingsolver “the queen of Nice Writing,” arguing that she offered a no-calorie version of life’s real tragedies, whether it was colonialism in Africa or American imperialism in Latin America. “Kingsolver does not exactly outrage me, because she is so damn nice; but she is becoming outrageous,” he wrote. “With the publication of ‘The Poisonwood Bible,’ this easy, humorous, competent, syrupy writer has been elevated to the ranks of the greatest political novelists of our time.”
“The Poisonwood Bible” drew on the experiences of Kingsolver’s family; she was finally able to finish it because she’d made a new family of her own. In 1993, divorced and raising her daughter alone, she accepted a teaching fellowship on the condition that she be placed on a college campus near enough to eastern Kentucky that her relatives could help with child care. She wound up at Emory & Henry University, in Virginia’s western highlands, where one day she got a phone call from Steven Hopp, a professor whose class on global wildlife conservation she had agreed to visit. Hopp asked what she’d be talking about, and, when she realized that she hadn’t planned anything, she made up a lecture based on a title the fellowship coördinator had chosen for her: “Ecofeminism and Personal Responsibility.”
What happened next remains a source of amicable contention thirty-three years later. Hopp tells me his version of the story while the three of us walk the timber road of their farm looking for mushrooms. Trumpets are in season, their dark, earthy umber contrasting almost comically with the neon-pink basket that Kingsolver carries. Irrespective of any sentence she might be in the middle of, she bounds ahead whenever she sees a big cap, to try to get it before Hopp can. He, meanwhile, is happy to lose the foraging competition in order to win the argument about their first meeting. He claims that during their initial conversation he made awkward small talk while inwardly worrying she might deliver a lecture on ridding the world of men. She claims that he told her, “Good luck parlaying that into an hour.” “In my defense,” Hopp interrupts, “I don’t think I would’ve known what the word ‘parlay’ meant.”
Kingsolver, in any case, parlayed it into a marriage. After the lecture, Hopp invited her to his farm, near Meadowview, where they walked the same trail the three of us are walking now. “The Jane Austen version would be ‘He had a beautiful farm; unpolluted acres,’ ” Kingsolver jokes. It was the night before she was supposed to leave town and they found that they couldn’t stop talking—they built a campfire, looked for glowworms, played music, and stayed up until daybreak. “I said, ‘I haven’t had this much fun in forever,’ ” Kingsolver remembers. “And he said, ‘Really? I have this much fun every day.’ ”
She returned to Tucson, but not before she and Hopp exchanged numbers; they got married, she says, when their telephone bills exceeded their mortgages. Hopp transferred to the University of Arizona, but they returned to southwestern Virginia every summer, and when Kingsolver’s daughter finished high school they relocated to Hopp’s farm full time. By then, they’d had a daughter, Lily, and they soon finished renovating the old farmhouse that had come with the property.
One of the most conspicuous luxuries there now is a Steinway piano. Kingsolver used to play with the Rock Bottom Remainders, a band of best-selling authors who perform rock-and-roll covers to benefit literacy and free-speech advocacy groups at glamorous venues such as the annual convention of the American Booksellers Association. “Barbara was like a bad girl from the Shangri-Las,” the novelist Amy Tan told me, recalling the outrageous outfits she and the other Remainderettes wore. Stephen King, a guitarist and sometime vocalist for the Remainders, described Kingsolver as “gorgeous and dryly funny,” adding, “I can remember her once saying, ‘I’m back here trapped in triplet hell.’ Talking about that rock beat, you know.”
Hopp is a drummer and guitarist, and he and Kingsolver have played music together from the beginning. “Ours is an egalitarian marriage,” Kingsolver explains while giving me a tour of their curing barn, which the chickens and guineas call home, and where practically all the other open space is taken up by this year’s garlic, onion, and shallot crop, drying on a rack almost the size of the Reflecting Pool, though already significantly less green. “He’s so supportive—the extrovert to my introvert,” she says. Hopp is also the first reader of her drafts and, at least during my visit, the baker of bread, maker of salads, brewer of coffee, checker of weather, and acquirer of U.S.D.A. land-use data on their farm when I ask about its acreage. No one is more surprised than Kingsolver by how happy she is living in Appalachia and being someone’s wife, though her husband is likelier to be called Mr. Kingsolver than she is Mrs. Hopp.
When “Animal, Vegetable, Miracle” came out, in 2007, some quipped that Kingsolver had always been trying to make her readers eat their vegetables. It’s difficult to summarize or even catalogue all the issues she has tackled in her work. An abridged list would include the complexities of tribal law, in “Pigs in Heaven”; the sanctuary movement, in “Animal Dreams”; censorship and artistic freedom, in “The Lacuna,” her 2009 novel about Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo, and the House Un-American Activities Committee; climate change and religious fundamentalism, in “Flight Behavior,” from 2012; and the kitchen sink, in “Unsheltered,” from 2018, which takes on evolution, poverty, racism, globalization, higher education, miscarriage, utopias, dystopias, and nearly everything else that was plaguing and polarizing America circa both 1875 and 2015. The critic Dwight Garner called the last “dead on arrival” in the
Times
, diagnosing a fault similar to one that had split readers of “The Lacuna”—a feeling that the novels were really each two distinct books, with a superior story crowded out by a lesser one.
“There was always a condescension toward Barbara and her work from literary circles,” Sam Stoloff, who took over Frances Goldin’s agency when Goldin died, told me when I asked about Kingsolver’s reception. “Barbara’s theory is always a prejudice against rural people, but I think there’s more to it than that. She straddles the line between commercial and literary fiction, and part of the condescension is people feeling she’s too popular. I also think it has to do with wearing her politics on her sleeve.”
Kingsolver has never lived in N.Y.C. and doesn’t have an M.F.A., and she says she doesn’t feel beholden to what either urbane readers or workshop leaders think a novel should or shouldn’t do. “I never wanted to be one of the cool kids,” she tells me, and, despite a keen awareness of the critical conversation about her work, her way of defending herself has been to make more of it. She delights in finding the right metaphor (relationships that “harden like arteries,” a pregnant woman who feels like “a universe with ankles”) and deploying aphorisms (“The wonder is that you could start life with nothing, end with nothing, and lose so much in between”) in just the appropriate tone and register for her wildly variable casts, which range from farmers, mechanics, and entomologists to fictional mid-century novelists. She has written in the first person, the third person, and an omniscient no person; she has written allegories, books within books, and collages of reportage real and imagined, plus epistolary novels, sestinas, and sonnets.
Kingsolver says that writing a poem is like “riding a unicycle, and the art is in balancing one idea,” but that her novels are more like station wagons that she fills up and then throws some other ideas on top of or tows a few more behind. That maximalist approach was out of synch with American literature for much of her career, but eventually the culture, at least when it came to fiction, veered in the direction her station wagons have always been driving.
For a long time, one of the things Kingsolver could neither let go of nor commit to the page was another kind of D.A.B.: a Damned Appalachia Book. She wanted to write a novel about the opioid epidemic and what it had done to the place she calls home, yet struggled to find a voice for it. In 2018, exhausted after the international tour for “Unsheltered,” she checked herself into Bleak House, a bed-and-breakfast that operates out of Dickens’s summer house in Kent, looking over Viking Bay, where guests are booked into such rooms as the Copperfield Bridal Suite and Little Dorrit’s Classic Double. Kingsolver didn’t get a character, though, she got the author himself: the Charles Dickens Room, and its adjoining study, complete with his old writing desk. That’s where she was sitting when, one night, unable to write and on the verge of sleep, she heard the ghost of Dickens say, “Let the child speak.”
Kingsolver still identifies as a scientist; she doesn’t believe in ghosts or talking with dead people, even beloved authors, which made the whole experience particularly bizarre. Perhaps it was a waking dream, she says, or a little glitch in her brain. In any case, she obeyed, conjuring, in the months that followed, one of the few child narrators to elbow their way into the American canon: Damon Fields, a Melungeon boy who becomes known as Demon Copperhead. Born in the caul to a teen-age mother high on pills and passed out on the floor of her trailer, Demon makes the best of an almost entirely unsupervised childhood, digging for sassafras and avoiding snakes, playing Nintendo Duck Hunt and wishing to be Wolverine. Next door is his best friend, Matt Peggot, a.k.a. Maggot. Everyone in this novel has a nickname—Fast Forward, Humvee, Hammerhead, Extra Eye, Baggy Eyes, U-Haul, Creaky, Swap-Out—partly because comedy is one of the only coins in this impoverished realm, but also because no one ever leaves or leaves behind their reputation. “Here,” Demon says, “all we can ever be is everything we’ve been.”
Plenty of novelists swear by Word, Scrivener, or Google Docs, but Kingsolver used an Excel spreadsheet to outline every chapter of “David Copperfield,” then marched Demon through a parallel plot. Somehow, the result doesn’t feel formulaic; it’s fierce and feral and, most improbably, fully original. Take the paragraph below, from soon after Kingsolver explains, in breath-catching detail, how Maggot’s mother ended up in Goochland prison for almost “Lorena Bobbiting” the boy’s father, and a few moments before she gives a Zola-like account of bringing in a tobacco crop, complete with the nicotine poisoning that can come with it. This is Demon, on getting to Elk Knob Elementary School from the farm where his case manager has temporarily placed him:
Riding the bus with high-schoolers was where you learned everything: how girls get pregnant, how to watch your back. Given the time we put in, the way-out country kids got the most education. I saw more than one guy fingering his girlfriend on a school bus, or her going down on him. More than one face slapped by a girl that wanted none of it. A lip or two busted. Once this fierce tiny towheaded girl got so fed up of a big guy calling her Q-tip, she stood on the seat behind him and cracked her Etch a Sketch over his head. Screen side down, the silver shit running down to cover his whole face. Picture Tin Man out of the Oz movie. That girl was going places. Probably she’s the president of something by now. At the least, not pregnant.
The slang, the syntax, the specificity, the sociology, all compressed, black-hole style, onto a school bus—Kingsolver keeps this up for five hundred pages, from Demon’s dashing “First, I got myself born” to an ending too good to spoil. Reading the book is like watching one of those mothers who lift up a car to rescue their child from underneath. Kingsolver wrote “Demon Copperhead,” she says, out of the grief and the anger she feels for what has happened to Appalachia, a colony of sorts within America where one extractive industry after another robbed its natural resources—first timber, then coal, then tobacco—until Purdue Pharma came peddling cures for all the pain those earlier industries had left behind.
Because of her Zip Code, Kingsolver has long been a kind of
MAGA
whisperer, an unofficial Ambassador of Real America. She hopes that that gig ends soon, and dismisses the possibility of Trumpism having a successor, insisting that the President has cultivated a cult of personality, not a lasting political movement. (“He chose a Vice-President with the charisma of a turd,” she adds.) America’s divisions, she says, are not attributable to any one person, and “Demon Copperhead” wasn’t intended to explain why half the country voted for Trump and was about to do so again. It was an elegy for the generation of children being raised by their mawmaws or thrown into foster care because their parents were dead from overdoses or locked away for selling pills, a rebuke of the well-meaning policymakers and nonprofit directors whose arrogance masquerades as helpfulness. It is, finally, an apologia for rural life by someone who came from and willingly returned to it.
Kingsolver’s daughters, Camille and Lily, both live near their mother, and her two grandchildren visit all the time. One of Kingsolver’s favorite local restaurants is a Mexican joint where she enjoys the Asian-pear Martinis and the grandkids enjoy the balloon artist who’s there every Tuesday. Camille’s husband runs Snow’s Fine Meats & Provisions, a butcher shop in Abingdon; while we ate a lunch from there one day, Lily and her husband came by to use the printer. Both daughters contributed to “Animal, Vegetable, Miracle,” and both have continued to collaborate with their mother: Camille’s work as a community mental-health counsellor and her familiarity with the foster system helped inform “Demon Copperhead,” and Lily’s training in science education led to her co-writing the children’s book “Coyote’s Wild Home.”
“I didn’t really expect my girls would be able to come back here after college, but I’m glad they could,” Kingsolver says. “I couldn’t get far enough away from my family.” When her mother died, in 2013, Kingsolver wrote, in a poem, “While we spoke kindly, / mostly, my mother and I did not love one another. / Ever, not even when I was a baby.” It was through reading old correspondence that Kingsolver learned about her mother’s postpartum depression. “For the first twenty-five years of my life, until therapy, I thought it was my fault,” she says. “How could a mother not love her child?” In the poem’s final line, with the last of her mother’s breaths drawn and a “wild stampede” of a storm outside quieted, Kingsolver writes, “Here begins my life as no one’s bad daughter.”
After Dr. Wendell died, in the spring of 2024, Kingsolver finally felt free to write about her origins. “I needed both my parents to be gone before I could write this,” she says of “Partita.” Its narrator, Livia Bohusz, is a small-town girl from Tennessee who learns to play piano at church, practicing endless hours for one recital after another, culminating in a guest appearance with the Knoxville Symphony Orchestra and then a scholarship to the Indiana University School of Music. Her ambitions are fuelled not only by a desire to perfect her talents but by desperation to escape her family: a brother whose suicide torments those who survived him; a mother who terrorizes her, emotionally and physically, for everything, including her musical gifts; a “Cross-to-Bear Methodist” father who is too cowed to protect his daughter or publicly champion her talents. “A child can’t hate her mother without putting the load-bearing walls of the known world at risk,” Livia confides in one early chapter. “I settled for hating her shoes.”
Plenty of people in “Partita” question whether the daughter of a dairy farmer could ever earn her place in the world of Satie and Schubert, and plenty of people who care for Livia don’t understand the universe of meaning she finds in eighty-eight keys. As she taps out Bach with her fingers on the back of a boyfriend’s shoulders one night, he asks her if she’s happy when she’s playing the piano. “I have no idea,” she tells him. “When I’m playing, I’m not me anymore. I go inside the music and disappear in there.”
That boyfriend is Sigurd, the Marxist organizer whose beliefs make Livia question hers. He disrupts her trajectory in other ways as well, and, in true Kingsolverish style, their affair draws a variety of crises down on Livia’s head. Kingsolver knows that it’s a lot to fit in. In one scene, Livia explains to Sigurd, and to us, that a partita “will never be all happy rondos, or all andantes in a minor key. You’ll usually have a prelude, a thrilling allemande, maybe a slow, sexy sarabande—the contrast is the point. The parts are all different, and the artist’s work is to make them all add up to a something that feels whole.”
Kingsolver can play a partita, too, but as much as she’s used her life as inspiration for this novel, she is emphatic about being its author, not its protagonist. “I think it’s similar to acting,” she tells me, “in that actors play all kinds of different characters that they would never be, including murderers. No one says, ‘Is this based on your own mother?’ To inhabit a character, they pull something from inside themselves that helps them understand that character, and that’s exactly how I would put it. I have written as many different kinds of people as Meryl Streep has played and more, and most of them are very different from me.”
So although Livia escapes Appalachia on a music scholarship, as Kingsolver did, and also returns there, she does so chastened, like the heroine of a Nathaniel Hawthorne or a Thomas Hardy novel, not like the world-famous artist Kingsolver has become. But the consolations of art do not depend on achievement, and that might be Kingsolver’s most direct riposte to her critics. Back home, Livia takes long walks with her sister-in-law, Mickie, the latest in a line of truthtelling public-school teachers from Kingsolver’s books. A former literature major, Mickie—or, per the Steele County High School Yearbook, Mrs. Michaela Barnes, A.P. English—finds meaning in pressing Dickens and Longfellow on farm kids, not so that they can become novelists or poets but so that they have a storehouse of beauty to sustain them for the rest of their lives. When a dispirited Livia is wondering what good there is in music, Mickie, like a windup Mary Oliver, tells her, “The point of art is to help you like your life better.”
I ask Kingsolver if she agrees with Mickie, and she says she isn’t sure. This claim about art is the kind of thing that would enrage her detractors, although it’s easy to imagine the credo tattooed on the arms of M.F.A. students and italicized in their bios on TikTok. “I haven’t Updiked,” Kingsolver tells me one day proudly, noting that, although she gets older with every book tour, her audiences seem to stay at least relatively young. Foster kids have written to her about how much they love Demon, new classes of students read about the Price family every semester, and Kingsolver still hears regularly from parents and grandparents who, moved by “Animal, Vegetable, Miracle,” have tried their own version of that book’s experiment, whether on hobby farms or with whatever pots they can plant on their front stoops or fire escapes.
These days, “nice” isn’t the withering critique it once was. The novelist Richard Powers, a friend of Kingsolver’s, told me, “All the qualities that are there in the books are magnified in fact—wisdom wrapped in warmth, commitment to community, wry pragmatism, a reverence for place.” Certainly, her life is like her work in at least one respect: it is far more difficult to dismiss once you’ve actually engaged with it.
During my visit, Kingsolver dumps the leftover water from our drinking glasses into one of her plants before answering a question I’ve asked her about charity. “The whole idea of charity is condescending,” she says. She prefers the category of generosity, because giving in that spirit lacks the coercive expectations of charity, the implicit hope that the recipient will become more like the donor. After Kingsolver’s advances grew large enough to support her family, she began passing along her royalties: one novel endowed the Bellwether Prize, which offered twenty-five thousand dollars and a publishing contract for socially engaged works of fiction; one of the essay collections contributes to the Environmental Defense Fund, Habitat for Humanity, and Heifer International; another novel became the engine for a new medical scholarship for Congolese students, named in memory of her father.
For fifteen years, Hopp ran Harvest Table, a restaurant in Meadowview serving food and selling goods sourced from a few hundred local farmers and craftspeople. It made no money, but embodied the principles he and Kingsolver had articulated in “Animal, Vegetable, Miracle,” serving grits made from Appalachian dent corn and burgers that came from nearby beef herds. Hopp closed Harvest Table in 2022 and Kingsolver sunsetted the Bellwether Prize in 2023, not because they gave up on their convictions, she says, but because they were becoming so widely shared: there are more locavores than ever, and the types of books the Bellwether championed (Jamila Minnicks’s “Moonrise Over New Jessup,” Hillary Jordan’s “Mudbound,” Lisa Ko’s “The Leavers”) no longer need as much help getting published.
After “Demon Copperhead” came out, Kingsolver convened some of the social workers and medical professionals who had helped her while she was researching the book by sharing their experiences of providing addiction and recovery care. Many came from Lee County, which is both where the book is set and one of the counties most ravaged by the opioid epidemic. Over breakfast at Shoney’s, she asked what she should do with her avalanche of royalties. To a person, they told her that what the region most needed was a recovery house for women—something small enough to let its residents feel like family and unhurried enough that they could really get back on their feet, whether they came from prison or the streets. Kingsolver and Hopp opened one: Higher Ground Women’s Recovery Residence, which, so far, has served more than a dozen women in Pennington Gap, Virginia, offering sober housing, education, and support for up to two years. When the women living in “The House That Demon Built” needed more opportunities for employment, Kingsolver and Hopp donated funds to buy the property next door, which will soon become Second Chances Thrift Store.
“Attention and money just feel like things you have to hold a mirror up to, directing them somewhere else,” Kingsolver tells me. “I guess partly I don’t want to be the tall weed that gets cut, and, partly because of my raising, I just don’t want to get too full of myself.” We’re cooling off from today’s walk in the woods, resting for a while in the oversized Arts and Crafts-style chairs in her sitting room, opposite the piano, with some of the music mentioned in “Partita” still on the rack. The chair Kingsolver has chosen is the one where she knits almost daily, using the wool of her own sheep, seventy-five pounds or so of which she and Hopp harvest every year, then take to a solar-powered mill where it’s spun into yarn.
Kingsolver picks up the sweater she’s in the thick of to show me her progress. But I’m distracted by what’s behind her: a broken window, stretching almost from floor to ceiling, the glass thoroughly fractured yet refusing to come apart, a dense spiderweb of cracks with the blur of her terraced vegetable garden behind it. “I forgot you’re looking at me with the backdrop of the shatter,” she says. Someone would be coming by soon to see about replacing the window, but in the meantime, ever since Hopp cracked it by kicking up a rock with his weed trimmer, Kingsolver has studied its brokenness, taping both sides to keep the glass together, admiring how it scatters the sunlight.
She turns back to look at it in the middle of a long answer to a question I’ve asked about reconciling her happiness with the injustices of the world. She ticks off just a few of the day’s news stories—the aftermath of an earthquake in Venezuela, the energy crisis in Cuba, the ongoing catastrophe in Gaza—and observes how easy it is to be overwhelmed by any one of these tragedies, and how easy it is to be distracted from them, too. “We are not wired for this,” she says of the endless scroll of suffering that people confront nowadays. “The machine is not built to handle all this information. There are limits to the human mind, a limit to the number of people the human animal evolved to care for.”
One antidote to this, she insists, is the novel. “Novels draw you into human conflicts the way our brains are wired to experience them—as feelings, and there’s a big difference between information and feeling. We enter into the realities of other people through emotion, not information, and that’s what a great novel does.” The newspaper, the home page, the grid, the feed: “A novel isn’t a few seconds and then on to something else—the hodgepodge of randomness, equating things that are not equivalent. A novel brings you into the one-to-one, the intimacy of human relationships and human conflicts, for hours at a time.”
Kingsolver says, “I’ll keep writing for as long as I can. Until I can’t remember words.” She doesn’t give a hoot about A.I., and she tells me that the same share of people read fiction today as they did in Cervantes’s time, so we should quit worrying about the end of reading. All she can do, she says, is what she’s always done: craft a novel, from page negative one hundred to page zero, then onward to the end. ♦

Israel’s Qatargate Scandal
A Reporter at Large
Israel’s Qatargate Scandal
Did Benjamin Netanyahu’s aides peddle influence to a foreign power?
By Ruth Margalit
September 19, 2026
As a young man, Yisrael Einhorn was a mainstay of Tel Aviv’s underground night life—an ebullient music producer and performer who billed himself as D.J. Cock and went around town costumed as a golden penis. It was fun, and sometimes he made some money, but over time the club life began to wear thin. He found a second career in advertising, then got into politics. In 2017, he founded a strategic-consulting company called Perception and went on to help run five election campaigns for Israel’s Likud Party. He became known for his close ties to the Party’s leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
While Einhorn built his influence in Israeli politics, his company also secured a lucrative foreign client: Qatar, the tiny Gulf emirate that is among the world’s richest countries. In 2022, Qatar was preparing to host the
FIFA
World Cup, and its communication ministry wanted to spread the idea that Qatar was a Jewish-friendly place. (Never mind that even the grade-school textbooks there were rife with antisemitism.) Perception set up a dummy news site and created fake social-media accounts highlighting the tournament’s amenities, which included kosher food in stadiums. After the games were over, Qatar still found the relationship with Perception valuable: it continued sending payments of forty-five thousand dollars a month through a third-party company.
In December, 2023, Einhorn went to the Ritz in London to discuss a new opportunity. His host was Jay Footlik, another ex-performer who’d had a propitious second career. Footlik grew up an aspiring actor in Skokie, Illinois, and as a young man he landed bit parts in such films as “Teen Wolf” and “Iron Eagle.” Later on, he, too, turned to politics: he worked on a campaign for Bill Clinton and served as a Middle East adviser to John Kerry. Since 2019, Footlik had been a registered lobbyist for Qatar; his company, Third Circle, was paid half a million dollars a year to enhance the emirate’s reputation among the D.C. élite.
At the Ritz, Footlik told Einhorn about Qatar’s P.R. objective. It wanted to be known as a peacemaker in the region. Both men knew that this would require a radical change in Israeli public opinion. It had been only two months since Hamas militants swept into Israel, killing some twelve hundred people and touching off a vicious assault on Gaza. Israelis, freshly traumatized, viewed Qatar as their enemy’s patron.
Since 2018, Qatar had been transferring as much as thirty million dollars a month to Gaza. The money was nominally to pay civil servants and prop up infrastructure in a territory sequestered by an Israeli blockade, but many observers agreed that Hamas diverted a significant sum to its military wing. “The Qatari grant is the main artery of the Hamas movement,” a Hamas leader told Qatar’s foreign minister in 2019, according to papers later seized by Israel. The October 7th attacks revealed what Qatar’s money had helped buy: Hamas forces assembled in a vast system of tunnels outfitted with ventilation systems, surveillance cameras, and communications networks; they emerged wearing body cameras and carrying antitank missiles.
When Footlik and Einhorn met in London, the war in Gaza had been intensifying. Strikes by the Israel Defense Forces had killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, while Hamas continued to hold more than a hundred Israeli hostages. Qatar wanted to intervene. The emirate had recently negotiated a ceasefire between the two sides, and, though the deal collapsed after a week, the Qataris thought that they could broker a more comprehensive agreement—as long as Israel and the U.S. accepted them as mediators.
Footlik and Einhorn began to plot a campaign to transform Qatar’s reputation. In the coming months, they are alleged to have worked with two aides in Netanyahu’s office on a scheme for which they were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars. The aides arranged press junkets, invented sources, and planted stories that brazenly inverted popular views. Hamas leaders were being sheltered in Qatar—but only at the insistence of Israel and the United States. Egypt was Israel’s longtime peace partner—but it couldn’t be trusted to handle the negotiations. As the stories gained currency, Einhorn wrote in a celebratory text that they were “giving birth to reality.”
From Qatar’s perspective, the campaign was a success: the Qataris became crucial players in peace talks over Gaza. Within Israel, though, it has become the center of a nearly unprecedented scandal—a legal case, now known as Qatargate, that involves a sweeping police investigation and potential indictments of several members of Netanyahu’s innermost circle. The government of Qatar rejects the allegations as “journalistic propaganda.” Netanyahu, with characteristic defiance, has dismissed the claims as a “bluff.” But, of all the corruption accusations that have plagued him over the years—taking gifts from business leaders, exchanging favors for friendly news coverage—the charge that his aides doubled as influence agents for Qatar may be the most politically damaging. Naftali Bennett, a former Prime Minister who is challenging Netanyahu in the upcoming election, has called it the “most serious act of treason” in the country’s history.
Along Israeli highways, a crowdsourced campaign has erected billboards to keep the scandal in view, with messages like “Qatar Funded the Massacre and Netanyahu’s Office.” When I stopped next to one such billboard in Tel Aviv recently, a driver pulled up in a Mercedes, rolled down his window, and spat on the ground in disgust.
The billboard also displayed photographs of the alleged conspirators. Among them was Eli Feldstein, a thirtysomething with a shaved head, a close-cropped beard, and a look of searching concern. Feldstein’s name had come up when Einhorn and Footlik were looking for someone with sufficient credibility to spread their pro-Qatar messages to journalists. Einhorn had a list of candidates, which included a number of seasoned media specialists—and also Feldstein, who worked as a military-affairs spokesperson for Netanyahu.
Feldstein was relatively young, and he didn’t speak English, but he had already distinguished himself as what Einhorn called a “master communicator.” He grew up in the ultra-Orthodox city of Bnei Brak and served for a decade as a media operative, working for a time in the chaotic office of Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s far-right national-security minister. There, he began ingratiating himself with the Prime Minister’s aides. On October 7th, as Hamas militants ravaged communities along Israel’s southern border, he was already managing optics from afar. Feldstein recommended that Netanyahu appear with “no suit, no tie, combat mode,” and demanded that the military spokesman’s office release photos of “soldiers on the ground, with helicopters.” When the photos failed to materialize quickly enough, he griped that members of the unit were “scumbags.”
Feldstein started work in Netanyahu’s office just four days after the attacks. The surroundings weren’t glamorous. In an atmosphere of national panic, the Prime Minister was running most of his operations out of a squat nineteen-fifties building near “the Pit”—the I.D.F.’s underground command center. But, Feldstein said when I met him recently near Tel Aviv, “I was thrilled to work there. I really wanted to prove myself.”
From his first day on the job, he was called on to defend the Prime Minister, Feldstein told me. As he was getting settled, Netanyahu walked by, pointed at a television mounted on his office wall, and asked if reporters were “still talking about responsibility”—his refusal to apologize for the military and intelligence failures that led to the attacks. Feldstein replied that they were. Netanyahu, he says, told him to “do something about it.”
Feldstein’s immediate boss was Netanyahu’s closest strategic adviser, Jonatan Urich. For years, Urich had been a constant presence at the Prime Minister’s side: a bearish man with black-rimmed glasses and an inscrutable smile. Feldstein described him as “Netanyahu’s first phone call in the morning and last phone call before bed.”
Urich had started off in the military press office, where he built a reputation as a social-media whiz. In 2015, he joined Netanyahu’s election campaign and helped secure an unlikely victory. “Jonatan turned negative campaigning into art,” a former senior adviser to Netanyahu told me. “He enjoys watching the other side suffer—
really
enjoys it.” He was fiercely loyal to the Prime Minister. When Urich was young, his father suffered a disabling stroke; Netanyahu became a father figure to him. “I would let him perform open-heart surgery on me,” Urich once said.
During his years working for Netanyahu, Urich also had what amounted to a side hustle, working for Perception. He was able to discreetly hold both jobs because he was paid for his government work as a consultant for Likud. At the same time, he received forty per cent of Perception’s payments from Qatar, through a third-party company founded by former Israeli security officials. (Urich denies any wrongdoing, saying, “I am being targeted because I advise the Prime Minister.” He has claimed that he “never received money on behalf of Qatar in Israel.” Although he doesn’t deny that Qatar paid him eighteen thousand dollars a month through most of 2024, he argues that he was being compensated for the World Cup campaign.)
After a few months in Netanyahu’s office, Feldstein, too, effectively went on Perception’s payroll. In his telling, it was almost accidental. He was hoping for a promotion and a higher salary, but he failed a security clearance because he had previously used drugs. Urich offered him a workaround, Feldstein said: he could receive an increased salary through an intermediary. That intermediary worked with Footlik. (Footlik says he has never sought to hire anyone who worked for the Israeli government, and that the funds he provided were for an effort to secure the release of the hostages. Feldstein argues that he never knew he was working for Qatar—though he and Einhorn referred in text exchanges to the “patients” and the “friends,” with the context clearly indicating Qatar.)
Footlik allegedly oversaw the Qatar influence campaign from outside, providing funds and giving strategic advice. Einhorn and Urich orchestrated the operation. Feldstein was their foot soldier, working to get news stories written and noticed. The campaign began in late April, 2024, and soon afterward Feldstein sent Einhorn two stories that he had helped place. In one, “senior Israeli officials” were quoted as saying, “No other country is capable of bringing about a deal except Qatar.” In the other, an Israeli reporter described Turkey as “Hamas’s big brother” and contrasted it unfavorably with Qatar.
Footlik sent Feldstein a text describing his patrons’ reaction: “Eli you are killing it. Really good.”
Feldstein forwarded it to Urich, with a self-congratulatory note. “Bingo,” he wrote. “They’re in shock.”
“They’re flipping out,” Urich replied.
Qatar was historically a land rich in pearls and oil. Yet, for decades after it gained independence from Britain, in 1971, it was regarded in the West as little more than an extension of Saudi Arabia, its vastly larger neighbor. Then, in 1995, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani took control of the country, deposing his father while he was away in Switzerland. Sheikh Hamad had lofty ambitions, and his wife Sheikha Moza bint Nasser had even loftier ones: they wanted their country to be not just independent but eminent. With only three hundred and fifty thousand citizens, Qatar lacked the manpower to establish physical dominance in the region. It barely had an army. Instead, the Sheikh and Sheikha pursued a strategy of self-defense through economic influence and self-promotion.
In 1996, Hamad founded Al Jazeera, a news network that gave the emirate enormous cultural influence throughout the region. Unlike other Arab media, the network aired interviews with Israelis and Iranians, and gave voice to dissidents across the Middle East. Before long, its broadcasts had “entered every household in Arab society,” Shaul Yanai, an Israeli historian of the Persian Gulf states, said. Ten years after its founding, three out of four Arabs identified Al Jazeera as a primary news source. Tamir Pardo, a former director of Israel’s intelligence agency Mossad, told me that Qatar became “not a state with Al Jazeera, but Al Jazeera with a state.”
The network also provided a vehicle for Qatar to project an ideological vision that was deeply at odds with Israel. Al Jazeera gave a prime-time slot to Yusuf al-Qaradawi, who was widely regarded as the spiritual leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, an influential Islamist group with offshoots around the world—including Hamas. Qaradawi defended Palestinian suicide bombings of Israeli civilians as a legitimate form of resistance.
The emirate’s stance toward Israel is bound up with a broader strategic concern: restraining Saudi Arabia’s power. For years, the Saudis have backed rival members of Hamad’s family, hoping to replace the ruling Emir and bring Qatar back under Saudi influence. At times, they also discussed a deal with the U.S., in which they would normalize relations with Israel in exchange for arms and the ability to develop nuclear energy—an arrangement that would have made it the dominant power in the region. For the Qataris, Yanai said, insuring that Saudi Arabia and Israel do not normalize ties “is existential.”
In 2013, Hamad ceded the throne to his son, Tamim. According to Dennis Ross, a former U.S. envoy to the region, Tamim views the Muslim Brotherhood more instrumentally and less ideologically than his father. But he has opposed normalization with Israel. “Are things
normal
in Israel? No!” he said in 2022. Between the Emir’s resistance, Israel’s harsh treatment of Palestinians, and the influence of figures like Qaradawi, “this has led to a generation for whom Israel is the greatest demon that exists,” Yanai said.
Nevertheless, Qatar treated Israel with what Yanai called “the famous Qatari duality.” In public, it called Israel the “occupation government” and provided aid to Hamas; in private, it maintained business ties and unofficial diplomatic contacts with high-ranking Israeli officials.
Ronit Marzan, a political scientist at the University of Haifa, describes Qatar’s approach to international diplomacy as “lulling empowerment.” In the U.S., for instance, it “buys weapons, invests in companies and in educational institutions. Then, slowly, the other state actor becomes addicted to the money.” Qatar shares the world’s largest natural-gas field with Iran, but has also backed the opposition to Iran’s allies in the Syrian government. It funds the Lebanese Army, but has also allegedly propped up Hezbollah. It hosts the largest U.S. military base in the Middle East, but also backed Islamist factions in Egypt and Libya. It gave a Boeing 747 to Turkey’s President, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and another to President Donald Trump. Ross told me, “The Qatari approach to the outside is to say, ‘The way we punch above our weight is by being uniquely situated to talk to everyone.’ ”
Perception held a similarly transactional view of power. By 2024, the firm was so entrenched in Netanyahu’s office that it was able to quietly dispatch the Prime Minister’s closest advisers to assist right-wing political candidates in Eastern Europe. Feldstein spent ten days on a campaign for a Perception client in Georgia. Netanyahu’s family spokesperson led one in Romania. Einhorn connected another senior adviser to a campaign that an acquaintance was running in Kosovo.
Einhorn himself worked on a campaign for Aleksandar Vučić, the President of Serbia. He told officials there that he had assisted the Israeli government with sensitive security matters. During the war in Gaza, he said, a shipment of arms to Israel had been held up in Eastern Europe, and he helped secure its release by arranging a phone call between Netanyahu and the Prime Minister of Montenegro. “I put myself on mute, and the two of them talked,” he said.
Feldstein never heard Netanyahu ask why his advisers were absent or where they were. (When the Qatargate story emerged later, this laissez-faire attitude outraged security veterans. “How can it be that the Prime Minister doesn’t know that his people are working for another government?” Pardo, the former head of Mossad, said. “And how come, once he learns it, he doesn’t tell them, ‘Guys, look me in the eye—you’re not coming anywhere near Jerusalem. As far as I’m concerned, you’ve betrayed me.’ ”)
In Einhorn’s view, it was natural that Netanyahu’s consultants were in demand around the world: they were shrewd campaign strategists and proven winners. Others concluded that the advisers were useful mostly for their proximity to Netanyahu. “These guys don’t know how to run a campaign for the State of Israel,” the former senior adviser to Netanyahu said. “They know how to be Bibi’s right hand.” In the lead-up to the World Cup, Qatar retained at least four of the world’s top public-relations firms. It didn’t need Perception—a company so small that it had no salaried employees. “It’s clear as day that they were approached because of their access to Netanyahu,” Aron Shaviv, a political strategist who oversaw Likud’s 2015 campaign, said. “And Qatar continued to keep them on retainer because now it had an asset.”
In May, 2024, I.D.F. troops pushed into the town of Rafah, on the Egyptian border, where more than a million displaced Gazans had evacuated on Israel’s orders and were now sheltering in makeshift tents. In the course of three weeks, Israeli soldiers destroyed much of the area, razing schools and mosques and commandeering buildings for use as military posts. The assault inspired worldwide outrage; the International Court of Justice demanded an immediate halt.
As the Israeli media focussed intently on the incursion, Einhorn grew restless about the progress of the pro-Qatar campaign. On May 24th, he asked Feldstein, “Anything for today?” There wasn’t. The previous night, the I.D.F. had retrieved the remains of three hostages from the sprawling Jabalia refugee camp. “Everyone is busy with recovering the bodies,” Feldstein replied, in messages published by Israel’s
i24 News
. But he said that he was happy to talk if Einhorn had “any ideas.”
Two minutes later, Einhorn wrote back to suggest that Feldstein give a briefing to journalists. Egypt had been deeply involved in talks over a ceasefire and a hostage-release deal. But Einhorn wanted to spread the message that “Egypt can no longer be trusted. From now on, only Qatar will lead the negotiations.” The quote should be attributed to “senior U.S. officials” in talks “behind closed doors,” he wrote.
That evening, during the prime-time news on Channel 12, a military reporter named Nir Dvori relayed the story nearly word for word. The network’s news anchor was astonished. “The
Americans
are saying this?” he asked.
“The Americans!” Dvori repeated.
This wasn’t the only time that the men apparently attributed made-up briefings to U.S. officials. The Biden Administration wasn’t surprised. “The assumption was that everyone was spinning everyone,” a former senior U.S. official in the region told me. But the Egyptians were furious. Mohamed Abu Hamed, an influential former lawmaker, wrote online later, “I haven’t seen anything dirtier than an Arab country paying money to cast doubt on the role played by another Arab country and create a fake role for itself.” (Qatar denied any effort to improperly influence Israeli officials. A Qatari spokesman said, “Put simply, if Qatar had somehow ‘infiltrated’ the Israeli government, it would have been a very bad investment.”)
After a blitz of pro-Qatar messaging, Israel’s Ambassador to the U.S. told Jewish groups, with no apparent evidence, that Egypt was violating its peace agreement with Israel. Feldstein and Einhorn seemed unconcerned about disrupting relations with Egypt, Israel’s most important peace partner in the region. “We’ve managed to really piss them off,” Feldstein texted at one point.
Days after planting the story on Channel 12, Einhorn prodded Feldstein again. “We’ve been too quiet,” he wrote. “Tomorrow we have to fire.” They came up with another story, saying that Qatar was growing disillusioned with Hamas. This wasn’t true—in fact, Qatar had declined to formally expel Hamas leaders from Doha, despite requests from American officials. But Feldstein devised an imaginary context: “a meeting held yesterday in Doha between the Qatari prime minister, the Egyptian intelligence chief, and senior Hamas officials.” That story, too, was picked up by Channel 12. “It’s a bombshell,” Feldstein wrote afterward. “Ballistic,” Einhorn replied.
The campaign seemed fuelled by such cheerful cynicism. In messages, Urich hailed Feldstein as the “No. 1 spinner.” In the course of several months, Feldstein told me, “there were dozens of reports in Qatar’s favor.” Einhorn flew the editor of the Jerusalem
Post
to Doha; he later produced two reports that seemed lifted straight from Qatari talking points. Footlik also paid tens of thousands of dollars to a columnist for
Haaretz
. (The columnist subsequently resigned but denies wrongdoing.)
Not every journalist was duped. One responded to a pitch from Feldstein, “Do you work for the Qataris?!” (Feldstein: “Hahaha.”) Yet many appeared eager to take Feldstein’s shifting attributions at face value. Dvori, the Channel 12 reporter, later wrote online that he had no reason to doubt that Feldstein’s briefings were given “on behalf of the Prime Minister.” At times, he said, Feldstein even put Netanyahu on the phone. “It never occurred to me that Netanyahu’s people were serving Qatar for a fee,” he wrote.
If Netanyahu wondered why pro- Qatar narratives kept surfacing in stories that originated from his office, he gave no sign of it. In Feldstein’s view, “that is proof that the messages were the Prime Minister’s messages. No one was rebelling in real time.”
Netanyahu’s position on Qatar had long confounded those who worked with him, according to a former senior Israeli defense official. Many of his decisions orbited around Gaza. In 2007, Hamas seized control of the Strip, and Israel imposed a punishing blockade. Five years later, Sheikh Hamad effectively broke the siege by visiting Gaza and pledging more than four hundred million dollars to reconstruction efforts there. Israel condemned the visit, but Netanyahu didn’t intervene.
Although Netanyahu publicly described Hamas as an enemy, he was privately intent on keeping it strong. Hamas competed for influence with the Palestinian Authority—the civil government that runs parts of the West Bank—which Netanyahu did not want to take control of Gaza. He reasoned that, as long as Hamas was in power, Palestinians would remain divided, and Israel would face less pressure to negotiate a land-for-peace deal. As Ehud Olmert, a former Israeli Prime Minister, put it, Netanyahu’s policy was “very clearly that Hamas was an asset and the P.A. was a liability.”
His instrumental approach to Hamas extended to Qatar, too. In 2017, a dozen Muslim-majority countries severed ties with the emirate, accusing it of sponsoring terror and fomenting chaos around the world. In the U.S., the House took up a bill to impose sanctions on Qatar. “For us, this was a golden opportunity” to cut off Qatar’s influence in Gaza, Roni Alsheikh, who served as deputy director of the Shin Bet security agency and as head of the Israeli police, said. Instead, a Netanyahu military adviser wrote a letter stating that “Qatar has not delivered weapons to Hamas” and was engaging solely in humanitarian work in Gaza. A pro-Qatar lobbying group sent the letter to members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Soon afterward, the bill was abandoned.
The following year, a roadside bomb targeted the Palestinian Authority’s Prime Minister as his convoy was driving in Gaza. Mahmoud Abbas, the President of the P.A., was enraged. He accused Hamas of an assassination attempt and slashed economic lifelines to Gaza. The result was surging unemployment, civil unrest, and mayhem on the border.
With Hamas squeezed, Netanyahu asked the Qataris to commit to official monthly payments to Gaza. He explained it as a strategy of buying stability: “I do what I can to restore peace to the southern communities.” But many defense officials considered it unconscionable to provide funds that Hamas could siphon off. Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman resigned in protest over the handling of Hamas. Even Netanyahu eventually acknowledged that Hamas leaders “take all the money that comes in from international support—and there’s quite a bit of it—and they put it into turning tunnels into a terror machine.” Yet he did not halt the transfers. Pardo, the former director of Mossad, described it to me as “a knife stab in Israel’s national security.”
Rumors began to spread that Netanyahu had covert links with Qatar. “There were definitely indications that there was a complex relationship there, including the idea that part of how Hamas was surviving was these understandings between Netanyahu and Qatar,” Ben Rhodes, a foreign-policy adviser under Barack Obama, told me.
On October 7th, the strategy of quietly propping up Hamas collapsed. In Israel, Netanyahu seemed finished politically; surely he couldn’t survive the biggest security failure in the country’s history. Yet, that morning, the first foreign leader he called, before he even gave a statement to the public, was the Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte, who has close ties to Qatar.
He also relied on his confidant Yossi Cohen, a former Mossad director with his own links to Qatar. Soon after the attacks, Cohen flew to Doha on a private plane, bypassing official Mossad channels. The agency’s new director issued an unusually harsh public rebuke. But Netanyahu defended his adviser, saying in a statement, “Cohen had initiated a meeting with an Arab leader with the approval of the prime minister.”
The following August, six Israeli hostages were executed by Hamas in a tunnel in Rafah, after more than three hundred days in captivity. Israelis poured into the streets, outraged that Netanyahu had squandered opportunities to reach a deal that might have saved them. Protests spilled onto the Jerusalem-Tel Aviv highway and lasted for days, representing a profound threat to the Israeli government.
Netanyahu grew nervous. Feldstein told me that he thought the Prime Minister should address the public immediately, but he was rebuffed. Then he had another idea to undercut the protests. An acquaintance from his father’s synagogue had told him about a Hamas document that he’d seen during his reserve service in military intelligence. The document, which was highly classified and written in Arabic, suggested that Hamas was planning to exploit the hostage families’ protests to fracture Israeli society. Feldstein says that he approached Netanyahu after a press conference and whispered to him about the document, saying that he and Urich were working on getting it out. The Prime Minister nodded in approval. (Netanyahu has denied having any knowledge of the document.)
There was an obstacle: the military censor barred publishing the memo, because it compromised Israeli intelligence. But Urich had a solution, Feldstein said. He told Feldstein to ask Einhorn to leak it to a foreign outlet, so that the Israeli media could legally report on the stories published abroad.
On September 6, 2024, the German tabloid
Bild
