published a story on the Hamas document. The article’s description of the memo was misleading: Though the headline suggested that it was linked to the Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, it was apparently written by mid-level officials. And though
Bild
presented the document as evidence of Hamas’s intransigence, it skipped over language showing that its leaders were willing to compromise. Still, in a Cabinet meeting two days later, Netanyahu referred to the story as proof that the protests were playing into Hamas’s hands. Urich texted Feldstein, “The boss is happy.”
The Qataris had reasons to be happy, too. Trump had placed Qatar at the center of a temporary ceasefire and hostage-release deal that went into effect in January, 2025. Netanyahu pulled out of the agreement that March, but Qatar remained the principal venue for indirect negotiations between Israel and Hamas. In October, a road-map peace deal was signed, and Trump thanked the Qataris, saying that they had been a “very big factor.”
Other negotiators were frustrated. Yair Barak, an Israeli official who served on the negotiating team, told Israel’s public broadcaster that Qatar was so biased in the talks that his peers referred to it as “Hamas’s representative.” Jonathan Schanzer, the executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, described the Qataris as both “the arsonists and the firefighters.” But Doha had succeeded in establishing itself as an indispensable player in the region’s politics. After October 7th, Qatar was vilified in Israel, but, as Uri Tuval, who has covered Qatargate extensively for the liberal magazine Telem, said, “Fast-forward three years—Qatar now has a foothold in the Mediterranean.”
Two months after
Bild
published the secret document, Feldstein was jolted awake at four-forty-five in the morning by pounding on his door. “Police!” voices shouted. Feldstein told me that he opened the door in his boxers, shaking so violently that he barely managed to turn the lock. Masked men carrying M16s barged in, handcuffed him, and pinned him to the floor. They seized his phone and laptop, and warned his roommate not to utter a word to anyone. “You’re suspected of harming national security,” they told him.
“I said, ‘I want an attorney,’ ” he recalled. “They said, ‘There is no attorney.’ ” He ultimately spent almost six weeks in detention and seven months under house arrest.
Feldstein’s arrest was kept under a sweeping gag order, for fear that disclosing it would compromise Israeli intelligence, but the
Haaretz
reporter Bar Peleg soon learned of it. Peleg had never before written about the Prime Minister’s inner circle; he spent the early days of the war mostly covering the hostage families. But, as he looked into Feldstein, a tip led him to a Google Doc that had two listed authors: Jonatan Urich and Yisrael Einhorn. Written in 2022, it described Perception’s pitch for Qatar’s World Cup campaign. “There was even a suggestion that Qatar host a soccer friendly between Israeli and Palestinian youths,” Peleg told me, with a laugh.
In November, 2024, Peleg exposed the connection between Netanyahu’s advisers and the Qataris. The police were reluctant to investigate, he says; a law- enforcement source had told him that they were “afraid of touching the Prime Minister’s office.” But the Shin Bet began gathering evidence, and, in February, 2025, a criminal investigation was launched. The next month, Feldstein, still on house arrest, was arrested again, as was Urich, on suspicion of contact with a foreign agent, bribery, fraud, breach of trust, and money laundering.
The revelations prompted renewed scrutiny of Israel’s relationship with Doha. Some observers speculated that, if Netanyahu’s closest aides were benefitting from Qatar, maybe he was, too. Among those who made accusations were several officials who had served at the highest levels of Israel’s security establishment. One of them, Udi Levi, told me recently, “I will say it plainly: I claim that the Prime Minister received money from Qatar.”
Between 2001 and 2016, Levi headed a division of Mossad that tracked terror-financing networks around the world. He worked closely with Netanyahu, and also voted for him, but has since become an impassioned, nearly obsessive critic. He is sixty-three, with the burly build of a former wrestler and the injuries to match. When I saw him, a bad back made him wince every few steps.
Levi’s suspicions began in April, 2021, when an unusual news alert appeared on his phone. The article was titled “Qatar Connection,” and Levi, a self-described “addict” of news about Qatari intrigue, clicked on it instantly. The report was from a French outlet called
Blast
, which publishes ambitious investigations in overheated prose. It included images of four documents from a decade earlier; three were on the letterhead of the Qatari finance ministry. They said, in Arabic, that millions of euros had been sent to prominent figures in France, including Bernard-Henri Lévy, a public intellectual who often commented on Middle Eastern politics, and Carla Bruni, the President’s wife. Millions more were supposedly earmarked for Laurent Platini, the son of the president of the European Football Association—and were to be paid around the time that
FIFA
announced that Qatar had been chosen to host the World Cup. (Both Bruni and Platini deny receiving any payments. Lévy sued for defamation, calling the documents fake, but lost his case and a subsequent appeal; a French court noted, “The journalists acted with sufficient caution and factual basis.”)
The reporters, Bernard Nicolas and Thierry Gadault, believed that the files had been hacked by Project Raven, a long-running surveillance operation conducted by Emirati intelligence. Their report was the first in a series of articles that accused Qatar of making payoffs to more than a dozen figures. Udi Levi followed the installments with growing interest. He had recently been hired as a consultant for families of Syrian victims of terrorism, who were suing a Qatari bank in the U.K. for sponsoring the terror group Jabhat al-Nusra. But half of the claimants dropped their suit, and Levi maintained that they were being threatened or paid off. (The defendants denied any interference.) “I was caught up in a crazy cycle of Qatari bribery neutralizing the prosecution,” Levi told me. The alleged payoffs he was reading about in
Blast
“fit like a glove.”
That October,
Blast
published a piece suggesting that, in 2012, Qatar’s Prime Minister had ordered his finance minister to provide “financial-aid packages” to two Israeli politicians. Fifteen million dollars were to be paid to “Mr. Benjamin Netanyahu, Chairman of Likud.” Five million dollars were to go to Avigdor Lieberman, who headed the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu Party. The two men ran on a joint ticket that year. The money, the order said, was for the “upcoming election campaign.” A subsequent letter, bearing the signature of the head of the Qatar Central Bank, seemed to confirm the transfer. (Both men have denied receiving funds from Qatar.)
As Levi examined the documents, he says, “a red light went on in my head.” The timing of the payments corresponded with unusual shifts in Netanyahu’s policies. The transfer from 2012 came a few days before Israel announced the end of a military operation in Gaza; not long after, Netanyahu effectively acquiesced to Sheikh Hamad’s visit.
Blast
also published documents detailing the alleged transfer of an additional fifty million dollars to Netanyahu in 2018. A letter from Qatar’s finance minister to the Emir’s office noted that the money “will be delivered in cash to the State Security Service.” This order came ten days before Qatar’s first cash transfer to Gaza.
Levi wondered whether the alleged payments had been reported elsewhere. He discovered that, two years earlier, the popular Egyptian newspaper
Youm7
had run a brief article. Citing “knowledgeable Arab sources,” it described a twenty- million-dollar transfer from Qatar to Likud for a campaign in 2012 and another fifty million dollars six years later—the same amounts in the
Blast
files.
Levi knew that the reports could easily have been based on forged documents. There was no shortage of state actors with an interest in discrediting Qatar and Netanyahu; it could have been the Egyptians, or the Emiratis, or Iran. Still skeptical, he conducted a forensic examination of the files. The Qatari names had the correct honorifics and salutations, he told me; the signatures matched the originals, though some looked digital. Perhaps most interestingly, the documents bore serial numbers. Levi later gained access to a cache of Qatari documents from roughly the same period, which Syrian hackers had taken from the offices of the Sheikh, among others. The serial numbers on those documents appeared to align with the sequence of the
Blast
files, forming a consistent chronological progression. “Everything seemed to match,” Levi recalls thinking.
The Qatari government adamantly denies making any payments. “The pattern is familiar: fake official documents are circulated to the media to support sensational claims about Qatar, only to fall apart when subjected to meaningful scrutiny,” the spokesman said. “We have strong evidence that, for several years, various parties, including elements of Israel’s far right, have been involved in circulating fabricated documents through the media in an effort to incriminate Qatar.”
A week after the first
Blast
piece ran, Qatar announced that its former minister of finance, Ali Sherif al-Emadi, had been arrested; he was subsequently sentenced to twenty years in prison for bribery and abuse of power. As news of the
Blast
allegations spread, Levi says, “I expected an earthquake.” For a time, Israeli journalists tried to follow up, but it soon became clear that there would be no conclusive proof of the documents’ authenticity. The files didn’t contain bank-account details, and, even if Qatar had ordered the transfers, there was no evidence that Netanyahu had actually received the money.
Still, some former security officials thought that the claims warranted a serious investigation. “You can’t
not
investigate it,” Roni Alsheikh, the former deputy director of the Shin Bet, told
Telem
. “These are suspicions of the highest level.” Yet there has been no official investigation related to the
Blast
files. Netanyahu dismissed the allegations, and is suing Levi and several other Israelis who have made similar charges. (His attorney has postponed hearings in one case so frequently that a judge finally fined Netanyahu and forced him to settle on a date this December.)
In the immediate aftermath of the October 7th attacks, Levi urged the hostage families to pressure the Israeli government to threaten Qatar with war if their loved ones “were not returned within forty-eight hours.” Instead, he watched with outrage as the Qataris took the lead on negotiations. He was not alone in his alarm. Yigal Carmon, a conservative retired colonel in Israeli military intelligence and the founder of
MEMRI
, a research center that monitors media across the Muslim world, had spent years insisting that Qatar was a sponsor of terrorism. In December, two months after the attacks, he republished the
Blast
files as part of a report warning about Qatar’s expanding influence. (Netanyahu is suing him, too.) When I met Carmon at
MEMRI
’s office in Jerusalem, he gestured at a framed photograph showing a Hamas chief shaking hands with a Qatari Emir. “Hamas is Qatar, Qatar is Hamas,” he said.
Soon after Carmon published the report, he became embroiled in a peculiar fraud. He was introduced to a man named Matthew Cohen, who he was led to believe had C.I.A. connections. In the following months, Cohen arranged for a source to sell Carmon two batches of documents, from Qatar’s finance ministry and Jordan’s anti-fraud authority, that he claimed corroborated the
Blast
files. Carmon raised a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars to purchase the documents, then published them online.
Levi, who has known Carmon for years, says that he called him as soon as he saw the files. “Yigal, are you crazy?” he asked. The documents should have raised immediate suspicion: they lacked the appropriate letterheads and serial numbers associated with those offices. The cache also included a copy of a ten-million-dollar check purportedly written by a company with ties to Netanyahu to a company associated with Hamas—yet a simple Google search showed that the check had the same number as one on an online template.
Levi urged Carmon to take the post down, but the damage had already been done. In July, 2024, the financial newspaper
TheMarker
reported that there was a booming trade in forged documents in Israel. The article mentioned the
Blast
files alongside the Cohen trove, suggesting that all the documents were fake. Matthew Cohen—who has also gone by Jason Goose—played his own part in discrediting the files. He bragged to the press that the documents were forged and that Carmon didn’t care. When I spoke with Cohen recently, he didn’t seem to regret the scam. “The whole concept of espionage is deception,” he told me.
Last April, a similar operation targeted Eliad Shraga, a prominent lawyer associated with Israel’s anti-government protest movement. An ultra-Orthodox private investigator named Avi Lehrer called Shraga and claimed to have bank records showing that Netanyahu and his family held millions of dollars in offshore accounts. Lehrer arranged a meeting to sell him the files—then never showed up. Instead, a recording of their conversation surfaced on Channel 14, a pro-Netanyahu television network. Lehrer later posted the segment on social media, tagging Yair Netanyahu, the Prime Minister’s son.
Lehrer has boasted in private about his connections with the Netanyahu family. Last year, he and Cohen met in Miami. During the meeting, which was first reported by TheMarker, Lehrer said that he had done “favors” for both Yair and his father, and had got work in return. (Yair has disputed this.)
Levi argues that the
Blast
files were deliberately compromised to distract from their contents. “It’s a well-known method—flood the scene with a lot of fake evidence until the entire investigation is contaminated,” he said. Alsheikh, the former Shin Bet deputy director, agreed: “Someone was interested not in strengthening the message but in shutting it down.”
A month after the
Bild
publication, Feldstein had a remarkable encounter with his employers. One night, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, summoned him to a parking lot underneath the I.D.F. headquarters, in Tel Aviv. When Feldstein arrived, around midnight, Braverman got into his car and asked him to surrender his phone to an aide standing outside. With the car secured, Braverman said he’d heard rumors that the I.D.F. had opened an investigation into a document leak. Braverman told Feldstein that he could “shut it down.” (Braverman denies this, and says that he can’t recall whether he met with Feldstein that night.)
It didn’t work. Feldstein was arrested three weeks later, and, in November, 2024, he was indicted for leaking the top-secret document to
Bild
, an offense that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison. Yet investigators have struggled to connect Einhorn and Urich with either the Bild case or Qatargate. A day after Feldstein’s arrest, Urich deleted his phone’s text history. (He said that he had bought a new phone.) Einhorn had relocated with his family to Serbia, and refused to return for questioning.
By this summer, prosecutors had finally added Urich to the Bild indictment and named Einhorn as a suspect in the case. But the progress of the Qatargate investigation remained uncertain. When Ronen Bar, the head of the Shin Bet, sought to expand the probe, Netanyahu moved to fire him. Bar resigned soon afterward, saying that he was being pushed out because of the investigation. (Netanyahu denies this.) The move was “particularly troubling,” Bar wrote in an affidavit, “given the extremely serious suspicions of harm to national security.” To replace Bar, Netanyahu selected a retired major general named David Zini—despite opposition from four former Shin Bet directors and hundreds of employees, who warned that Zini was a Netanyahu ally who would prioritize loyalty over the rule of law.
Israel’s attorney general cautioned that the appointment was mired in conflicts of interest, and insured that the Qatargate investigation would continue. But the investigation was completed months ago, and no indictments have yet been made. The Shin Bet has since circulated an opinion among security officials, suggesting that the conduct of Netanyahu’s aides did not amount to a national-security threat. A law-enforcement source told
Haaretz
that the serious allegations remain unchanged: “The only thing that changed was the person at the top of the Shin Bet.”
In March, Netanyahu cleared his schedule to give public testimony about Qatargate. By all accounts, the aide he was most intent on protecting was Urich. He testified that he didn’t know Urich had been working for Qatar. Even if he had known, he added, “There is nothing wrong with that. Qatar is not an enemy state.” (Six months later, Netanyahu ordered a strike on Doha during a meeting of Hamas leaders, after which Trump forced him to make a public apology to the Qatari Emir.)
Urich is being represented by Netanyahu’s personal attorney, and Likud is reportedly financing his defense. Netanyahu also staged a supportive photo opportunity: on a blustery evening, he embraced Urich outside his office in Jerusalem, and the two men walked away hand in hand, while cameras flashed. By then, Urich had gone back to work for the Prime Minister. He had also signalled a redemptive spiritual conversion. After his arrest, he began sporting a thick beard and a large black kippah associated with the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. He recently wrote on a Chabad site that the late Lubavitcher Rebbe had “delivered a message to me in prison.”
But every day in Israel, it seems, brings fresh accusations against the Prime Minister’s office. Even the right-wing daily
Israel
Hayom
recently ran a front-page story alleging that Urich and the other advisers had passed classified information to Qatar (something they denied). The election, scheduled for October 27th, will be the first one since the Hamas attack and the war that has shattered Israel’s standing in the world. Earlier this year, sixty-one per cent of Israelis described the Qatargate affair as “serious.” Among voters of Netanyahu’s Likud Party, less than a third viewed it that way.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who is Netanyahu’s most serious competitor in the coming election, said he believes that the Prime Minister was aware of his advisers’ connections to Qatar. When a voter asked about Qatargate during a campaign stop in August, he answered, “Netanyahu knows what [Urich] did. Anyone who engaged in criminal activity will pay a very heavy price and, as far as I’m concerned, will sit in prison until their last day.”
Feldstein told me that his time in prison was disillusioning. For the first nine days, he was barred from meeting with an attorney. At one point, guards brought a television into his cell, and Feldstein tuned in to “The Patriots,” a talk show on Channel 14. He watched as the host displayed family photos of the Feldsteins and played a Hebrew song that he loved, one that his parents had requested. “It gave me a lot of spirit,” Feldstein recalled when I met him, in July. “But then I understood that I wasn’t the story for them—Bibi was. It was meant to serve his interests, not mine, and that hurt me a little.”
We were sitting in his attorney’s office on the thirty-sixth floor of a high-rise in the city of Ramat Gan, overlooking the Tel Aviv skyline. Feldstein appeared no different from any other young resident of Tel Aviv. He has a broad, animated face, and wore a T-shirt and jeans; the distinctive black kippah I remembered from photographs was gone. He is a fast talker who stuttered as a child; occasionally, during a three-hour conversation full of recrimination and regret, the stutter returned.
On the fifth day of Feldstein’s detention, Netanyahu’s office issued a terse statement: “No one from the Prime Minister’s office has been arrested or questioned.” In the days that followed, Netanyahu suggested that he barely knew who Feldstein was, and that he’d never worked for the Prime Minister. A few weeks later, as Feldstein’s attorney was going on Israeli television to publicize the case, Netanyahu defended his former aide as an “Israeli patriot, an ardent Zionist.” He later changed course again and described Feldstein as “a nothing.”
Feldstein told me that his parents were offered the services of an attorney close to Netanyahu, free of charge, but they refused. Feldstein said that his father argued, “I need a lawyer who will defend my son, not the Prime Minister.” The family instead hired Oded Savoray, a prominent litigator who has been outspoken in his opposition to the government. During their first meeting in prison, Savoray told Feldstein that Netanyahu and his advisers were not standing behind him, but Feldstein refused to accept it. Savoray returned the next morning with printouts of news articles showing that Netanyahu was disavowing him. That day, Savoray recalled, “I saw a broken man.”
Feldstein still awaits trial in the leak case and may be indicted for his part in Qatargate. When I met him, however, he did his best to project confidence. Since his house arrest ended, he has started a strategic-consulting business. Though his notoriety had driven away some prospective clients, he said that his “experience in crisis management” had attracted others. Recently, he ran into a Channel 14 host, who yelled at him for breaking ranks with Netanyahu. “It’s been difficult for my family and also for me personally, because it’s not like I’m here for revenge,” Feldstein said. I asked whether he felt disappointed with Netanyahu. He rose from his chair and began to pace the room. “In some respects yes, and in some respects no,” he said eventually. “At the end of the day, Netanyahu cares about Netanyahu.” ♦

epub_24.title: Why I Free-Solo El Capitan
epub_24.text:
Why I Free-Solo El Capitan
Shouts & Murmurs
Why I Free-Solo El Capitan
By Mike O’Brien
September 21, 2026
I’m going live right now because I’m, well, about sixteen hundred feet up the side of El Capitan. I currently have no ropes or harnesses on me. Just a chalk bag on my waist belt and a mike pinned to my shirt.
This is my third time doing a free-solo pass at El Capitan. And some of you asked if I’d record my thoughts as I hang by my fingertips over my impending death. I thought, Why not?
And there they go . . . So I just lost my sunglasses. Wait for it . . . I always love that. Anything you lose up here takes ten to twelve seconds to hit the ground. Anyway, I’m rambling on this live stream so I can give people some explanation for why we do this. Maybe even inspire someone to live a better life.
But first, in order to get my next foothold, I’m going to have to rely solely on fingerholds as I swing my foot over to a crevice. I’ve got a half-crimp hold with my left hand, and a mono with my right index finger. Aaand I got my toe in the crevice. O.K. Let’s find the next one.
That was perfect, actually. Just now, every part of my body and brain was focussed on the task at hand. Otherwise, I’m dead. So it’s very relaxing.
You have living, and you have dying. And zero time on life’s drama, spam calls, bills . . . Thankfully, debt collectors don’t tend to climb El Capitan, last I checked. And if they start to, all of us rock-jocks are in trouble! One second, I don’t like this sloper. I’m gonna need to get a better grip. Gonna push off my right leg and see if I can find a pocket up above me. Got one. Feels solid enough . . .
It’s the forced unplug for me. Like all of you, my inbox is filled with stressful e-mails, but those will have to wait. Like, “You took all our money blah blah your climbing school is a Ponzi scheme blah blah why did we have to get more students in order to pay the same thing we paid last year?”
O.K., this is a part of the wall I’ve never done. And I think that’s very sick. Or, as some of my friends would call it, very dumb. Especially because some of the rocks are flaking off. Like that one. Damn it.
So all I’m focussed on is: How do I navigate a new path around this chossy area? Goes without saying that right now I’m not worried about some Karens complaining, “Oh, you never taught our kids anything. You were smoking outside while they climbed up a little fifteen-foot-wall thing.” Or, “My son fell off your plastic wall and fractured his tailbone. I’ve informed the police.” Well, which is it? Is my climbing wall too small, or are kids fracturing tailbones when they fall from its great heights? Can’t be both.
And I hate to be that guy, but there’s also no girlfriend when you’re on El Cap. Trust me, I love Maya, but I think we both benefit from little breaks. Frankly, anyone would be open to taking a break from someone who lately just screams, “I hate youuuu . . . I’ve got evidence of what you did! I’ve got video evidence.”
O.K., I’m navigating out of the looser rocks and over to the Dawn Wall, which I’ve done before. It’s steeper, but there’s better footing.
Again, present moment taking priority over outside noise. Like the girl I cheated on Maya with
one time
, mind you, texting me, “I deserve half of that climbing-school money because you used all my pillow-talk ideas. Don’t make me destroy you online.” I’m, like, Destroy me how? Ya too late.
And, in some ways, the most stressful text of my morning: “Bro, you know why I’m reaching out. You cheated on my little sister and I don’t need to remind you I’m a Triple O.G. in my set of the Crips. I’ll see you later today when you do your little rock-climb thing.” Top ten suckiest text I’ve ever gotten probably.
So, yeah, in some ways I’d rather be dangling by three fingers than dealing with life’s day-to-day headaches.
Thankfully, Crips don’t tend to climb El Capitan, last I checked. They tend to park at the top and play loud music. Next to the police, apparently. Funny to see those two getting along. Do I get a Nobel Prize for that? Kidding. I’m thinking more about toeholds than whether I’m going to get a Nobel. That’s why I free-solo El Capitan. To not worry about whether I’ll win a Nobel Prize. ♦

epub_26.title: Dark Horse
epub_26.text:
Dark Horse
Fiction
Dark Horse
By Sarah Anderson
September 20, 2026
In my mind, my father is fucking the horse again. From the front, you can hardly tell. She blinks slowly; she is still. A web of thick veins branches up and across her hind leg, tributaries rushing toward one vast river. Behind her is my father, pants around his ankles.
Over time, my brain has refined the loop, adding a warm evening light that silhouettes him as he moves, the rustle of Claudia’s hooves against the sticky candy-cane wrappers all over the floor, cast off from the treats he was always giving her. The scene has played out in my head every day for almost three years.
The Thought has a way of sitting in the back of my mind—really sitting there, like it takes up physical space, and it is impossible not to touch it. I have tried, many times. But at least once a day I press it like a bruise, and if I don’t it eventually starts to play anyway. The sound of their asynchronous breathing: Claudia’s a deep sigh, a snort, my father’s a pant, quick and uneven.
Read an interview with the author for the story behind the story.
I believe the vision was born the day I went out to the barn to tell my father that it was time, that my mother was about to die. His hands were on Claudia’s flank, his cheek resting against her. He didn’t turn around. “I’ll be there in a minute,” he said, and didn’t come. Not for hours, not until the coroner had arrived to take away the body.
My father acquired Claudia in the early nineties, when he worked for the Bureau of Land Management in Wyoming. It was there that he learned about the Horses and Burros Act of 1971, which declared wild horses “living symbols of the historic and pioneer spirit of the West” and made it a federal crime to kill them. In the years following the Act, the wild-horse population exploded, wreaking havoc on the land and leaving the horses to fight it out with one another or starve. Slaughterhouses in the U.S. shuttered, and the government contracted cowboys to round up the horses into pens, spending millions every year to keep them alive.
The act is a topic about which my father can speak at great length. The ways in which it has failed to do what it set out to—protect the horses—the ways it is not more humane at all, really, and its secondary sin: that it is carried out in
his
name; i.e., at taxpayer expense. “If I were President,” my father often says, “the first thing I would do is overturn the Horses and Burros Act.” And, gathering steam, “The real problem is that Americans can’t look themselves in the face anymore. Everyone wants to be Jane fucking Goodall, but without getting their hands dirty.”
All through the night in those years with the B.L.M., my father helped do population surveys from helicopters, counting the white-heat outlines on a screen in the dark—ghost horses, the ones that had escaped the gatherers. During the day, he inspected the government holding facilities.
The first time my father saw Claudia, she was one of hundreds of warehoused young horses in a crowded pen. She was never a particularly attractive horse, nor particularly charismatic, in my opinion. But while my father was standing at the fence, back turned, she wandered up and bit him on the ear, and that was that. He offered to buy her at auction, but the manager gave her to him for free, since it would save the government thousands of dollars in food and upkeep.
My father named the horse after the model Claudia Schiffer, who had been in the news recently for dating a high-profile magician. He took the horse home to the house he had just bought with my mother, who was about to give birth to me. “You shoulda seen the legs on Claudia when she was young,” he would say wistfully, and I never could tell which Claudia he was talking about.
Podcast: The Writer’s Voice
Listen to Sarah Anderson read “Dark Horse.”
As a teen-ager, when I couldn’t sleep, I would spend hours looking at every photo of Claudia Schiffer I could find. When I think of her now, I see the 1991 Spanish
Playboy
cover. In the photo, she kneels in wet sand in a pair of unzipped shorts, breasts poised to break free of the arm across her chest at any moment.
My mother did not look anything like Claudia Schiffer. She was brunette, and thick in the calves. At the end, she had no breasts to speak of, and, if she had, no one would have wanted to look at them anyway.
Horses are easy to injure but difficult to kill. Occasionally, euthanasia doesn’t take—some alchemy in their huge bodies fighting sedation. It’s also expensive, and sometimes a horse will react poorly, stumble around and fall hard, tongue lolling.
The other option is a bullet. It is less expensive, because the cost is the cost of a bullet. But you still have to figure out what to do with the body. At a slaughterhouse, they will shoot the horse for free and pay you a couple thousand dollars for the meat. You can guess which option my father chose when the time came.
For a long while, my father did not acknowledge the fact that Claudia was in the twilight of her life. Not when the tendons in her legs started causing too much pain for her to walk some days. Not when she shifted her weight back onto her heels, a telltale sign of hoof disease, from age and too much sugar. Not as her compulsions, which he called “her habits,” escalated and she began cribbing, a repetitive behavior in which she grasped the fence with her front teeth and yanked her head back, grunting. “Hey, lady,” my father would say softly. “Just relax.”
“The internet said we should try putting herbal tea in her feed,” he told me early one morning when I came into the kitchen to start the coffee, before my shift at the dentist’s office.
“Who?” I said, still half asleep.
“What do you mean ‘who’? Claudia. To help with her habits.”
He ordered camomile in bulk, but Claudia kept cribbing. The fence started to splinter, and her teeth started to wear. They had never been great to begin with. My mother had insisted on brushing them regularly, making me hold up Claudia’s rubbery top lip so she could reach every one of the yellowed, stonelike teeth. Even when my mother was too sick to go anywhere else, we went to the barn together once a week. The task seemed to soothe her. “Better?” she asked at the end of a session. “Much,” I said, in the affected mid-Atlantic accent she and I would use to channel Claudia. Lately, my father and I had been lax with the brushing.
In June, four months into the camomile regimen, a particularly loud plane from the military base flew overhead. The sound of it spooked Claudia so much that she ran the length of the fence back and forth for more than an hour, until she could no longer bear weight on her right front knee. At first, my father stood by the fence trying to calm her, calling to her and offering food, but eventually he went back into the house and sat in his armchair in front of the TV, without turning it on. “I can’t reason with her,” he said, shaking his head. A few hours later, when she finally lay down in the paddock, still shivering, skin rippling, I watched through the window as he went to her, wrapping his fingers in her mane and whispering something. He led her slowly back to the barn, and I didn’t see him again until the next morning, when I found him back in the armchair, slivers of hay clinging to his shirt.
That day, the day he finally realized he could no longer keep Claudia alive, my father declared that together we would drive her seven hundred miles to the Mexican border, where slaughterhouses abound.
“Please,” I said. “Please, can we just call the vet?”
“Claudia hates the vet, and I do, too,” he said. “He’s smarmy. I don’t want him to be the last thing she sees. And besides, I like the idea of her body being put to use. She would want that.” I felt the Thought coming on, felt myself drifting into the blurry space between thinking about the Thought and actually having it.
“You do it then,” I said. “You take her.”
“Dylan can come,” he said.
I paused. It felt like he was suggesting something drastic and incongruous. Taking our mailman on a cruise. Bringing a cat to a christening. My boyfriend, Dylan, existed in a different part of my brain from both Claudia and my father, and frankly I sometimes forgot him completely. But my father was right; Dylan loved both road trips and concrete tasks. He was an acts-of-service guy. My father sensed weakness in my pause and moved in for the kill. “You two can keep the money, make a vacation out of it. Should be almost three thousand dollars, for a horse like her.”
It was pointless to argue with my father when he was like this. And I needed the money, having spent all I had finishing the dental-hygiene program at the community college the previous year.
“Fine,” I said.
“We’ll leave Saturday,” he called as I stormed out of the kitchen. I made it to the porch before the Thought reared its head, my father and the barn and the click of his belt buckle, and I wished desperately that I could hate him the normal way.
In the five days before the journey, my father threw together his version of a hospice program. He fed Claudia all the things she liked most—red Skittles and candy canes and strawberries. Her favorite color was red, he explained. “She’s glamorous like that.” Every January, for as long as I could remember, we’d gone to the post-Christmas sales at the dollar store and at Walmart and bought up all the candy canes on clearance. Only the peppermint. “None of those bullshit pussy flavors,” my father said, glaring at a pack of multicolored Sour Patch Kids-flavored canes.
He also sprayed my Calvin Klein perfume around the stable, because he had heard a radio story about how animals like it. I tried to explain to him that it was just big cats. “Because of civetone,” I said. “It’s a pheromone, from the anal glands of a civet.”
“You don’t think Claudia can appreciate a good smell?” he said. I started hiding my perfume in a Tampax box behind the mirror. He used what was left of my mother’s Chanel No. 5 instead.
My mother took up drinking when she became a lost cause, and I took it up with her, in solidarity. I didn’t have the balls to shave my head, or anything like that, so I did what I could. I did not let her get fucked up alone.
We spent most of her last months drunk on the porch together, me sneaking inside to get another bottle of gin without my father seeing. “Did you get it?” she’d whisper, and I’d whip it out from behind my back or from up my shirt and we’d crack up. At some point in the night, when we weren’t really talking anymore, just looking out at the fireflies glimmering in the throats of the plants, we would light up her chemo weed. She watched me smoke the jay down, and then, when the only thing I could hear was cicadas, I set the still-lit joint on a little blue plate we kept outside for that purpose and went into the house. She had so few private moments by then, her body everyone’s business. I could give her this: let her smoke it alone, like a secret.
Inside, I forced myself to stay awake and listen for her footsteps. Sometimes she fell asleep out on the porch, and I would half carry her to the bed, which was empty, my father having moved to the guest room. “She sleeps better that way, and she needs her rest now,” he said. “We both do.”
My mother stopped drinking when she died, but I kept going, for both of us.
The thing about constantly seeing the image of your father fucking a horse is that there are very few people you can tell about it. Practically none.
The summer after my mother died, I used some of the money she had left me to go to Australia. I went because it was as far away as possible and because I wanted to learn to scuba dive. I had just started having the Thought, and I was hoping it would go away with travel and new experiences, such as going to the bottom of the ocean.
My father thought it would be good for me to spend some time on my own. He had noticed that I had been acting strangely around him, struggling to make eye contact, and I suspected he had found my stash of empties in the cupboard under the bathroom sink. “Go,” he said. “Get right with God.”
“I will,” I said, though I didn’t know what he meant by that, or how to approach doing it. I had never known him to be religious.
In Australia, I met a man, a boy, really, twenty-one and insufferable. “I’m young, but I’ve just done so much with my life already,” he said to me at our hostel’s wine-and-cheese night, in a packed, dingy common room. “I hate you,” I thought with a little thrill of pleasure, washing down a sweaty cube of cheddar with red blend. The next morning, he caught me on my way to breakfast, and soon he began accompanying me on every excursion.
It wasn’t until the third day, as we waited for a bus on an island known for its wild koala population, that he revealed to me that he had been a child star on a popular TV show my mother had been a fan of. His character flaws suddenly crystallized in a highly satisfying way.
On our last day together, the former child star suggested we go to a nude beach, falling over himself to explain that it was not sexual in any way, merely an experience he wanted to have.
“Sure,” I said. Naked with the child star. My mother wouldn’t even believe it.
“If you’re not comfortable with it . . .” he said.
“I’m fine with it.” He seemed disappointed by my readiness.
At the beach, there was a sign with images of four jellyfish in order of escalating concern, from unpleasant sting to instant death. Next to it was a sign that read “Clothing Optional.” We walked to a small cove, stripped down without looking at each other, and waded awkwardly into the shallows, sitting down on the sandy bottom. I was lulled by the heat and the shifting patterns of sunlight in the water. As often happened when I began to relax, I felt the Thought shift restlessly in a corner of my brain.
“Do you ever have really fucked-up thoughts?” I found myself saying to the former child star, before I could stop myself.
“Probably,” he said. “Like what?”
“Like sex stuff.”
“Like choking?”
“Maybe,” I said. “Or, like, fucking animals.” I said it in a weird voice that was meant to be jokey but wasn’t.
“Not really, but people do all kinds of shit. My friend showed me a whole website of it. Really sick stuff.”
“Were there horses?”
“Oh, yeah,” he said. “Sheep, too. Everything.”
We fell silent, and I closed my eyes. When I opened them, his face was close to mine. He gazed at me a moment, then leaned in.
“What are you doing?”
“Can I kiss you?” he asked.
“No,” I said. “Why would you ask that?”
“We’re at a nude beach together,” he said. “We’ve spent the past four days hanging out. You asked me for a piggyback on the way here.”
“I’m sorry,” I said, but I wasn’t. “There’s been a misunderstanding.”
He looked out at the horizon for a moment, then abruptly stood. “Well,” he said. “At least I’m not a fucking pervert.” He splashed back to shore, pale ass shining in the sunlight.
That night, I attended a free sound bath at the hostel, run by a thin British woman, who had given me a towel at check-in. The child star was already there, in butterfly position, ostentatiously meditating.
“Feel the rise and fall of the breath entering and exiting your body,” the British woman said, as she began to work the bowls. “If any thoughts do arise, allow them to pass through you like clouds in the sky.”
At the sound of its name, the Thought rolled over but remained silent. Instead, I found myself thinking over and over, “The antidote to jellyfish is vinegar.” I wished it was my own original thought, but I was fairly sure it was just from that cautionary sign at the beach. To my right, the child star was taking very loud, deep breaths and emitting low “om”s.
“You will likely find yourself feeling a bit raw for the rest of the night,” the woman said, when the bowls quieted, as she opened a beaded tip box. “And experiencing strange dreams.” I wished she had mentioned this beforehand.
That night, as I fell asleep, I thought I had finally done it. Escaped the Thought for an entire day. That maybe telling the child star had done something after all. Purged it. But then I dreamed it instead.
For the first time, it wasn’t happening inside the barn but on the nude beach, little sprinkles of sand in Claudia’s mane and stuck in the hairs around her prehensile lips, as if she had been grazing at the water’s edge. Dead jellyfish littered the shoreline, a pile of them at my father’s feet.
I did not tell anyone about the Thought again.
The morning of the drive, Claudia did not want to get into the trailer. My father went through the last two boxes of candy canes trying to coax her in, step by step. Dylan stood off to the side watching YouTube how-tos and offering nuggets of wisdom. “This guy says the issue is either about fear or lack of respect,” he said. “We’re supposed to act as much as possible like the trailer isn’t there.” Eventually, I sent him to the garage to look for the extra set of jumper cables, which we kept in the barn.
When Claudia finally climbed into the trailer, my father jumped down and turned to me. “We need to be prepared to ask them to shoot her in front of us. So that—” He broke off midsentence. “Stop doing that,” he said sharply.
“Doing what?”
He gestured at his chest, cupping his hands in the universal symbol for tits. Lately, my right hand had developed a mind of its own, wandering up my body and across my chest, gently palpating my breast tissue in moments of distraction. Two fingers pushing inward, seeking abnormalities. The worst part was that I didn’t even notice it anymore. Like nail-biting. I dropped my hand back to my side. “Sorry,” I said. “Go on.”
“To make sure they do it right,” he said, and walked back toward the house.
For the first two hours, Dylan drove, and we were quiet, the sun climbing higher and warming the car as I drifted in and out of sleep in the front seat, twitching awake every so often to check the trailer in the mirrors. My father sat in the back, staring out the window, an odd, blank look on his face.
At hour five, Dylan turned on a podcast about sustainable building practices and tiny homes, put the car in cruise control, and started eating pistachios, cracking them open and dropping the shells into his empty coffee cup. Sleep became impossible. I knew he was thinking about what we could do with Claudia’s blood money.
“Are you listening to this?” Dylan said. “It’s a lot easier than people think to build your own house. It’s actually really intuitive.”
“Can we stop soon?” I asked. “I have to pee.”
“Already?” my father groaned from the back seat. As we whizzed past several promising exits, I distracted myself by making a themed playlist, which I could only hope might nip the podcasts in the bud and discourage conversation.
At a 7-Eleven on the border of Colorado and New Mexico, I peered into the trailer’s little upper window to check on Claudia. She was sweating, her muscles twitching slightly. “We’re almost there,” I told her. “Keep your shit together for a few more hours and you’re home free.” I pictured her in Heaven, a silent, peppermint-scented place. “God loves horses,” I added.
Inside, I bought a cherry Slurpee, then quickly went back to the truck to locate the two airplane bottles of vodka Dylan kept in the glove compartment. They were tucked next to the first-aid kit, as though he thought he might one day need to perform a field surgery. I poured both through the straw hole of my cup to create a delicious cocktail and returned the empties to their place.
My father emerged shortly afterward with a rope of bison jerky, Dylan with three oversized Rice Krispies bars.
“Are you kidding me?” I said, as Dylan climbed back in.
“What?”
“Do you even know what those are made of?”
He started the car.
“Horse!” I said. “Hooves or some shit. Everybody knows that’s what marshmallow is made of.”
“There’s no way,” Dylan said.
“Gelatin,” I said once he was driving again. “Look it up.”
“You look it up.”
“I don’t need to. I know I’m right.”
“I really don’t think Claudia cares,” Dylan said.
“Gelatin is an extremely useful product,” my father said. “And versatile.”
“Have some respect,” I said, and went back to my playlist.
“A Horse with No Name.” “Black Horse and the Cherry Tree.” “Wild Horses,” by the Rolling Stones, Natasha Bedingfield, and Garth Brooks. “The Funeral,” by Band of Horses. That one was going to hit hard closer to the border.
Less than an hour later, my father asked where we would be stopping for lunch.
“We’re not stopping,” I told him. “We just stopped. You got food.” I sucked on my straw, hitting the vodka slush at the bottom of the giant cup, each sip a different combination of metallic and sweet.
“I’m hungry,” he said. “I had one piece of jerky. We have at least five hours left.”
“No.”
“Dylan, keep an eye out for an exit,” my father said. “Jesus, what’s the rush? Claudia gets carsick. She could use a break. Horses can’t vomit, you know. So she has to just suffer through it.”
“We’re not stopping,” I said.
Twenty-five minutes later, I was sitting across from my father at a Red Lobster. He was thoughtfully paging through the menu and trying to persuade Dylan to go in on a Shrimp Your Way with him.
“Do you like coconut?” he asked.
“Just a Bahama Mama for me,” I told our server, a pallid young man called Zachary.
“And to eat?” he asked.
“That will be all,” I said.
“Don’t they have cheesecake here?” my father asked, frowning at the last page of the menu. “Isn’t that their thing?”
“I think you’re thinking of the Cheesecake Factory,” I told him.
“Do not patronize me,” he said. “I mean it.”
When my drink came, my father dipped his fingers into it without asking, to fish out the cherries for Claudia. I slapped his hand away. When his food came, the Thought and I watched him bite into the veiny pink flesh of the shrimp, discarding the tails into a little pile, and I excused myself from the table. I had resisted the Thought all day, and pressure was building in that corner of my mind. In the parking lot, I opened the side hatch of the trailer to let Claudia stick her head out. She nuzzled my face, an act of tenderness quite unlike her. Her breath was atrocious.
Around hour seven, my father finally fell asleep, chin tucked to his chest like a giant toddler. Dylan checked the rearview mirror to insure he was out before asking if we could please talk about the money now. He was of the opinion that we should use it to seed a joint savings account, with which we would one day buy a tract of land somewhere, on which we would build our own homestead by hand. He had attempted some version of this with his first wife. It had not gone well. We had been fighting proxy wars about this plan since he first presented it, mostly through opposing allegiances with halves of the couples who tour houses on “Property Brothers.”
Dylan had been married twice before, and the second marriage was still in the process of dissolution, from a legal standpoint. He talked about the marriages as if some act of God had ended both of them. Like they were casualties of an earthquake, or a drunk-driving accident. “Sometimes it makes me so sad that I’ll never see her again,” he once said, on the topic of his first wife.
“Why can’t you see her again?” I asked. “Doesn’t she still live really close to us?” He ignored me.
“You go from knowing a person so well. To, all of a sudden, nothing. Hard to grasp the permanence of it all, really.”
“Gee, I can’t even imagine.”
“It’s tough,” he said, without any sense of irony. “Hard to even find the words.”
In the car, he fiddled with the air-conditioning. “Did you hear me?” he asked.
“No,” I said.
“Well, what do you want to do with it?”
“Stop scraping teeth,” I said. “And live alone.” He dropped it.
I wondered if, once we were rid of Claudia, the loss would feel permanent. If I might finally be free of the Thought, of my father’s pistoning hips. Outside, the landscape was opening up, drying out, turning from trees to scrub. My tongue was still red from the Slurpee, like a slab of raw meat inside my mouth. I guess that’s basically what a tongue is, technically speaking. I saw it in the side mirror while I was singing: “At every occasion, I’ll be ready for the funeral.” The song ended and started over, and I became aware that it had been on repeat for a while, that my hand was on my breast. I had lost track of time.
I palpated clockwise, like the internet told me to. Imagine the face of a clock over your breast, or the slices of a pie, it said. If my tits were a pie, I think they would be one of the nutty ones. Pecan. Or maybe Key lime. If my tits were from a state, they would definitely be from Florida.
“Dylan,” I said.
“Unh,” he said, just a sound at the back of his throat. He was pouting.
“Dylan.”
“What,” he said, not like a question.
“Dimpling, puckering, or skin that looks like an orange peel.”
“What?”
“Dimpling, puckering, or skin that looks like an orange peel. That’s what you should look for. Not just lumps.”
“Cool.”
“Could you maybe not be sarcastic when I’m telling you I might have cancer?”
“You don’t have to indulge the behavior, son,” my father piped up from the back seat, apparently awake now. “You can tell her no.”
Dylan sighed and ignored him. “I’m not being sarcastic, babe. We just checked last night.”
“No, really,” I said. “It’s dimpling. Give me your hand.”
He centered his left hand on the wheel then gave me his right, feeling my breast for the obligatory minute. “Nothing,” he said. “I don’t feel anything. There’s nothing there.” I squeezed the flesh again, then pinched it, trying to make the dimple reappear, the skin growing red and angry. But I couldn’t.
“Christ,” my father said.
Once, I had made my mother check a red bump on my vulva. She had grown tired of listening to me try to describe it. “Just show me,” she said. I sat on the closed toilet seat and opened my legs. “Ingrown hair,” she said immediately.
“Are you sure?”
“I’m sure.”
“Sorry,” I said. “For making you look.”
“Oh, sweetie,” she said. “I changed your diapers.”
Out the window, scrub had given way to desert. The ground was a deep orange now, the color of thirst. I thought about a world where my mother sat on the toilet seat instead of me, where I stood in front of her, or my father did, and we told her to raise her arms above her head, and we put our hands where she told us to and said, “Yeah, I feel it.”
To understand horses, you must start by understanding that they are always afraid. I was never able to love Claudia, but, as a creature driven by fear, I could understand her.
“A horse is all about flight,” my father often said, when he was railing against the Horses and Burros Act. He was always quoting from this book about how animals make us more human, or something to that effect. He was especially proud of himself for reading it, because the author had autism.
Around the eleventh hour of our journey, as the sun was beginning to set, an unsettling banging started coming from the trailer. Claudia hitting her face against the wall, maybe, or cribbing on the metal window bars. I checked the mirrors, then the back seat. My father was asleep again, having exhausted all delay tactics. Asking to stop for a Coke, to check the trailer hitch, to see the World’s Largest Pistachio. I suspected that he, too, had ordered something to take the edge off at the Lobster, after I had left.
Dylan and I both tried to ignore the sound, but it got louder and more regular. “Pull over,” I said.
“We’re so close,” Dylan said. “It’s going to get dark soon. She’s fine.”
“Pull the fuck over,” I said, and something in my voice made him listen. He pulled into a gas station six miles from the border. He slammed his door and headed for the convenience store with long, angry strides. My father stirred, mumbling something and frowning.
I went around to the back. One of Claudia’s wild eyes was pressed to the window, like how I imagined a squid might peer into a submarine. The eye rolled slightly. My father appeared at my side. “What’s going on?” he asked, his voice rough with sleep, then turned to Claudia without waiting for an answer. “Hey, lady,” he said, softening his tone. “I’m here. I’m right here.” His voice broke, and I saw tears on his cheeks. This man who had stood dry-eyed as we put his wife in the ground.
He opened the door and Claudia started backing up frantically, then became frightened by the sound of her own feet clanging on the metal. “Whoa,” my father said. He jumped up behind her and pushed hard against her hindquarters to get her back in. He grunted with the effort of it, put his hips into it, and Claudia gave a snort. “Good girl,” he said, as she took a step forward. “Just like that.” I felt a wave of nausea as he slammed the door and turned to me. “I’m going to see if they have peppermint candies in there,” he said. “Keep talking to her. Make sure she knows she’s not alone.” As he walked away from us, Claudia started cribbing again, biting down on the metal bars and throwing her head back, grunting with pleasure or pain. Blood on her lips. Another name for cribbing is windsucking. It sounds nicer that way. Something you do because you want to, not because you have to. The Thought had hardened to a knot behind my eyes. It pulsed with the sound of her teeth against metal. Bite, grunt. Bite, grunt.
Finally, the pulsing gave way to a rushing in my head, like I’d stood up too fast, and then I was back in the barn. It was night, lit only by the floodlights at the back of the house, flickering in a storm of moths. The smell of dust and wood, cut with some animal thing. My father thrusting behind Claudia, a moving shadow. In front, asleep at Claudia’s feet, was my mother in a nightgown, her body as small as a child’s. When my father emerged, he stood over her, trying to rouse her, to get her to stand. “Good girl,” he said. “Just like that,” as she awoke, rolling clumsily onto her knees.
As I came out of it, I found myself standing with one hand curled around the warm metal of the trailer’s door handle, the other on my breast. The sun was bleeding now, too, color pooling in every crevice of the sky, and Claudia was still going at it. Bite, grunt. Bite, grunt.
Make sure she knows she’s not alone,
my father said.
I flung the door wide open. Claudia released the metal bars and looked suspiciously over her shoulder at the open door.
“Go,” I told her. “Go. Get out of here.” She blinked.
“We’re trying to kill you,” I said. “You have to save yourself.”
Still, she refused to move.
And so I climbed in with her. I put my lips next to her hollow, pointed ears, two furred halves of a papaya, and screamed. She bolted, stumbling backward out of the trailer and running across the parking lot. At the Mobil sign, she tripped, steadied herself, and turned right, galloping down the center of the empty road.
The door to the convenience store burst open, and Dylan emerged, the glint of a blue-foil Rice Krispies Treat in his hand and my father on his heels. Dylan froze a few feet from the door, squinting at the scene. My father pushed past him and charged toward me, his face contorted in a way I had only ever seen in my mind. We locked eyes for the second that it took for him to process the empty trailer and then Claudia, at least a hundred yards up the road now and fading fast. Her body so quickly becoming silhouette. In that second, I saw the future: the long white grin of a horse skull picked clean, smiling with all of its teeth. The strange siren call of coyotes gathering in the night. My father, on his knees. Alone.
I screamed again, with the fury of some kind of visionary, some kind of witness, as he took off after her. He looked, for the first time I could remember, old. I stopped only when I was sure he could never catch her.
“I will think of you often,” I said, as Claudia disappeared over the horizon. And I did. ♦

Hernan Diaz’s Grand Experiment
