Hernan Diaz’s Grand Experiment
In the novel “Ply,” the Pulitzer Prize winner imagines a ruined New York, a fractured society, and the ultimate structure of existence.
By Kathryn Schulz
September 21, 2026
Twenty-five hundred years ago, the Greek philosopher Zeno set about making the case for the counterintuitive claim that all motion is an illusion. Imagine a footrace, he said, between a tortoise and Achilles. As everyone knows, tortoises are gelatinously slow, whereas Achilles, at least per Homer, is famously fleet. So let’s grant the tortoise a head start, Zeno declared—say, a hundred yards. Off it lumbers. When it reaches the hundred-yard mark, Achilles starts running and rapidly reaches it, too. By then, however, the tortoise is ten yards farther along, so Achilles must close the new gap. Zeno’s point was that this process will never end: to pass the tortoise, Achilles must first get to where it was, but the tortoise will always have moved on, however incrementally—by one yard or 0.1 yard or 0.01 yard, and so on in an infinite sequence. Since you can’t complete an infinite number of steps in a finite amount of time, Zeno concluded, Achilles can never catch up, even though common sense suggests that he swiftly will.
This famous paradox appears twice in “
Ply
” (Riverhead), a new novel by the acclaimed Argentinean American writer Hernan Diaz. In a startling departure from his previous two books, which were set in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, “Ply” takes place hundreds of years hence, in a version of New York City rendered almost unrecognizable by the collapse of the United States and the demise of modern democracy. We first hear about Zeno’s paradox when the book’s unnamed protagonist is a child, traumatized by the murder of her father for his alleged role in an incipient political uprising. When her mother tells her the story of Achilles and the tortoise, the girl experiences it less as philosophy than as lullaby—her mother’s way of saying that, although they live in a world without legal or political protections, “no one, no matter how hard they tried, would ever be able to reach us. We would always be a step ahead.”
Years later, when the protagonist is grown, she encounters a scientist named Pola, who pauses while explaining some complex theoretical physics to ask, “I don’t suppose you are familiar with the paradox of Achilles and the tortoise?” Pola recounts that paradox the way the philosopher originally conceived it—as a puzzle about the nature of reality. Although Zeno was wrong about the mathematics of infinity, his hypothetical footrace still captures a fundamental question about the universe: Can space-time, that four-dimensional weft in which all of existence unfolds, be endlessly subdivided? Or is it made up of some ultimate, indivisible particle, like an atom as the ancients imagined it, only unimaginably smaller?
Scientists don’t know the answer, for an intriguing reason: once you divide space-time into small enough units, quantum mechanics and the theory of relativity start contradicting each other, and our understanding of the universe falls apart. In Diaz’s novel, Pola is aware of this, but she believes both that a fundamental particle exists and that she is on the verge of discovering and controlling it, thereby acquiring world-altering powers. Here she is, standing beside a D.I.Y. particle accelerator that she has rigged up in the basement of an abandoned uptown art museum, waxing abstrusely grandiose about her plans:
By accessing this seemingly indivisible, final, discrete unit, we will be able to manipulate the popping bubbles that make up the effervescence of spacetime. Because, to use that other imperfect image, we would be in control of the very knots in the threads that weave the fabric of spacetime itself.
Good luck to her. It’s hard enough to be in control of the very knots in the threads that weave the fabric of a novel, and you might as well know up front that this one unravels. On the plus side, unravelling is what “Ply” is about: what is lost, what is gained, and what possibilities emerge when all of our usual laws, societal as well as physical, break down.
Lawlessness is familiar terrain for Diaz. His first novel, the magnificent “
In the Distance
,” follows one Håkan Söderström, the younger of two brothers growing up in rural Sweden around the eighteen-forties. Diaz sets the plot in motion in three efficient pages: when Håkan’s father earns some unexpected money, he buys his sons passage to New York. Their transatlantic journey is slated to begin in Portsmouth, but once there Håkan loses sight of his brother in the crowds along the wharf. Alone and increasingly desperate, the boy goes from pier to pier, asking for a boat that is headed to “Nujårk,” a word no one around him understands. Then he tries “Amerika” and is waved onto a ship that sets sail for its destination: San Francisco.
The rest of “In the Distance” is an inverted and eviscerated Western. Hoping to make his way back to his brother, Håkan disembarks in California and immediately heads East, against the flow of all the homesteaders and forty-niners streaming West. As he travels through the United States, he occasionally encounters kindness or wisdom, but he never encounters anything like the rule of law; preëmptive or retaliatory violence is the chief recourse of everyone from prospectors and pioneers to Mormon vigilantes, and the sole sheriff to appear in two thousand miles of wilderness is vicious and corrupt. Eventually, Håkan is forced to participate in this omnipresent bloodshed, at a terrible cost to his soul and his reputation. Soon, he is turned into a myth, wanted across the West for crimes he didn’t commit. Now known as the Hawk, a mangling of both the name and the nature of this singularly unpredatory man, he goes into hiding, the dream of New York receding as he is consigned, like an American Moses, to endlessly traversing the desert without entering the promised land.
When Diaz wrote “In the Distance,” he had no agent; he submitted the manuscript in response to a call for new work by Coffee House Press, a nonprofit publisher in Minneapolis. The book came out in 2017; six months later, it was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. Diaz won the prize for his second novel, “
Trust
,” which recounts, in four ways, the story of an astronomically wealthy Roaring Twenties-era financier and his enigmatic wife. The first version is a compact novel-within-a-novel in which this fictional couple is further fictionalized, to an uncertain degree but scandalous effect. The second is the financier’s incomplete autobiography, which he intends as a riposte to the novel but which reads as the kind of boastful yet vacuous legacy burnishing beloved of powerful men in their waning years. The third is a memoir by a woman—part secretary, part ghostwriter—whom the financier hired to help him with the autobiography, while the fourth is a fragment of the final journal of his wife, the largely invisible force who sets the whole story spinning.
If “In the Distance” is about the lawlessness of a region that has not yet cohered into a nation, “Trust” is about a lawlessness more familiar to us today: the exploitable anarchy of the financial markets—in this case during the early twentieth century, when checks on financiers were minimal to nonexistent. Diaz’s main character sees the crash of 1929 coming and shorts the entire stock market, so that, when the economy collapses, his private fortune soars. It is unclear whether he is lucky, brilliant, or abetted by a keener mind, just as it is unclear whether he is amoral or immoral, or whether he believes his own self-justifying pablum. (“Profit and common good are but two sides of the same coin.”) As that pervasive uncertainty suggests, “Trust” is also about a kind of literary lawlessness—about whether this novel and its several narrators can be relied on to follow the rules of storytelling.
Despite this thematic overlap, you could read “In the Distance” and “Trust” back-to-back and never guess that they shared an author. Diaz’s first book is simultaneously mythic and intimate; it stays close on Håkan and the vast landscape that he moves through—seldom has the American West been written about more gorgeously—and you are always inside the story, right at its tragic hero’s heels. By contrast, “Trust” is cool and distant; you don’t enter it so much as peer into it, as into a skeleton clock, watching the turning of its gears.
“Ply” continues this trend: although it, too, is concerned with the breakdown of laws, it reads nothing like its predecessors. This is partly because its future setting makes it feel like science fiction, even though the world it depicts has backslid from the scientific standards of today. In fact, it has backslid from every standard of today: in a sort of ultimate triumph of Project 2025, centralized government is a thing of the past, which means there are no public services in this future New York—no public health, no public education, no public utilities.
One consequence is that life expectancy has plunged. Without affordable medical care or social welfare, people die of tooth decay and childbirth and exposure to the cold come winter. Fertility has also collapsed for reasons no one understands—maybe an unknown disease, maybe environmental toxins, maybe a genetic mutation. The demographic impact is drastic: late thirties is the new old age, reaching fifty is almost unheard of, and the over-all population has plummeted.
As a result, much of “Ply” has a distinct “World Without Us” feel. In Diaz’s version of New York, dolphins arc through the East River, black bears browse on acorns from SoHo’s abundant oak trees, and whole avenues’ worth of buildings, their tops caved in, have turned into “massive planters.” Even island biogeography is having its way; the moose that dwell in the Bronx are unusually small, the feral cats of Manhattan strangely large. The human residents of this de-urbanizing city live a hybrid life, part modern, part ancient. They watch things called projections and possess iPhone-like devices called stells, but they get around mainly on foot and by bike, barter goods and services, gather to gossip at water stations, and settle down after sunset into an almost primordial darkness.
That’s because electricity, like every other commodity in this new New York, is privatized, under the control of a company called Tensor. Since few people can afford power bills, almost everyone relies on the thriving black market for “bricks,” portable batteries whose charge is illicitly siphoned from the grid. The people who do that siphoning are known as “pinchers,” and our unnamed protagonist is one of them. That puts her in the crosshairs of CTS, a private security company that has taken over another former function of the state: public safety. The difference is that, like early insurance companies, CTS extinguishes only the fires it is paid, including by Tensor, to put out.
It was CTS that murdered the pincher’s father, in an Argentinean-style disappearance of anyone who agitated against this privatization: no trials, no Gulags, just gone. When her mother dies some years later, the protagonist, then age eleven, is left adrift. Eventually, she makes her way to a man named Acevedo, a prominent tinker in a city that is full of them because “nothing new is ever really available and nothing old is ever really thrown away.” Acevedo’s workshop looks like a junk yard and functions like a food pantry, but, in a familiar trope of science fiction, it operates like a religious order, with shaved-headed apprentices expected to be silent, selfless, and entirely without need.
Acevedo himself functions as both the book’s moral authority and its political theorist. In a lecture to his apprentices, he explains what brought about the long-ago collapse of liberal democracy: basically, an unchecked continuation of everything filling the op-ed pages today. Social mobility gave way to impermeable class divisions; the idea of inalienable rights withered on the vine; a profound skepticism of government replaced an understanding that some problems are too large or challenging or unremunerative for any other entity to solve; and artificial intelligence undermined the belief that humans are unique and extraordinary—the very conviction that had undergirded all those other ideals since the Renaissance.
Many books about the future are ways of thinking through the problems of the present. One of the difficulties with “Ply” is that it seems to want to do this but never quite settles on what to say. It doesn’t really mourn the lost world order; at one point, Acevedo lists the superior qualities of his own times, from the decline of the patriarchy to the end of the carceral state. Only reluctantly does he acknowledge all the misery around him, which both he and the pincher choose to regard as a sign that they are living through the painful birth of a better era. Elsewhere, however, the book suggests that the present lawlessness is itself that better outcome. “There was freedom in dissolution, joy in disorder,” Diaz writes, as if advocating for anarchy, though most of his characters appear to subscribe only to the political philosophy known as making the best of a bad situation.
If the book has one consistent political sentiment, it is a kind of Occupy Wall Street-style anti-capitalism. In “Ply,” as in Zuccotti Park circa 2011, people with different and sometimes incompatible views have exactly one thing in common: anger over the untrammelled greed of the private sector, its steady hijacking of public services, and its ruinous impact on everyday citizens. A similar sentiment lay at the heart of “Trust,” where its fictional treatment was clear and spare, but in “Ply” it is both more emphatic and more confusing. Somehow, we are to believe that New York is no longer a monument to commerce and consumption, yet also that it is controlled, down to matters of life and death, by private corporations.
To further muddy these waters, our protagonist abandons Acevedo, the strongest critic of capitalism in the book, when she falls in love with a fellow-apprentice named Sol, who craves a different life. “I want to be free to want,” she declares, and the two run off together to begin their careers as pinchers. Acevedo regards pinching as pure theft, and thus “the ultimate affirmation of private property.” But Sol thinks of it as “profit . . . and fun,” and, for a while, she’s right, especially because the two women settle into a particularly glamorous niche of the business—powering concerts for the city’s thriving music scene.
Music is a constant presence in “Ply,” as it was in “Trust”: proof that the arts can flourish even in a culture seemingly too preoccupied with other things—wealth accumulation, survival—to care about them. Diaz, who is gifted at describing sound, packs “Ply” with bands both new and retro, some of which arguably represent a different sort of anti-capitalist impulse, although only in that vague way best summarized as Fuck the Man. But, the more time we spend with them, the more the book’s inchoate political energy dissipates. Moreover, the pincher herself gets something else from the music scene. A literal purveyor of power, she finally feels like a figurative one, too, and the sensation is exhilarating. “It was short-lived,” she tells us, “but while it lasted it was a long, pure now.”
What shatters this high is the slightest of accidents: Sol cuts her hand on a nail. Two days later, she is dead of sepsis, and our heartbroken protagonist takes a hard turn toward suspicion and solitude. Functioning now mostly as a lone wolf, she spends her time tinkering with a new model of brick she’s designed, twice the size of the typical version but capable of holding forty times the charge. When others grow interested in it, she senses danger and decides to stop pinching. But then along comes Pola, the scientist, who is ready to begin her world-altering experiment, except for one hitch: she needs electricity.
A curious thing happens at the start of the second half of “Ply.” The narration switches, not from one character to another but from the first person to the third. Having spent two hundred pages following along inside an “I,” we are suddenly kicked out and find ourselves reading about “the pincher.” That shift coincides with two others. First, Diaz turns his attention from the nature of society to the nature of the self and the universe. Second, we swap mentor figures, with Acevedo the tinker replaced by Pola the scientist—an austere and ethical fixer of real objects for the benefit of the people replaced by a volatile, drug-addicted, possibly crazy theoretical physicist. (Diaz has a fondness for maybe-mad scientists; “In the Distance” has one, too, who is more consistently kind than Pola but similarly single-minded.)
At the beginning of this second half, the pincher agrees to help Pola acquire the electricity she needs. This turns out to be all of it: the two plan to drain Tensor’s main power grid and store its energy for use in Pola’s experiment. To do so, they develop a heist-y plan, promising to hand over prototypes of the pincher’s new brick to a couple of interested parties in exchange for staging a riot that will distract CTS when Tensor most needs it. First, though, they must build a battery capable of storing the power they intend to steal. As they work on it, the women grow close, despite Pola’s sometimes difficult personality and despite the outrageousness of her experiment. This involves not only the particle accelerator but a mysterious golden disk that Pola believes can manipulate space-time and therefore reshape the universe.
You either do or don’t have a taste for this sort of thing. The pincher, for one, does not, but she falls under Pola’s spell anyway, coming to see her as a mother figure. Soon, the pincher also acquires a surrogate daughter—a young orphan named Ines, whom she takes in after finding her badly beaten outside their museum turned laboratory. Ines takes a shine to both women, and the time the trio spends together, like the time the pincher and Sol shared in the first half of the book, forms a temporary idyll.
Eventually, though, the moment arrives to implement their plan—which, like many such plans, works until it doesn’t. The heist appears to go off without a hitch, but the experiment does not: when a fire engulfs the lab, the pincher rushes to put it out and, in the process, stumbles into the golden disk. She survives but suffers serious burns, and before long starts showing signs of radiation sickness. Yet she is more consumed by what she saw when she looked into the disk—a vision, as difficult to re-create as dreams by day, of merging with space-time.
Soon, the pincher floats free of her consciousness, briefly inhabiting the mind of Pola or Ines before flickering back into herself. Accordingly, the narration starts flickering as well, between “the pincher” and the “I” of firsthand experience. Meanwhile, the other characters grow unstable, too, seeming to become alternate versions of the pincher or her mother. The pincher attributes this loosening of the boundaries of the self to her contact with the disk; the reader wonders if it’s just part of the process of dying. In the end—I’m not spoiling anything; I am doubtful, for many reasons, that the concept applies to this book—there is a great betrayal, and a great explosion, and a great many unanswered questions.
Partway through “Ply,” a minor character named Anton launches into an irritated monologue about the saying “I am here for you.” As a non-native English speaker, he finds these words meaningless, and he has a point. “I,” “here,” and “you” are all examples of indexical words, those whose meaning changes depending on their context.
Much of the second part of “Ply” is a meditation on those words, too. I, here, you—we change in relation to one another and to where we are, including, Diaz suggests, on a map of coördinates we cannot even fathom. His book is interested in not only whether the universe is composed of some fundamental particle but whether we are: whether there is an irreducible essence of selfhood or whether that is just an illusion, as Zeno claimed motion was—a local experience of reality that occludes another one, so hidden or vast or mysterious that it falls almost entirely outside our comprehension.
You can’t fault Diaz for lack of ambition. As a title, “Ply” is a slippery, clever choice, a word that means “layer” while containing other layers of meaning. So, too, the book itself, which is preoccupied with many things at once: what people are made of, what society is made of, what the universe is made of. And the whole of Diaz’s career is similarly ambitious. As different as his three books are, together they form a kind of new “U.S.A.” trilogy—or, more aptly, an “N.Y.C.” trilogy. “In the Distance” features a New York that is both a longed-for destination and an imagined locus of civilization; in “Trust,” it has become the heart of an all-devouring financial industry and its ethos of pure greed; in “Ply,” that ethos has been fulfilled, turning the city into a site of radical decay and, potentially, the birth of something new.
Regrettably, the grand intellectual ambitions of “Ply” finally overwhelm the other desiderata of fiction. One of these is storytelling. Diaz excels at this, as his previous books attest—“In the Distance” is genuinely impossible to put down—but the narrative energy of “Ply” keeps getting derailed, not least because two of its main characters exist mostly to lecture us. This sort of works with Acevedo, the proxy political theorist, but doesn’t work at all with Pola, the proxy cosmologist, whose ten-page discourse on space-time fails not only to clarify the relevant particle physics (admittedly a tall order) but also to provoke our awe or pique our curiosity about her character.
That last problem is not limited to Pola. Although some bit players in this book are wonderfully drawn—especially Anton, a bombastic but bighearted black-market kingpin—the pincher herself seems as if she exists only to do the author’s bidding. Learning about her is more like reading a personnel file than meeting a person, which proves fatal for the novel’s stakes. I understood what Diaz was doing with all those chameleon pronouns near the end, but it is difficult to care about the dissolution of a character who never quite felt real in the first place.
Still, there is something in Diaz that wants to be reckoned with, something that brings to mind those black bears in SoHo, startling and powerful and rare. At one point, the pincher comes across an old Hawthorne story and is struck by how effectively it does what Pola can only dream of doing centuries later: set someone loose on multiple chronologies simultaneously. The reference is heavy-handed, but the idea is the right one. With due respect to the innovations of science, fiction remains the most powerful microscope, telescope, seismograph, X-ray machine, and particle accelerator we’ve ever discovered—a way to examine the world at every scale, to reverse causality, to alter time, to identify fundamental properties, to reveal our inner workings and control the conditions of the universe. Best of all, and happily for Diaz, you can run as many experiments as you want, and no one is harmed when the odd one fails. ♦

Tom Brady’s Endgame
Books
Tom Brady’s Endgame
A new biography argues that the star quarterback’s divorce was his biggest fumble.
By Jennifer Wilson
September 21, 2026
There is a certain YouTube clip that I watch from time to time, when I need a pick-me-up, or when I’m in a giddy mood and want to push it further—to the upper reaches of euphoria. The video, from 2018, is titled “Eagles strip sack on Tom Brady - Local Announcers / Multiple Languages,” and it captures seven seconds from the fourth quarter of Super Bowl LII, as witnessed by stunned sportscasters across the globe. On one side were the New England Patriots, led by the clutch quarterback Brady and coached by Bill Belichick, a partnership that had produced five Super Bowl rings. On the other were the hobbled Philadelphia Eagles, my home team, with a second-string quarterback named Nick Foles (Carson Wentz, the team’s top draft pick from 2016, had been sidelined by a torn A.C.L.) and a coach, Doug Pederson, who had previously only ever been in charge of a high-school team (which never won a state championship during his tenure). As Brady gets ready to throw, in what most presumed would be a game-winning drive, it happens. The Eagles defender Brandon Graham fends off a Patriots offensive lineman, reaches his left hand out, and knocks the ball loose from Brady’s grip. “Fuhmble! Fuhmble!” the announcers in Germany scream. “
Incroyable
,” the French commentators say. “Tom Brady bereft on the turf,” the Australians observe of the legendary quarterback, who by then was sitting on the field in shock.
It is a testament to Brady that whenever I watch this clip I feel a touch nervous. If anyone could break open the space-time continuum to retrieve a loose ball and connect with the tight end Rob Gronkowski for a first down, it would be him. By the time he retired, in 2023, Brady had seven Super Bowl rings, the most of any player in the game’s history; his first came in 2002, his last, two decades later. He seemed immune from time itself, as though he were part god. That the quarterback who first found the Patriots’ Achilles’ heel in a Super Bowl was Eli Manning—the younger, bumbling brother of football’s true prince, Peyton Manning—added to the sense that Brady could only be taken down by an accident of fate. After Super Bowl LI, when Brady’s jersey was stolen from a locker room, the Patriots’ owner, Robert Kraft, compared the heist to “taking a great Chagall or Picasso.”
As if all that weren’t enough, in 2009, Brady married Gisele Bündchen, a woman for whom the moniker “supermodel” was deemed insufficient.
New York
magazine dubbed the Brazilian glamazon, who has a reported net worth of four hundred million dollars and twelve hundred magazine covers on her résumé, an “
Über
-model.” She frequently posted photos of herself on social media doing yoga on the beach, like
Forbes’s
richest water sprite. After the Eagles converted Brady’s fumble into the franchise’s first Super Bowl victory, she congratulated every player in green she saw on her way out, leaving them so awestruck it was a wonder that the Patriots hadn’t sent her into the tunnel before the game instead. And she wasn’t just beautiful; she was warm and whimsical. Bündchen, who had two children with Brady, told
People
magazine, “My kids never got sick when I was breastfeeding. If they had something in their eyes, I’d put milk in their eyes.” She was, you might say, the ultimate catch.
And so it has fascinated observers of football and celebrity marriages alike that, when Bündchen nudged her husband to retire, after he won his fifth Super Bowl ring, in 2017, he did not go one further and set Gillette Stadium on fire. Brady did eventually retire, in February of 2022, only to “unretire” forty days later. By August, the couple were living apart, according to tabloid reports. By October, they were divorced. That winter, Brady said that he was retiring “for good.”
Since then, his image has taken a harder hit than any he endured on the field. He popped out of a coffin in a cheesy W.W.E.-inspired skit at Fanatics Fest. He appeared in a Pizza Hut commercial shouting, “Hut!” (Get it?) His attempts to be an on-air sports analyst have underwhelmed. “As a broadcaster, Tom Brady isn’t just Capt. Obvious,” the former Fox Sports commentator Skip Bayless tweeted. “He’s the Commander in Chief of Obvious.” Brady has become a punch line, and the jokes always seem to circle back to his split with Bündchen. One fan referred to his post-retirement antics as “divorced dad side quests.” In Netflix’s 2024 “Roast of Tom Brady,” the comedian Kevin Hart said, of Brady’s final season, “When you got a chance to go 8–9, and all it will cost you is your wife and your kids, you gotta do what the fuck you gotta do.”
Still, I didn’t expect “Brady: An American Story and the Price of Greatness,” a new biography by the former
Sports Illustrated
journalist Lars Anderson, to tell the story of Touchdown Tom’s life through the prism of his divorce. The book—surprisingly intimate despite the fact that Anderson didn’t have access to the golden couple—reads like “Scenes from a Marriage” with a lot more blitzing. It opens with Bündchen and Brady’s first date, in 2006, at the West Village wine bar Turks & Frogs. Anderson writes with exactly the amount of restraint you’d expect of a man whose subjects are a football legend and a Victoria’s Secret model, which is to say—he leaves every metaphor on the field. That night, Bündchen’s eyes were “the mossy green of a primeval forest” while Brady’s were “the glacial blue of a winter sky.” Over drinks, he tells her that he intends to play for ten more years and would be happy to win just one more Super Bowl. Anderson tries to understand why, in the end, Brady couldn’t stick to the game plan, even when the woman whose teeth “glistened with the flawless geometry of freshly fallen snow” asked him to.
The quarterback who averaged a 64.3-per-cent completion rate over his career was almost never born. His father, Tom Brady, Sr., had studied to become a priest. Born in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury neighborhood in 1944, he left home at fourteen to attend a seminary in Chicago, but, Anderson forewarns, he had “wandering, lustful eyes.” A Latin instructor urged him to reconsider his path: “Mr. Brady, you ought to propagate the faithful, not propagate the faith.” Brady’s mother, Galynn Johnson, had grown up on a dairy farm in Minnesota; in high school, she was a cheerleader. In 1968, Johnson was twenty-two, working as a flight attendant for Trans World Airlines, and living in San Francisco, when, one day, there was a knock at the door. It was Brady, Sr., then a travelling insurance salesman. The two soon married and moved to San Mateo, where they had three girls—Maureen, Julie, and Nancy—and then a boy, Thomas Edward Patrick Brady, Jr., born on August 3, 1977.
By most measures, Brady’s childhood was idyllic. (On Google Street View, the home where he grew up resembles, fittingly, the house from “The Brady Bunch.”) But Anderson paints a picture of a boy living in the shadow of his athletic-superstar sisters. Maureen made the U.S. Junior Olympic softball team, Julie was a starter on her college’s soccer team, and Nancy won a softball scholarship to Berkeley. In contrast, Brady was scrawny, slow, and repeatedly picked last for games. Maureen later recalled to the
Eagle-Tribune
a time when “some boys were throwing a football around our street and they told Tommy to go deep. He ran all the way down the street waiting for the football and they turned around and left.”
Tom, Sr., stepped in. When Brady began playing football in high school, his father hired the head coach at the College of San Mateo to train him. He also enlisted a video editor to create a sizzle reel for college scouts. In December of 1994, Billy Harris, who was on the coaching staff at the University of Michigan, noticed a “mystery tape” on his desk. He was used to receiving film from high-school coaches, but this had been mailed from a residential address. Harris hadn’t heard of Brady. “Nobody on the recruiting trail was mentioning him,” he told the
Athletic
in 2020. The university recruited Brady only after its top pick, Bobby Sabelhaus, pulled out at the last minute. (Sabelhaus, who never played in the N.F.L., is now a real-estate agent in Nantucket.)
At Michigan, Brady began as the seventh-string quarterback. “The coaches don’t believe in me,” he told Greg Harden, a counsellor in the athletic department. “You’re right, they don’t,” Harden said, before offering a mantra: “If it was to be, it was up to me.” Brady became a relentless preparer. He did one drill, wherein he would drag his planted foot after throwing the ball, so many times that the nail on his big toe came off. His senior year, during a nationally televised game against Notre Dame, Michigan was trailing at halftime. The coach, Lloyd Carr, replaced the team’s hot-shot sophomore quarterback with Brady. The crowd let out a “wave of boos,” Anderson writes, “the instant his cleats hit the grass.” Brady responded with a fourth-quarter, game-winning comeback.
His ability to produce in big moments was one of the “intangibles” the newly hired Patriots coach Bill Belichick kept seeing in scouting reports. The tangibles were less stellar. At a scouting combine ahead of the draft, Brady had registered the second-slowest forty-yard dash for a quarterback in the event’s history; one coach complained that he looked “more like a damn aluminum siding salesman than a professional quarterback.” The night of the 2000 N.F.L. draft, as the sixth round began, Brady was lying in bed beside his father in his childhood home, realizing that he might never play professional football. Then a call came. The Patriots were selecting him in that round, at No. 199. (Only one Super Bowl-winning quarterback had ever been drafted lower.)
According to Anderson, a key part of the Patriots’ winning formula was Brady’s sense that Belichick had plucked him from obscurity. Anderson quotes Lee Smith, who briefly played alongside Brady in 2011; if Brady had been a first-round pick, Smith suggested, “he could have told Belichick to kiss his ass whenever he’d jump on him. But instead Tom had to impress Belichick.” He went on, “And when your star player is walking on eggshells around the head coach, everyone on the team is doing the same thing, which is what Belichick wanted.” Brady’s history of being undervalued helped him bond with the offensive linemen, who are often treated more like equipment than people, bodies there to protect the brains, i.e., the quarterback. “He’s one of us,” the offensive tackle Clint Oldenburg said during Brady’s first season.
It helped that Brady’s teammates saw him put in the work. One morning, the Patriots safety Rodney Harrison thought that he had finally beaten Brady to the gym by arriving at 5:30
a.m
., only to find him watching film in a meeting room and jotting down notes. “Good afternoon. Did you enjoy sleeping in?” Brady asked Harrison, grinning. In Anderson’s hands, scenes like this read as foreshadowing the marital discord to come, as does a sound bite he includes from the documentary “Tom vs. Time”: “If you compete against me, you better be willing to give up your life, because I’m giving up mine,” Brady says.
In 2002, during his second season, Brady became the youngest quarterback to win a Super Bowl, leading the Patriots to a 20–17 finish over the St. Louis Rams. They won again in 2004, and yet again in 2005. (I watched the latter game, against a Donovan McNabb-led Eagles team, through tears.) With fame came curiosity about his personal life—“His favorite color was blue. He really,
really
loved onion rings,” Anderson writes—and new opportunities. He shadowboxed Muhammad Ali at a charity event. He made a cameo in the Farrelly brothers’ film “Stuck on You” at the urging of the Patriots fan and Boston native Matt Damon. He judged the 2002 Miss U.S.A. pageant in Gary, Indiana. Donald Trump, the pageant’s owner, told the press, “Let me tell you, if one thing stands out about Tom Brady, it’s that he loves those women. And guess what? They love him, too.” That hadn’t been true before; Brady’s teammates, who recalled his failed attempts to pick up women at Boston bars, were taken aback when, during a flight on a private jet to Hawaii for the Pro Bowl, a call came from the “American Pie” actress Tara Reid’s personal assistant, asking whether Brady would like to take Reid out on a date.
Fame also brought out Brady’s quirks. He began working with a “body coach” named Alex Guerrero, whom his teammates referred to as “Mr. Miyagi” from the film “The Karate Kid.” The two developed a strict diet-and-exercise regimen that became known as the TB12 Method. Brady abstained from sugar, caffeine, refined flour, dairy, and “nightshades,” a food group that includes tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant. He began to experiment with fashion. When mocked in the locker room for carrying what looked like a woman’s purse, he yelled back, “It’s a European handbag!” He filled his locker with cologne and aromatic emollients. “I’ve never seen too many Caucasian brothers with cocoa butter,” his teammate Deion Branch told
USA Today
at the time. The Patriots wide receiver Wes Welker said, at a press conference, “He’s probably the toughest metrosexual I’ve ever come across.”
Like David Beckham before him, Brady needed a partner who could understand highlights and the spotlight. In December, 2006, Brady, freshly broken up with the “Sex and the City” actress Bridget Moynahan, received a call from Ed Razek, the chief marketing officer of Victoria’s Secret. (Razek was the subject of a 2020 investigation by the New York
Times
into sexual harassment at the lingerie company; he denied all wrongdoing.) Razek told Brady that he had a “girl version” of the star quarterback. Razek also called Bündchen—whose five-year, on-and-off relationship with Leonardo DiCaprio had come to an end—to say that he had a “boy version” of her. By January, Bündchen was smitten enough to attend her very first game of American football, a playoff matchup with the San Diego Chargers. (In the 2021 ESPN+ documentary “Man in the Arena: Tom Brady,” she admitted, “It was the most boring thing I’ve ever seen in my life. I was, like, ‘What are they doing? Why do they stop all the time? Where is the goal?’ ”) A month later, they were vacationing together in France. While there, Brady received a call from Moynahan. She was pregnant. Anderson takes pains to back up Brady’s claim that things were over with Moynahan by the time he met Bündchen at Turks & Frogs, writing, “A certified obstetrics nurse estimated that, based on the infant’s being born at forty weeks, the date of conception would have been close to November 29, 2006, at least two weeks before Brady’s blind date with Gisele.” That summer, Brady’s first child was born.
Bündchen and Brady were married in a small ceremony in Santa Monica in February of 2009, followed by a vow renewal two months later in Costa Rica. “Each guest was gifted a copy of Don Miguel Ruiz’s pop-psychology guide
The Mastery of Love
about overcoming emotional wounds,” Anderson notes.
Brady was completely under her spell. “You’re lucky you married a witch,” she told him. She gave him “protection stones,” altars for his locker, and new mantras to chant. She “concocted special liquid drops he’d release into his mouth,” Anderson recounts. (We never learn what’s in them.) Brady’s enemies were hers, and, unlike him, she could drink on game day. After the Patriots lost to the New York Giants in Super Bowl XLVI, she was heckled by fans who shouted, “Eli owns your husband!” Bündchen, “emboldened by a glass or two of wine,” Anderson writes, shot back, “My husband cannot fucking throw the ball and catch the ball at the same time.” Her retort made headlines around the world. “I thought I was, like, mild—what I said,” she recalls in “Man in the Arena.” “I mean, it’s true.”
She stood by her husband through Deflategate—Brady’s only major scandal, in which it was discovered that the Patriots were using balls with less air than N.F.L. guidelines required—even when it drew unwanted attention to her. The New York
Post
ran a front-page story titled “COVERUP!”; alongside a picture of Brady, it featured a paparazzi photo, allegedly of Bündchen disguised in a burqa as she entered a Parisian plastic-surgery clinic. Like him, she could stay calm in the pocket. “She is always looking at, you know, the positive side of everything,” Brady’s oldest sister, Maureen, said. “She always says, ‘Why is this happening
for
me?,’ not ‘Why is this happening
to
me?’ ” She also helped in material ways. The Patriots were able to surround Brady with an unusual level of talent because he could accept a salary below that of other élite quarterbacks. “My wife makes a lot of money,” he told Jimmy Kimmel.
I’m a fan of books about sports. (I once almost created a podcast on the subject; I planned to call it “The Bookie.”) The best ones situate athletes in history. Buzz Bissinger’s “Friday Night Lights” is about high-school football the way that the documentary “Hoop Dreams” is about basketball. Both capture the shrinking aperture of opportunity in a country founded on the idea of limitless possibility. David Maraniss’s “Path Lit by Lightning: The Life of Jim Thorpe” considers how the Native American football legend wrestled with what it meant to be “all-American.”
The ambitions of Anderson’s book are slight by comparison, its stakes those of a preseason game. Brady is a man who began playing professionally at the dawn of a new millennium, but you wouldn’t know it here. In his era, the football field became the site of a bold act of protest against racial injustice, yet the name Colin Kaepernick does not appear once. (In 2017, Brady did not join his teammates who kneeled during the national anthem, though he did lock arms with others, in a small show of solidarity.) Anderson rushes through Brady’s relationship with Donald Trump. In 2015, a week after a
MAGA
hat had been spotted in Brady’s locker by reporters, he said that he hoped Trump would win. “There would be a putting green on the White House lawn,” he quipped. (The next year, when an Instagram user asked if Bündchen and Brady supported Trump, she responded, “NO!,” and Brady skipped the Patriots’ White House visit after winning the Super Bowl in 2017, citing “personal family matters.”)
We hear about Brady’s teammate Aaron Hernandez being arrested for homicide, but Anderson doesn’t bring up the player’s subsequent suicide or the autopsy finding of Hernandez’s severe case of chronic traumatic encephalopathy. The closest we get to any discussion of C.T.E. comes from Bündchen. “He had a concussion last year,” she said to Charlie Rose in 2017. “He has concussions pretty much every—I mean, we don’t talk about it, but he does have concussions. And I don’t really think it’s a healthy thing for your body to go through. . . . I’m planning on having him be healthy and do a lot of fun things when we’re, like, a hundred, I hope.” It was a shocking claim, as there was no record of head trauma on any of Brady’s injury reports, which would have required that he comply with the N.F.L.’s concussion protocol; her allegation prompted an inquiry by the league.
There’s no sense in Anderson’s book that Brady is a man of our age, except in the worst possible ways. Brady could choose when to retire, but some of his own fans were deprived of that option. Michael Livieratos, a Patriots supporter, put his life savings into FTX after seeing his hero promote the cryptocurrency firm. (Sam Bankman-Fried paid Brady fifty-five million dollars for sixty hours of promotional work, and Gisele eighteen million to appear alongside her husband.) No, the big question of the book seems to be this: Can a man really claim that he’s won it all if he fumbled Gisele? I must confess I took some pleasure in seeing a man subjected to the narrative that the end of his marriage is a life-defining moment, his most important story. If he were a woman, this book would be a best-selling memoir.
Anderson, noting that Bündchen’s star sign is Cancer, quotes an astrological report from the summer before their divorce that appeared in
Cosmopolitan
: “Honest, raw conversations will be necessary as power struggles and hidden agendas are exposed. This is your opportunity to transform the dynamics in your closest ties.” When Brady arrived at training camp ahead of that year’s season, the coaching staff found him “gaunt and cadaverous,” Anderson writes. In 2025, a little more than three years after their split, it was reported that Bündchen had married her jujitsu instructor, Joaquim Valente. Soon after the news broke, Brady posted a selfie on Instagram from a car, wearing a sweatshirt that read “
Forever Young
,” with the song “1-800-273-8255,” by Logic, playing in the background, the title a reference to the national suicide-prevention hotline.
In the end, it’s Bündchen’s objections to Brady’s insatiable desire for more—more rings, more wins, more record-breaking—that give the book its heft. Brady retired at forty-five, when he was the oldest starting quarterback in N.F.L. history. He played his final seasons with Tampa Bay, which I could understand; perhaps he hoped to prove that he could win a Super Bowl without Belichick, and he did. But he wanted another, and another—which does, one could argue, tie him to this moment in our country, when no quest for more feels out of bounds. In “Tom vs. Time,” Bündchen tells the camera that football was her husband’s first love. “And I think it’s, like, his main love, really,” she adds. Brady jokes that if she had it her way, after his Super Bowl LI victory the pair would have moved to Costa Rica, where as of late she has been photographed walking hand in hand along the beach with Valente. She was done with this “American story.” How many more times could she say,
Enough, you already have enough.
♦

What’s Really Behind the Baby Bust?
Books
What’s Really Behind the Baby Bust?
People say they want more children than they’re having. Is modern life stopping them—or have our ideas about a good life changed?
By Margaret Talbot
September 21, 2026
If you’ve followed the debate over falling birth rates in the United States, you could be forgiven for thinking that most of the fretting comes from the anti-feminist right. In recent years, Vice-President J. D. Vance has emerged as a cranky pro-natalist, deriding “childless cat ladies,” blaming “secular global liberalism” for population decline, and, in happier moments, as at an anti-abortion rally last year, declaring, “I want more babies in the United States of America” and more “beautiful young men and women” eager to make and rear them. A report from the conservative Heritage Foundation earlier this year sounded the alarm over the drop in U.S. fertility, linking it to “second-wave feminism” and other familiar culture-war culprits: “casual sex, abortion, childlessness by choice, and no-fault divorce,” all of which menaced “the natural family,” which was helmed by a heterosexual husband and wife. Many of these voices agree with the determinedly fecund Elon Musk (at least fourteen kids and counting), who has said, “Population collapse due to low birth rates is a much bigger risk to civilization than global warming.” Recent polling shows that, among the growing percentage of Americans who think we should be at least somewhat worried about the birth rate, men worry more than women, and Republicans more than Democrats.
Running through this conversation is a theory about what people want. A big reason people have fewer children, the argument goes, is that they no longer want them enough. Feminism, secularism, individualism, and sexual freedom have weakened the old attachments to marriage and family. In this account, the explanation is largely cultural.
Another story about falling fertility, however, begins from almost the opposite premise: plenty of people still want children, often more than they wind up having. What has changed are the social and economic conditions people need to create the families they’d hoped to have. Housing is ruinously expensive. Child care is costly, too. Jobs are demanding and insecure. Finding a reliable partner can feel harder than ever. From this perspective, the fertility slump is a record of frustrated longing.
Anna Louie Sussman, the author of “
Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty
” (Dey Street), forcefully makes this second case. She is not a social conservative or a soapbox pro-natalist. The censorious baby boosters at Heritage would not be fans of the way she chose to reproduce. Sussman, a single journalist in New York, travelled to Bologna to retrieve eggs that she’d frozen there six years earlier, when she was thirty-four (egg freezing was cheaper in Europe), then flew to another European city, charged about three thousand dollars to her credit card for an embryo-transfer procedure (it would have cost about fifteen thousand dollars in the U.S.), and got pregnant. Her gay best friend, Anthony, became her daughter’s adoptive father, and his parents joined a small, devoted community of caregivers for their child.
Sussman nevertheless shares Vance and Musk’s conviction that something has gone seriously wrong when so few babies are being born. She just views the shortage as symptomatic of societal woes that conservatives have little to say about: the costs of housing, health care, and higher education; fear of a climate-changed future; feelings of precarity, immediate and anticipated; and obstacles to finding a potential co-parent. She largely attributes these phenomena to the workings of modern capitalism on our bank accounts and psyches. She is less concerned with the birth rate per se than with the experience of forgoing children. She is not, she writes, “arguing for people to have more or fewer children, or about the importance of children for economic purposes”—shoring up tax bases, saving pension systems, and the like.
What troubles Sussman is the gap between how many kids people say they want and how many are born. A 2025 U.N. study asked fourteen thousand people across fourteen countries how many children they wanted and how many they expected to have. Most wanted two; not even four in ten expected to achieve that. A Gallup poll that year showed something similar among Americans surveyed: forty per cent said that having two children was optimal, and twenty-seven per cent said three. (That’s roughly in line with results from previous decades.) But at current rates many families won’t get there.
“When so many people hesitate to have children,” Sussman writes, “what is lost is not simply future taxpayers or consumers. We miss out on the rich relationships that bond us across generations, on the flood of love and tenderness that caring for children, or simply being around them, can unleash.” She adds that the “retreat from parenthood also encapsulates a dissatisfaction with our present so extreme it has become a vote against the future.”
The scale of the fertility decline makes the issue hard to dismiss. Global fertility rates fell from an average of about five births per woman in the nineteen-sixties to 2.2 in 2024. Most countries, representing about seventy per cent of the world’s population, have rates below the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman. In the United States, the rate is now 1.6. In South Korea—where dog strollers outsell baby strollers, and playgrounds and elementary-school classrooms can be eerily empty—it is below one. In the U.S., almost half of women aged thirty are childless, compared with eighteen per cent in 1976.
So who has the better analysis of what is happening? Have people’s priorities changed, or has building the families they hoped for become more onerous? If millions still want children but are discouraged from having them, then the fertility slump marks a substantial social failure. And there is plenty in contemporary life to bolster Sussman’s case.
Consider what parenthood now asks of people. A big part of the story is the shift toward what the economists Melissa Kearney and Phillip Levine describe as “much more resource and time-intensive” parenting. Many young adults who started families in the past twenty years were raised this way, which shaped their own conceptions of how to rear children. If families want to invest in extracurriculars and a college education for their children, while lavishing time and attention on them, then doing so for five, rather than, say, one or two, may seem impossible.
Time-use studies have shown a steady increase since the nineteen-seventies in the hours that parents in rich countries devote to child care. Millennial mothers and fathers in the United States spend more time tending to their offspring than Gen X-ers did. Recently, as I was reading research papers on declining birth rates, an unfamiliar finding glinted up at me like a penny on the sidewalk. In countries where male involvement in child care and housework is highest—Norway, for example—male parents tend to oppose having additional children. You might see this as a bummer: Mr. Moms overwhelmed by ordinary domestic duties. Or you might see it, as I did, as evidence that men who participate more actively in such tasks develop a healthy respect for what they require.
Turning to South Korea, contemporary demographers’ favorite example of a reproductive desert, Sussman examines one particularly punishing form of souped-up child rearing: the culture of
hagwon
, or afternoon and evening cram schools. These institutions are de rigueur for children hoping to reach university in a hypercompetitive system, and they require parents, almost exclusively mothers, to collect their exhausted, fact-stuffed kids late at night, up to six days a week. People in Seoul told Sussman that the system had turned them against parenting: they felt unable to avoid
hagwon
and unwilling to subject future children to it.
For many would-be parents, the demands of child rearing are not the first hurdle. Before having kids, they want to find someone to raise them with. Here, too, Sussman assembles a formidable catalogue of impediments. Dating apps are too much like online shopping. (There’s some overlap here with the Heritage Foundation’s critique of dating apps, which similarly targets their profit-driven, algorithmic incentives for “continuous scrolling and swiping,” as its family report puts it.) Plastic surgery and inflationary beauty standards impose dizzying upkeep. A surfeit of online porn scrambles young men’s expectations of sex. And social media encourages “relentless packaging and marketing of the self.” A 2020 Pew Research Center survey found that thirty-five per cent of never married, single American adults hadn’t ever been in a committed romantic relationship. In a 2024 survey, eighty per cent of singles reported “emotional fatigue or burnout” from online dating. The research shows, Sussman says, that the biggest reason women choose to freeze their eggs is that they haven’t found the right partner. “At a time when we have more social and sexual freedom than at any point in history,” she writes, “it can feel harder than ever to find genuine connection.”
Sussman’s portraits both illustrate and complicate these diagnoses, as individuals tend to. In a chapter about dating, she introduces Michaela, who, in her late thirties, is dating “more diligently than anyone I know,” mostly through apps. Michaela is multilingual, outgoing, and, Sussman tells us, “tall and voluptuous, with lush, dark eyelashes.” She is an Ivy League graduate and business owner who wants a partner and a child but has gone on some two hundred dates without luck. By the book’s end, though, she does find a partner, IRL, and has a baby with him. She told a stranger on a train that she was single, and the woman introduced her to an American living in the South of France. It would have been fan service to tell us more about the romance, but this is all we get. Another subject in the book, Marwan, also wants to be a parent, and gets many online matches when he lists his job as a McKinsey consultant. But when he quits to start his own firm and makes time for friends, reading, sports, and volunteering, his profile draws much less interest. He is still “tall and handsome, with a gregarious smile,” and an Oxford Ph.D., according to Sussman—but “self-employed” is evidently a turnoff. (Message to Marwan: I know some delightful women for whom “McKinsey” would be the turnoff.)
Yet the closer you look at the gap between desired and actual fertility, the harder it is to know what it measures. Some parents probably change their minds without much regret after one or two children—content with the family they’ve created, persuaded by the solidity and particularity of its configuration that it, not some theoretical alternative, is right, or sobered by child rearing’s demands (perhaps a child has special needs). The South Korean example suggests a related possibility.
Hagwon
culture is a grim version of a more benign, mutually rewarding form of cultivated, small-batch parenting—one in which adults and children know one another well because they’ve spent time trying to, parents foster their kids’ interests and eccentricities, and people find in family life what the historian and social critic Christopher Lasch called a haven from the heartless world.
More tellingly, wanting two or three children already represents a domestic vision far removed from the teeming households of pioneer families, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” or even “The Brady Bunch.” The fact that people want smaller families than they once did isn’t necessarily a vote against the future. It’s a vote against past family sizes, from eras when more people relied on children for labor, expected extras to make up for ravening child mortality, or felt religiously bound to multiply bountifully. (These motivations persist even in affluent countries, such as among Orthodox Jewish families in the United States and Israel. But Mormons are having fewer children; Utah’s birth rate has declined more than any other state’s, by thirty-seven per cent since 2007.) In the 2025 Gallup poll, only eleven per cent of Americans surveyed said that four kids was ideal, and just four per cent said five.
“Inconceivable” is not a policy book; it’s a reported social critique sauced with stories. Inevitably, though, Sussman touches on what societies might do, or have tried to do, in order to arrest falling fertility. As she suggests, and as recent studies demonstrate, interventions aimed at boosting birth rates—such as tax credits or baby bonuses—tend to have modest or short-term effects. Eleven Swiss cantons have introduced birth allowances over the years, and one study found that the payments increased fertility, mainly among lower-income immigrants, but the effect quickly faded. When Hungary, under Viktor Orbán, devoted about five per cent of its G.D.P. to an elaborate system of family subsidies, the spending seemed to stabilize the average age at which women first gave birth. But it had little effect on over-all fertility; mainly, it nudged people into having the children they would have had anyway, just a little earlier.
Other policies that might be expected to hike the birth rate by making it easier to combine work and family life often have transitory or relatively small effects, too. In the nineteen-eighties, Sweden extended a provision in its family-leave system that rewarded parents for having another child relatively soon after the previous one, and many did so. The result, as the economists Kearney and Levine report, was “a temporary baby boom, that was subsequently offset by a baby bust.” Of all the family-friendly policies, spending on early-childhood education and child care appears to do the most to goose birth rates—especially when aligned with the right leave policies. But, according to a U.N. report, child-care provision is “more likely to influence the fertility behavior of highly educated women, who are more active in the labor market.” And, for those of us still capable of being surprised at how hard and costly it can be to budge human behavior, the numbers are a little underwhelming: in one study, every extra percentage point of G.D.P. spent on early-childhood education and child care was “associated with 0.2 extra children per woman.”
The unfettered free market of the U.S. certainly hasn’t boosted birth rates—but neither have Scandinavia’s generous social guarantees. Birth rates have plunged in social democracies and capitalist autocracies alike. Norway and the U.S. are about equally fecund. “Strong family policies and social supports,” Sussman writes, “are just a baseline. They should ensure that if and when someone would like to become a parent, they do not face job loss, financial ruin, or catastrophic health bills, and that children and their parents have enough to eat and quality child care if parents want to work. But they are no longer themselves capable of producing the conditions under which people want to, or choose to, have children.”
That qualification seems significant. If making parenthood materially easier does little to restore birth rates, perhaps some part of the fertility decline reflects a change in what people want from their lives. Fewer people consider marriage and children indispensable to a rewarding adulthood. In a 2023 Pew poll, seventy-one per cent of American adults said that an enjoyable job or career was very important to a fulfilling life, whereas only twenty-six per cent said children and twenty-three per cent marriage. (Sixty-one per cent said close friends.)
Sussman is inclined to see such preferences as further evidence of capitalism’s moral failings. I’m sympathetic. Loving your work is great, but career obsession can be its own form of sterility; corporations aren’t people, and most employers would sooner lay you off than understand your ineffable you-ness. Sussman cites one study in which women who had substantial student-loan debt were around forty per cent less likely to have kids than those who didn’t carry debt. That seems bleak, too.
But the poll’s answers can also point to a genuinely enlarged sense of what a satisfactory life might contain. People can experience love and tenderness for younger generations without biological parenthood, as any devoted aunt or teacher can attest. They can build lives around friendship, work, art, travel, activism, or community, in ways less constrained by old ideas about virtuous adulthood. Some changes associated with lower fertility are plainly gains. Teen-pregnancy rates have dropped dramatically, women have far more educational and professional opportunities, and social norms that stigmatized childlessness have loosened. (For a horrified laugh, check out
a 1968 episode
called “Spinsters” from the BBC documentary series “Man Alive,” on YouTube. Sample line of narration, about an unmarried woman in her thirties: “She fills her life with activities which some might call substitutes—she paints and is learning the classical guitar.”)
So it makes sense to be cautious about treating peoples’ stated preferences about children as a kind of buried truth, and the gap between what people say they want and what they wind up having as chiefly a measure of the obstacles placed in their way. Having a child is the most overdetermined of choices: intimate, nearly instinctual, and yet deeply embedded in cultural norms and social structures. That makes the birth rate a particularly inadequate barometer of whether a given family policy is worthwhile. The reason to institute strong family supports—for example, to have a national policy offering paid leave for new mothers and fathers in the United States, the one wealthy country that does not do so—isn’t because they act like levers to push out more babies. It’s because they make people’s lives better, and societies kinder, more equitable, and more forbearing.
Every time I read about declining fertility—whether it’s a right-wing pro-natalist screed about permissive, secular culture; an earnest, progressive account of how contemporary capitalism constrains our most fundamental choices while presenting a simulacrum of infinite options; or, for that matter, a sober statistical analysis from the O.E.C.D.—I realize that I can’t quite imagine the combination of forces that would reverse the worldwide trend toward fewer babies and smaller families. So many modern humans seem to want many things at once: children, autonomy, absorbing work, a certain standard of parenting, and a particular sort of romantic partner. The fertility rate reflects the priorities that emerge when decisions have to be made. Economic factors play a role, but culture plays a larger one and is less amenable to policy interventions. Culture encompasses ideas about what adulthood should entail, what parents owe their children, how much sacrifice family should require, how parents and other caregivers should divide their child-rearing duties, and whether having children makes a life bigger or smaller.
Those ideas can’t be legislated into existence, yet institutions, social movements, customs, and habits can shape them over time. Norms do shift, sometimes unpredictably, as people watch one another live. If smaller families arose partly from changing ideas about a good life, we can’t assume that those ideas have reached their final form. The postwar American baby boom itself reversed a century-long decline in family size. Whether or not we see another baby boom, my vote is for giving up on policies aimed at coaxing or prodding people into having children, and for making family life easier for the people—and they will always be with us—who dearly want them. ♦

Briefly Noted
“The Maltese Version,” “That Summer’s End,” “Berlin Before and After,” and “Jean Toomer.”
September 21, 2026
The Maltese Version
, by Katy Simpson Smith (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)
. The timeworn saying about there being two sides to every story gains new dimension in this probing novel, which posits that “two sides means there are two stories.” Here, readers are presented with four sides, each belonging to a different woman connected to the same man: Max, a literary translator. One of the women, Max’s mentor, Herschel, induces him to go to Malta, to work on a collection by a local poet, Ana. When his girlfriend, Leonie, can’t get ahold of him, she deploys her friend Rhoda to investigate. As their lives intersect, Smith asks, How do we make meaning, and how do we convey it?
That Summer’s End
, by Lee Seong-bok, translated from the Korean by Anton Hur (Knopf)
. Nature, loss, and longing inspire these quiet verses, which conjure a sense of the immense mysteries governing the observable world. “How do feelings come / a bough first blossoms,” the book’s opening poem, “Feeling,” begins. “Is that how feelings come / a bough first drops its blossoms / Is that how feelings fall.” Lee’s lines have the intimacy and metaphysical heft of prayer; their elegant recursions and repetitions call to mind the cycles of life, death, and rebirth. Many of his poems are titled simply, in reference to the people, objects, animals, and abstractions on which he trains his attention—“Sea,” “Mountain,” “Cat,” “Child.” Throughout, Lee’s invocations imbue his subjects with an air of divinity.
What We’re Reading
Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
Berlin Before and After
, by Wendy Lesser (Harper)
. This adoring tribute to Berlin considers the city’s history as a “cautionary mirror” for the present. Lesser, as a secular Jew born in California in the shadow of the Second World War, confesses to having once possessed an “ingrained distaste” for Germany. Yet when she began travelling there, in 2003, she developed an intense fondness for its capital. As her narrative moves from the vivid cultural ferment of the Weimar Republic to the era of Berlin’s division and on to today, it touches on figures such as Bertolt Brecht, Gerhard Richter, and Jenny Erpenbeck, and examines how Germany has memorialized the crimes perpetrated by the Nazis and the German Democratic Republic. Ultimately, Lesser’s goal is to show what other cultures can learn from the fact that, there, “the desire to wipe out the disparaged past did not prevail.”
Jean Toomer
, by George Hutchinson (Yale)
. This illuminating biography focusses on the Harlem Renaissance writer, best known for the experimental work “Cane,” from 1923, which has since become a highlight of modernist and African American literature. As Hutchinson makes clear, Toomer had a complex relationship to Blackness; his grandfather was the mixed-race son of an enslaved woman—a heritage that Toomer embraced, before pretending ignorance of it. He also rejected the overtly racialized way that his work was categorized, a view that sprang from his belief that all people belong to the same “basic human stock,” and that, as Hutchinson writes, “the so-called separate races were products of false labeling.”
