The Curious Power of Punctuation
A Critic at Large
The Curious Power of Punctuation
Commas, dashes, semicolons, and spaces have shaped how we read for centuries. What happens when machines start crafting the sentences?
By Louis Menand
September 21, 2026
Do you know the first sentence of “
Pride and Prejudice
”? You probably think you do, but I bet you don’t. The answer is “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” Did you remember to put in the commas?
What are those commas doing there, anyway? By modern usage, they should mark off a non-restrictive clause, but they don’t. Nor are they marking items in a series or natural pauses in speech. Did Jane Austen even write them? Probably not. Judging by her few surviving manuscripts, Austen didn’t much use commas (or paragraphs). She used dashes.
Here is a passage from the manuscript of her last finished novel, “
Persuasion
”:
“To see you, cried he, in the midst of those who could not be my well-wishers, to see your Cousin close by you—conversing & smiling—& feel all the horrible Eligibilities & Proprieties of the Match!—to consider it as the certain wish of every being who could hope to influence you—even, if your own feelings were reluctant, or indifferent—to consider what powerful supports would be his !”
Here is the same passage from the published book:
“To see you,” cried he, “in the midst of those who could not be my well-wishers, to see your cousin close by you, conversing and smiling, and feel all the horrible eligibilities and proprieties of the match! To consider it as the certain wish of every being who could hope to influence you! Even if your own feelings were reluctant or indifferent, to consider what powerful supports would be his!”
And so on. The published version replaces five dashes and three ampersands, and lowercases four capitalized nouns. It sounds more like Austen, but maybe Austen really sounded like Virginia Woolf.
Austen must have made some of these revisions herself, but it is believed that the grammar and punctuation in her later novels were cleaned up by a man named William Gifford, who was an editor at Austen’s publisher, John Murray. (“Pride and Prejudice” was an early novel, published by a different house.) Which might mean that the polished, quasi-epigrammatic sentences we find so Austenian may not be sentences Austen actually wrote.
Florence Hazrat, the author of “
On the Mark: From Periods to Interrobangs, How Punctuation Remade the World
” (Basic), would wish to point out that the difference for the reader in these two versions of “Persuasion” is entirely a function of the punctuation. Change dashes to commas, smooth out the prose, and the whole Austen experience is altered. What was pell-mell and excited becomes thoughtful and decorous.
Hazrat’s book is a history of punctuation—or some punctuation, since it barely mentions the apostrophe, the serial comma, or quotation marks. “On the Mark” is a “the X that changed the world” book, which is a popular genre. Its claim is that “the history of punctuation is the history of humanity.”
This ambition inevitably leads to overreach. If punctuation played a role in everything, what about, say, the war in Gaza? Hazrat finds a link. “Punctuation marks in Hebrew,” she explains, “are relics of a brutal colonial system that is far from over.” Adding punctuation turned Hebrew into a spoken language, “paving the way for an artificial sense of unity among Jewish people from all over the globe, encouraging them to move to the land that already had people—a people made to suffer and bear the brunt of European anti-Semitism in the most horrendous ways for generations.” It seems (the reason is not altogether clear) that, had Yiddish been the official language of Israel, atrocities might have been avoided.
Zionist complicities aside, Hazrat is a punctuation enthusiast, though there are a few marks that she is not very fond of. The semicolon is one. She calls it “a dreamy kind of mark for meandering minds.” I would have said that the comma splice is the dreamy mark for meandering minds, not the semicolon, whose function is to replace the comma splice. But she doesn’t seem to know the semicolon’s correct usage. She thinks it’s a big comma, when it’s actually a small period.
On the other hand, she can’t get enough of the parenthesis, which, she says, dates to antiquity. I had always thought of parentheticals as subversive, a teasing or skeptical interpolation, the equivalent of a raised eyebrow. Hazrat understands them in pretty much the opposite way. “The parenthesis is a gentle kind of interruption, stable and predictable and balanced,” she says. “The parenthesis in word and deed is an ethical way of life.” (Since I use a lot of parentheses, this was encouraging.)
She tells us that the sentence-ending period was invented by Aristophanes of Byzantium, the head of the Library of Alexandria, in the second or third century B.C.E.; that the earliest known question mark is in a fifth-century document written in Syriac, a language close to Aramaic, which Jesus spoke; and that the exclamation mark dates from the mid-fourteenth century. The invention of the printing press, around 1440, let loose what she describes as “a flurry of signs,” including the semicolon, quotation marks, the dash, and the ellipsis. No new marks have been added since 1600 (unless you count emojis, which we will get to).
In Hazrat’s view, the greatest changed-the-world punctuation mark of all time is the space. She tells us that it was invented in the eighth century by Irish monks to separate the words in a sentence. She calls this hack “revolutionary.” “Perhaps,” she says, “it would be a stretch to say that the Irish monks’ invention led to the liberations of classes and genders, caused wars and peaceful pacts, and paved the way for economic booms and busts, literary masterpieces from
Hamlet
to
Les Misérables
, and the development of the internet. Perhaps that’s going too far, and perhaps not far enough.”
I would say too far. But she has a point. The history of punctuation
is
the history of humanity in the sense that changes in the technology of writing—changes in how we write and how we make what we have written available to readers—correlate with changes in the distribution of social power. The purpose of punctuation is to make writing easier to read, and making writing easier to read means giving greater and greater numbers of people access to the written word. Literacy is no longer the monopoly of a privileged class. Today, even the gatekeepers are gone, or have turned into paywalls.
The excitement that Hazrat feels about punctuation—little marks that make a big difference—is a lot like Sarah L. Kaufman’s enthusiasm for verbs. Verbs, Kaufman tells us in “
Verb Your Enthusiasm: How to Master the Art of the Verb and Transform Your Writing
” (Penguin Press), “can leap off the page and land in our bodies. They tickle the senses. They delight the instinct for movement. At times, they may tell you something true about yourself. All that in a word.” Verbs are infinitely adaptable, she says. They are “the Cate Blanchetts of language.”
The book is about how to use and misuse the different parts of speech (there are nine), with an emphasis on the verb. Kaufman has a favorite sentence that serves as a touchstone. It’s the last sentence of “
The Great Gatsby
,” and I bet you do know this one: “So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.” She grows eloquent on the magic of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s diction. “You might feel his verbs in your body, so delicately you’re not quite aware of it,” she says. “The repeated
B
sound—beat, boats, borne back—is percussive. The physical resonance of the verb
beat
may echo internally in many ways, as you feel a soft drumbeat, as your heart beats. Reading ‘borne back’ may light a brief, indistinct flickering inside, a sense of how your own consciousness can whoosh backward in time.”
Apart from the fact that I have never understood what Fitzgerald is trying to say here—isn’t the whole point of the book not that Gatsby is doomed to return to the past but that he can’t?—I think that “beat” and “borne” lack visual concreteness. Shouldn’t it be “paddle”? “Paddle” sounds a little silly, but that’s the metaphor Fitzgerald is using. (Those boats must be canoes, not steamboats. A steamboat wouldn’t care that much about a current.)
Kaufman spent many years as the chief dance critic for the Washington
Post
, a job that must demand novel and unexpected ways of saying “leaping,” “lifting,” and “pirouetting”—hence her verb fascination. But she has thoughts about other parts of speech as well, and she offers a good deal of usage advice. Basically, “Verb Your Enthusiasm” is a style guide for newspaper writers: cut down on adjectives and adverbs, avoid the passive voice, prefer monosyllabic words, always say “he said” (not “he shouted,” “whispered,” “stated,” “averred,” and so on).
These tips make for good newspaper writing, but unless you are Ernest Hemingway, who began his career as a newspaper reporter and credited the Kansas City
Star’s
style guide with forming the basis of his style, they do not define good writing per se. Newspaper writing differs from most other writing because print-newspaper space is finite. The fewer words you use, and the more recognizable they are, the more you can say and the faster you can say it. That is where this modern minimalist verbal style comes from. Joan Didion, the mistress of concision and a Hemingway admirer, began her career writing captions and sidebars to fit around pictures in women’s magazines. Most writers don’t have those constraints, real or imaginary.
Still, Kaufman thinks that, if we are looking to speed the eye and save space, one part of speech we should be happy to throw overboard is the adverb. Her point is that if you have picked the right verb it won’t need to be modified. And many adverbs (“really,” “truly,” “literally”) do seem to be empty intensifiers. “Adverbial crutches are everywhere and misused in the extreme,” she warns (or, if you prefer, “says”). Her particular bête noire is “actually,” which she calls “one of the most annoying and overused words in the English language.”
Microsoft Word doesn’t like “actually,” either. It tells me that “more concise language would be clearer for the reader.” I know this because I have already used “actually” twice in this piece, and I set off a Word alarm both times. Did they annoy you? Wouldn’t it have been more annoying if I had used, for example, italics, as in “sentences Jane Austen
wrote
”? Adverbs and italics often do the same work, but unless you are J. D. Salinger, who had a genius for them, italics can seem like an artificial pumping up of significance, verbal Viagra. Still, I have used italics in that manner once in this piece. And adverbs, even the intensifiers, can add shading and tone to a sentence. I can see giving them up for directness, but it is a trade-off. Writers have a toolbox. Why not use the whole kit?
E-mail, text messaging, and the internet have swamped us with new signifiers. I no longer need parentheses; I can use a raised-eyebrow emoji instead. I don’t write to someone anymore; I e-mail or D.M. them. “E-mail” is a denominalization, a noun turned into a verb. E-mail was a thing before it was a thing you did.
Denominalizations are not new. They happen constantly, and Kaufman, as a verb person, has an attraction to them. She says that Fitzgerald used “to cocktail” as a verb, as in “
Cocktailest thou? Dost cocktail? Wilt cocktail?
” But she notes that the coinage dates from the eighteen-sixties. Much of denominalization amounts to a brand war. Today, we say “I Googled it,” but not “I Binged it” or “I DuckDuckGo-ed it,” just as we say “I Ubered to the restaurant,” but not “I Lyfted to the restaurant” or, God forbid, “I Hertzed to the restaurant.” I can FedEx a package, and maybe UPS one, but at the post office it’s always “I mailed the package.”
It is, of course, all a corporate plot to insinuate commercial products into our everyday lives, a strategy that has been colossally successful for brands like Scotch Tape, Band-Aid, and Kleenex. Someday, “I Ubered” will just mean “I used a car service”; maybe it does already. There are also what I guess could be called deverbalizations: “the reveal,” “the ask.” But Kaufman doesn’t get into those. (A super-annoying and omnipresent related usage is “weaponize.” Use of that non-word must stop, today.)
These books are reminders that we are in the middle of a revolution in the phenomenology of reading, a major change in what it is like to consume writing. Many written texts we simply decode—instruction manuals, advertising copy, legal boilerplate. But, when we read for pleasure or for edification, we imagine a person “behind” the words. We treat writing as substitute speech. We say “That’s Jane Austen” or “That’s Virginia Woolf.” We feel we get to know writers by the sound of their words. More grandly, we experience writing as a way of transmitting an author’s state of mind, or set of emotions, to our own.
But, today, digital systems can generate Austen-like and Woolf-like sentences. We had feelings about our imaginary Austens and Woolfs; we “knew” them. But we are starting to realize that it is pointless, or stupid, to have feelings about sentences that a program spews out at an alarming rate. At some point, we will stop anthropomorphizing the words on the page or on the screen and start treating them the way we treat numbers, as marks to decode. When that happens, what will be left of the reading experience?
Hazrat and Kaufman subscribe to the theory of embodied cognition. They want us to understand reading as a somatic experience. “Verbs ignite emotions, transform our thoughts, and stimulate our bodies,” Kaufman says. That’s why she hears a heartbeat in Fitzgerald’s famous sentence. Hazrat puts it this way: “Punctuation enables us to access a text as a multidimensional full-bodied, full-mind experience.” Their books are therefore, in some respects, elegies to a conception of reading and writing which seems to be nearing an end.
We talk back to our G.P.S., and we say rude things to Siri. But that’s because we are mainly still living in a pre-A.I. world. The A.I. world itself still feels foreign. There is a creepy fascination with stories about people who fall for their chatbots, lawyers who submit A.I.-generated briefs, students who hand in ChatGPT-ed writing assignments. But we will adapt. Soon, people will no longer make a distinction between writing made by a human and writing made by a machine. It will all simply be writing. In that world, reading will no longer be the kind of embodied experience that Hazrat and Kaufman memorialize.
Hazrat complains about the disembodied feel of text messaging, and the fact that, as she reports, ninety-one per cent of Americans believe they can express themselves better in emojis than in written words. “No video conferencing or instant text messaging can replace presence,” she says, “and so we cling to the make-believe of technology.” What we are experiencing, she thinks, is not an ordinary shift in language use: “Generative AI confronts us with the possibility of a near-total abandonment of thinking work, that is, reading and writing. The surface engagement (if it can be called even that) of having ChatGPT read articles for us is already impacting our cognitive faculties negatively.”
She admits that chatbots have all sorts of personalized features, but they’re all fake. The conversational tone keeps us “talking” to the computer “because it feels like a real person,” she says. “Feedback functions like the typing awareness indicator and feel-good marks like emojis keep us online, keep us sending one more message, and another, and another, trying to finally get what we crave, connection, through something that simply cannot provide that, technology.”
Texting has virtually eliminated punctuation, undoing the centuries of innovation that gave sentences rhythm, shape, and meaning. Texters often forgo capitals and question marks (although they do overuse exclamation marks), and the period is avoided. “The polite way to be rude now is to use correct punctuation,” Hazrat says.
Kaufman is less apocalyptic. “No bot—so far—can craft poetic physical language that makes us feel something,” she assures us. Surely it’s only a matter of time. L.L.M.s already write poetry; the question is how good they can become at it. Right now, there is little money to be made from making them better poets. When there is, or even if there never is, they will keep improving in much the same way human beings do: by reading lots of poetry and learning what works. In the end, writing is just a technology. There is nothing magical about it. The usual worry is that we will mistake a machine’s poem for a person’s. The more dispiriting prospect is that we will dismiss a person’s poem as A.I. slop. We admire the person who can make good sentences, like Austen or Fitzgerald. Can we admire the makers of a generative A.I. that can do the same? ♦

Waiting for Jay-Z
Pop Music
Waiting for Jay-Z
In a sold-out run at Yankee Stadium and an eight-part documentary on HBO, the rapper makes the latest case for his own singularity.
By Hua Hsu
September 21, 2026
It was nearing midnight on a balmy Sunday in July, and there was still no sight of Jay-Z. This was the last of three sold-out concerts at Yankee Stadium, and somehow the tens of thousands of fans gathered inside didn’t appear too aggrieved, peaceably bopping along to old soul tunes on the P.A. and eating chicken tenders out of souvenir boxes shaped like Timberland boots. We take the magnitude of Jay for granted. “I made the Yankee hat more famous than a Yankee can,” he once rapped, a boast that’s come to seem less outlandish with time. No other artist has withstood hip-hop’s changing winds over such a long span, let alone won so many of the bets he placed on himself. Rap shows aren’t known for being tidy, punctual affairs anyway—what was another hour?
Then again, this was a crowd over-indexed in forty- and fiftysomethings, a demographic that would really feel the consequences of a late night come Monday morning. What drew so many people to these concerts, as well as to recent stadium shows in London and Paris this fall, was a sense of nostalgia and a perception of scarcity. Jay-Z’s previous solo tour was in 2017, after the release of “4:44,” an absorbing, stripped-down record full of post-therapy insights meant to repair his image after rumors of infidelity—transgressions that might have been bad enough even if his wife was not Beyoncé. The following year, the couple released “Everything Is Love,” a renewal of vows in album form, and toured Europe and North America as a double bill. In the near-decade since, Jay-Z has chosen his moments of visibility sparingly, appearing mostly as a power broker playing in one-per-center sandboxes. Although his gravitational effect on how people dress, what they sip at the club, and how they structure their bars has weakened, his presence is felt. “We tote guns to the Grammys, pop bottles on the White House lawn,” he rapped on “So Ghetto,” and it was a good, mischievous line back in 1999. But he has since become someone who texts Barack Obama, and who curates the most high-profile concert in the world, the Super Bowl halftime show.
The first night of the Yankee Stadium residency celebrated the thirtieth anniversary of Jay-Z’s début album, “Reasonable Doubt,” which he performed in its entirety, bringing out guests such as Beyoncé, Nas, and Alicia Keys. The following night, he did “The Blueprint,” from 2001, again with high-wattage support. Neither of these victory laps was preordained: hip-hop is a young person’s sport, and when “Reasonable Doubt” was released there was little reason to believe that Jay-Z, then twenty-six years old, would end up one of the greats. In the mid-nineties, the genre was dominated by prodigious, fully formed young talents such as Nas and the Notorious B.I.G. Jay had emerged a few years earlier, as the sidekick to a playfully spry Brooklyn rapper named Jaz-O, and had returned to selling drugs when both of their careers stalled. He eventually began to release his music through Roc-A-Fella, an independent record label that he’d started with some friends.
Jay-Z was early to realize that New York’s influence on hip-hop was waning, and that the lines dividing styles, regions, and genres were no longer as important as they once were. After “Reasonable Doubt,” a soulful, bruising masterpiece inspired by his native Brooklyn, he proved to be a shape-shifter and a shrewd collaborator, working with rappers from the South when this still seemed like a daring thing for an East Coast artist to do. In the five years between “Reasonable Doubt” and “The Blueprint”—which was released on September 11, 2001—he went from being yet another New York rapper scrapping for relevance to being hip-hop’s undisputed king. And then he somehow kept ascending, sanding down the edges of his persona until he became the quintessential celebrity of the Obama era, back when the notion of doing unprecedented things and entering off-limits rooms felt transgressive enough. He invested in restaurants, created beverage and clothing lines, and became a part owner of the New Jersey Nets, helping oversee the team’s relocation to Brooklyn. In 2005, he rapped, prophetically, “I’m not a businessman, I’m a business, man.”
This last concert of the Yankee Stadium run promised to be a career-spanning revue—an enticing pitch, as the later albums have felt more like exercises in brand management. “Magna Carta Holy Grail,” released in 2013, was initially a free download exclusively for Samsung customers; “4:44” seemed partly an attempt to boost subscriptions to Tidal, a streaming company that he owned. Maybe, for Jay-Z, these were the only victories worth pursuing anymore. Perhaps after years of fending off challenges from rival New York rappers, there was a novelty to hanging out with Bono and Chris Martin—or Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner—instead. This was as plausible an explanation for the delay as any: a guest on the level of a world leader. With Jay, anything seems possible.
When Jay-Z first announced his return to the stage, he sat for an extended interview with
GQ
, complete with a photo shoot by the artist Rashid Johnson, whose work he collects. His comments illustrated the unique burden of the hip-hop superstar, straining to stay in touch with the grimy realism of his earliest rhymes. He wondered aloud if rap’s hypercompetitive battle culture, as recently embodied by Kendrick Lamar and Drake, had become too much of a liability. (“I don’t know if it’s worth it at this point.”) He called the rising tide of anti-billionaire sentiment in America a “cop-out,” sounding slightly defensive. His wealth hasn’t changed his sense of morality, he explained. “A person with more money can do more good. . . . This is the system that we have. And with the system that we have, what are you going to do?” The elephant in the room was a lawsuit, filed in 2024 and withdrawn in 2025, in which an anonymous woman had accused him and Diddy of sexually assaulting her when she was a teen-ager. “That shit took a lot out of me,” he said. “I was angry. I haven’t been that angry in a long time.”
Jay-Z opened the first night at Yankee Stadium with a kind of State of the Union freestyle. He hinted that Colin Kaepernick, the former N.F.L. quarterback, whom many believe to have been blackballed by the league for his advocacy against police brutality, wasn’t as righteous as we thought. Jay argued that he had chosen a less showy way to make change, advocating for criminal-justice reform out of the spotlight. “I’m the one they can’t control,” he rapped, suggesting that Kaepernick had taken an unreported payout from the N.F.L. and dismissing the “Twitter activists” who didn’t see the long game of his backroom advocacy.
The backroom becomes literal in “Jaÿ-Z in 8,” a new eight-part documentary series on HBO featuring the rapper in conversation with the producer Rick Rubin, who has been anointed a mascot of sorts for the notion of creativity. Each episode shows the two men sitting in the Palais Brongniart, in Paris, listening to Jay’s songs on a very nice sound system, and talking about them. “This is like elder wisdom,” Rubin says excitedly, after playing “Don’t You Know,” a preternaturally mature track from 2002. “It’s really wild,” Jay agrees. “I don’t know where it was coming from.”
Their conversations drift from Jay’s memories of his late, long-estranged father to his experience with therapy, measuring the distance between the brash playboy of then and the fifty-six-year-old family man of now. The series ends up being the latest retelling of a story that fans know well at this point—I still prefer “Fade to Black,” from 2004, a behind-the-scenes film about the making of “The Black Album,” and “Decoded,” from 2010, an autobiography co-authored with the journalist dream hampton. What distinguishes this new project is Jay’s obvious delight in having Rubin, the eccentric naïf, as his interlocutor and audience. (Rubin played the same role for Paul McCartney in “McCartney 3,2,1,” a six-part documentary from 2021.) “You knew so much,” Rubin effuses about the early music. “It’s amazing.”
The pair’s narration of Jay-Z’s life doubles as a history of America in the past half century, beginning with the economic collapse of New York in the seventies, running through the rise of rap, the crack epidemic, and the war on drugs, and landing on the eventual pathbreaking successes of the hip-hop generation. Jay has always skillfully folded each turn into his larger mythology, going from drug dealer to rapper to label boss to executive with an air of inevitability, every choice subsumed into the glory of the hustle. “Have you been the same person the whole time?” Rubin asks innocently. No, Jay replies. He was constantly becoming someone different.
It was Monday by the time Jay-Z took the stage. As the introduction to “The Dynasty: Roc La Familia” pulsed through the Stadium, he stepped out wearing a Yankees cap and a bespoke pin-striped workwear suit, looking like the most elegant handyman on Earth. His band turned the song into a headbanger’s delight; Jay remained steady and regal over the crunching guitar chords and cathartic drum kicks. When it was over, he took a moment to explain the delay. Some fans had breached one of the entrances without paying, leading security to shut down the entire Stadium. Jay had insisted on waiting until every ticket holder was allowed in before performing. But he promised that he would not be shortchanging us.
Jay was limber and cocky, unhurried as he prowled the stage. We had been waiting for four hours, desperate for a release, yet he was assured and deliberate with every move. His strength in the late nineties was a kind of calm under pressure, and his power in the next decade was translating that swaggering cool for ever-larger stages. Songs that felt tense and claustrophobic on the records—such as “Where I’m From,” a track from 1997 about the Marcy Projects—became seismic events when performed live.
At one point, Jay removed his jacket and revealed what appeared to be a bulletproof vest—a nod to the “Streets Is Watching” video, from 1998, when his paranoia toward his rivals was at its highest. The delirium of the late hour only deepened as the guests came out: Jeezy, Teyana Taylor, Jermaine Dupri, Usher, Swizz Beatz, Rihanna (who briefly out-swaggered Jay), Pharrell, and Beyoncé, backed by the Mayyas, a Lebanese dance group. These were all stars he could either claim credit for making or consider of equal stature. Even more impressive was how they had all stayed hours past their presumed call times. I felt silly for thinking that the evening’s guests might have been fellow nineties stalwarts such as M.O.P. or Cam’ron. The legacy that Jay wanted to broadcast was not one in which he acknowledged his generational peers, many of whom are more likely to feature on back-in-the-day podcasts than on new tracks.
For a couple of hours, it was easy to forget who Jay had become, and to instead marvel that he was still here at all. So many of the supporting characters of his rise were absent, whether they had lost their place in his inner circle, such as his Roc-A-Fella co-founder Damon Dash, or died before their time, as with the Notorious B.I.G. and DMX. Of course, there was no Diddy or R. Kelly, both incarcerated for sexual misconduct. The most auspicious absence was Kanye West, Jay’s estranged former protégé, who is arguably the only other solo rapper who could draw crowds of this size.
An elevated subway train rumbled by in the distance, just past the outfield, a reminder of the city beyond. How could Jay-Z possibly stay connected to the world that his music was designed to escape? Standing in the audience, I thought about hearing “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)” for the first time, recognizing that it was sampling the musical “Annie,” and finding this both absurd and totally irresistible. I remembered how effortlessly Jay took to hip-hop’s evolutionary turns in the late nineties and early two-thousands, moving from New York’s stoic classicism to the squeak and space-age funk of producers like Timbaland and the Neptunes. I thought about the hours I’d spent in the d.j. booth trying to figure out how to mix in and out of “Big Pimpin’ ” or admiring the blunt simplicity of “Money, Cash, Hoes,” which still sounds to me like someone getting frustrated with a keyboard and throwing it down a stairwell.
I looked around and imagined everyone was similarly adrift, all of us in our own orbits, with Jay the common gravitational center. Yankee Stadium felt small and intimate. My friend and I left during the encore, as he began “Empire State of Mind,” a song that became so ubiquitous during the Knicks playoff run this spring that I never need to hear it again. It seemed more sensible to beat the traffic. ♦

Debt
Poems
Debt
By Daniel Poppick
September 20, 2026
What debt is this whose currency is sleep?
What clued me in
To your delay? What’s the content of a leaf?
Who’s fool enough
To commune in them? What choice poisons
Commingle with chlorophyll
To chase us to the other end
Of decay?
To what address can we send the flowers
Or in lieu of flowers
What fund should we invest with this thousand-mile
Stare through flaming
Fields of aster, star-torched tendrils of our
Vision insisting
In pale ashy patterns to leave some room
For the ghost’s donation?
Can I ask who’s calling? Aren’t you
Sleeping in?
When will I wake, erased by a glacial gaze
Frozen out
Like a convex plinth of air’s obsession
With a pyramid?
What’s a poem compared to a mouth?
Who’s there to hear it?
Why are all your texts written in
Invisible ink
At this late hour? To whom
Do I owe the pleasure?
This is drawn from “Lines and Circles.”
